en: *Pūrvāvadāna-sūtra*, Scroll One, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter One: On the Single Dharma (1–2). Part One of Chapter One: On the Single Dharma.
I have heard these words from the World-Honored One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!
When I observe the world, I see no other single dharma that so obscures sentient beings and causes them to rush and wander along the long path of birth and death as does the veil of ignorance."
Why is this so? Because the multitudes of sentient beings in the world are shrouded and obstructed by the veil of ignorance, they gallop and wander along the long road of birth and death.
Therefore, you all should train yourselves in this way:
"How should I cultivate and give rise to the light of wisdom, so as to shatter the veil of ignorance and emerge from the net of craving?
You, bhikṣus, should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"There is no other single dharma that so obscures and obstructs all sentient beings,
causing them to rush along the paths of birth and death, as does the veil of ignorance.
Through this great delusion and darkness of ignorance, they have wandered for a long time."
There is mutual coming and going, with beings rising and falling through high and low realms.
If one shatters the veil of ignorance and unties the net of craving,
one will not dwell within the stream of birth and death, for the causes thereof no longer exist.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!
When I observe the world, I see no other single dharma that binds sentient beings and causes them to race and wander through the long road of birth and death as much as the fetter of craving."
Why is this? Because the multitudes of beings in the world are bound by the fetters of craving and attachment, they gallop and wander along the long road of birth and death.
Therefore, you should train yourselves in this way:
"How should I cultivate and polish the sword of wisdom to sever the fetters of craving and destroy the mass of great darkness?
You bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"There is no single dharma that binds all living beings and causes them to rush through the paths of birth and death like the fetter of craving.
Craving is a great bondage; because of it, one wanders for a long time."
There is mutual coming and going, rising and sinking, high and low destinies.
If one severs the bonds of craving and destroys the mass of great darkness,
one does not dwell within the stream of birth and death, for the cause thereof no longer exists.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!

If a single sentient being were to wander through birth and death for the duration of an eon, the bones of the bodies they have received, were they to be able to be accumulated without rotting, would form a heap so high and vast as Mount Vipula in Rājagṛha."

How much more so for those sentient beings who, having no beginning or end, have galloped and wandered along the long road of birth and death; could the bones of the bodies they have received ever be measured? Why is this so?
"O Bhikṣus, you should know!

I say that because sentient beings do not understand, do not clearly see, do not realize through direct insight, do not penetrate, and do not thoroughly examine the Four Noble Truths, they gallop and wander along the long road of saṃsāra, receiving these bodies of bone."
Therefore, you should train yourselves thus:
"How may we thoroughly understand, clearly perceive, realize, penetrate, examine, and fully master the Four Noble Truths?"
“O bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“If the bones of a single sentient being were to remain for an eon, Without decaying, they would form a mountain as high as Mount Sumeru.”
The mass of these [bones] would be as high and vast as Mount Vipula;
how much more so for one who has wandered through birth and death for a duration without beginning or end?
The quantity of the skeletal remains one has received throughout that time is truly immeasurable.
This great mass of suffering is experienced because one does not see the Noble Truths;
therefore, one should cultivate sublime wisdom to correctly contemplate the four realities:
namely, the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Cause of Suffering, and the Cessation of Suffering.
The Noble Eightfold Path is able to extinguish the cause of the suffering of suffering.
Such a person (pudgala) will transmigrate through rebirths for at most seven more times;
they will certainly sever all fetters and be able to reach the end of all suffering.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!
With my Buddha-eye, I survey the world and see that all karmic fruits arise in dependence upon the mind and its intentions."
A certain class of sentient beings, driven by their own minds, engage in such conduct and follow such a path;
when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the various evil destinies and are reborn in the hells, as if casting off a heavy burden.
Why is this so? Because those sentient beings have defiled minds.
With this as the cause, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into the evil destinies and are born in the hells.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"A certain class of sentient beings, Whose minds give rise to defilement—
I shall now, for your sake, Prophesy the place of their rebirth."
When that person’s body breaks up and life ends, like casting off a heavy burden,
they will surely fall into the various evil destinies and be born within hell.
One should know that such a person of evil wisdom does so because their mind and intentions are defiled.
"Because of such defilement, one shall be born within the hells.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
With my Buddha-eye, I survey the world and see that all karmic fruits arise from the mind and its intentions.
A certain class of sentient beings, driven by their minds and intentions, engage in such conduct and follow such paths;
when their bodies perish and their lives end, they cast off their heavy burdens as if discarding a load, ascending to the higher realms and being born among the devas.
Why is this so? Because those sentient beings possess pure minds and intentions.
With this as the cause, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they ascend to the higher realms and are reborn in the celestial worlds.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“There is a class of sentient beings Whose minds have given rise to purity;
I shall now, for your sake, Prophesy the place of their rebirth.”
When that person’s body perishes at the end of life, like casting off a heavy burden,
they will surely ascend to the higher realms and be born within the celestial worlds.
One should know that such a person of noble wisdom does so because their mind is pure.
"Because of this purity, one shall be born within the celestial realms.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
All sentient beings are governed by their own karma; karma is their companion, karma is their gateway to birth, karma is their kin, and karma is their refuge.
Karma determines the inferior, middling, and superior categories of all sentient beings.
Therefore, you should thoroughly understand:

the intrinsic nature of actions, the causes and conditions of actions, the categories of actions, the maturation of actions, the exhaustion and cessation of actions, and the causes, conditions, and requisites for the path leading to the cessation of actions.
"O bhikṣus, you should correctly understand what I have taught.
How should one understand the intrinsic nature of karma?
The intrinsic nature of karma refers either to volitional karma (cetanā-karma) or to karma following volition (cetayitvā-karma)."
In this way, one should understand the intrinsic nature of all karmas.
Having correctly understood the intrinsic nature of karma, how should one understand the causal conditions of karma?
The causal conditions of karma refer to all forms of craving.
In this way, one should understand the causal conditions of all karmas.
Having correctly understood the intrinsic nature of all karmas and their causal conditions, how should one understand the categories of all karmas?
Regarding the categories of karma: there is a distinct category of karma that leads to a body in the hells;
a distinct category of karma that leads to a body among animals;
and a distinct category of karma that leads to a body in the realm of hungry ghosts.
There are distinct categories of karma leading to bodies in the asura realm;
distinct categories of karma leading to bodies in the human realm;
and distinct categories of karma leading to bodies in the celestial realm.
In this way, one should understand the various categories of karma.
Having correctly understood the intrinsic nature of karma, the causes and conditions of karma, and the categories of karma, how should one understand the maturation of karma?

Regarding the maturation of karma (*karmavipāka*): it refers to the various karmas performed in this life that are capable of producing further existence (*bhava*) within this very life, whether they have already been experienced or have not yet been experienced.
In this manner, one should understand the maturation of all karmas.

Having correctly understood the intrinsic nature of all karmas, the causes and conditions of all karmas, the categories of all karmas, and the maturation of karma, how should one understand the total extinction of all karmas?
Regarding the "exhaustion and cessation of karma," this means that because craving ceases, all karmas are exhausted and cease.
In this way, one should understand the exhaustion and cessation of all karmas.

Having correctly understood the intrinsic nature of karmas, the causes and conditions of karmas, the categories of karmas, the maturation of karmas, and the exhaustion and cessation of karma, how should one understand the causes, conditions, and requisites for the path leading to the cessation of karma?

The causes, conditions, and requisites for the path that leads to the cessation of karma refer to the Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
In this way, one should understand the causes, conditions, and requisites for proceeding upon the path to the cessation of karma.
"Bhikṣus, you should know!

Any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who can correctly understand the intrinsic nature of all karmas, the causes and conditions of all karmas, the categories of all karmas, the maturation of all karmas, the total extinction of all karmas, and the causes, conditions, and requisites for proceeding upon the path to the cessation of karma—they are able to have faith in my Dharma and Vinaya."
If one can have faith in my Dharma and Vinaya, one is able to enter my Dharma and Vinaya.
If one can enter my Dharma and Vinaya, one is able to attain the practice of the holy life within my Dharma and Vinaya.
If one can reach my Dharma and Vinaya and practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one will be able to ultimately and completely exhaust all karma. Why is this?

Because these śramaṇas or brahmins, having correctly understood the intrinsic nature of karma, the causes and conditions of karma, the categories of karma, the maturation of karma, the cessation of karma, and the causes, conditions, and requisites for the path leading to the cessation of karma, are then able to become weary of, detach from, and extinguish all karma; they attain ultimate liberation and well-liberated deliverance.
Being well-liberated, one is able to stand independently.
Being able to stand independently, one possesses excellent cultivation.
Possessing excellent cultivation, once that body has disintegrated, by the very nature of things (dharmatā), there is no longer any further designation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"All sentient beings in the world, Throughout the past, present, and future, Are all subject to their own karma; Karma is their companion."
Karma is the gateway for their birth; karma is their retinue;
karma is that upon which they rely. Karma determines the three grades [of rebirth].
Following karma, they are born here and there, revolving without fixed end like a wheel.
Sometimes dwelling among gods or humans, sometimes residing in the four miserable realms—
all sentient beings in the world are driven by the power of karma.
Neither kingdom, wealth, wife, nor children follow one into a future birth.
At the time of their death, they must suddenly abandon everything;
alone they follow their karma as it leads them, for all things arise from one's own actions.
Thus, when sentient beings in the future undergo such karmic results, [they too shall experience them].
If one can rely on the Buddha’s teaching and leave the household life out of right faith,
then among those who are foolish and lack a teacher to guide them,
such a person is called one who practices well and is not deluded regarding the True Dharma.
Therefore, you bhikṣus, exert yourselves with diligence and do not be heedless;
you should thoroughly understand all karmas and practice correctly in their continuity.
This is for the sake of exhausting the intrinsic nature of karma, as well as its causes, conditions, and so forth.
"By cultivating the Noble Eightfold Path, one shall swiftly attain its full perfection.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
When any evil or unwholesome phenomena in the world arise, all those categories of the unwholesome and all types of the unwholesome are preceded by the mind.
"Why is this? Because once the mind has arisen, all evil and unwholesome states follow and arise after it.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"When unwholesome states arise, which act as causes for the experience of suffering,
they are all preceded by the mind and co-arise with the afflictions;
the mind is the precursor of these states, the mind is their sovereign, and the mind is their driver."
"Because the mind is defiled, there is speaking and there is acting;
suffering arises following this, just as a wheel turns because of the hand.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
“Bhikṣus, you should know!
Regarding all pure and wholesome dharmas that exist in the world, at the time of their arising, every category and type of the wholesome is preceded by the mind.”
"Why is this so? Because once the mind has arisen, all pure and wholesome dharmas arise following it.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to summarize this meaning, spoke these verses:
"When various pure and wholesome dharmas arise, they are causes capable of inducing happiness;
all have the mind as their precursor and arise together with wholesome dharmas.
With the mind as their precursor, the mind is the sovereign, and the mind is the driver."
"Because the mind is pure, there is speech and there is action;
joy arises following this, just as a shadow follows the movement of a form.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One these words:
“Bhikṣus, you should know!
There is one dharma in the world which, when it arises, brings harm and lack of peace to many sentient beings;
it leads the great multitudes of gods and humans in the world toward what is meaningless and profitless, resulting in the experience of great fruits of suffering.”
What is this one dharma?
It is called the schism of the Saṃgha. Why is that?
"Monks, you should know that if the Saṃgha is divided,

the entire assembly will engage in mutual disputes, mutually reproaching one another, mutually contemning one another, mutually reviling one another, mutually disparaging one another, mutually resenting and hating one another, mutually provoking and offending one another, mutually opposing one another, mutually slandering one another, and mutually abandoning one another."
At that time, those in all the world who had not yet developed respectful faith will become even less respectful and faithful;
and those who were already respectful and faithful will turn away from their faith.
Monks, you should know this!

Thus it is said that there is one dharma in the world which, at the time of its arising, brings harm and lack of peace to many sentient beings, leads the great assemblies of gods and humans in the world toward what is meaningless and disadvantageous, and results in the experience of great suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to summarize this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“When a single dharma arises in the world, It can give rise to immeasurable evils;
Namely, the schism of the Saṃgha, In which the foolish take delight.”
"To cause a schism in the Saṃgha is suffering; to cause a division among the assembly is also suffering.
To break the harmony of the Saṃgha brings the suffering of the Avīci Hell for an entire kalpa.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!
There is one dharma in the world which, at the time of its arising, brings great benefit and great happiness to many sentient beings;
it draws in the great assemblies of gods and humans throughout the world, performing great purposeful benefit and bringing about the fruit of great bliss.”
What is this one dharma?
It is called the harmony of the Saṃgha. Why is that?

"Monks, you should know that when the Saṃgha is in harmony, the entire assembly has no mutual disputes; they do not reproach one another, do not despise one another, do not insult one another, do not revile one another, do not harbor resentment or aversion toward one another, do not cause each other distress or offense, do not act in opposition to one another, do not slander one another, and do not abandon one another."
At that time, those in all the world who had not yet developed respectful faith will develop respectful faith,
and those who already possess respectful faith will increase it further.
Bhikṣus, you should know this!
Thus it is said that there is one dharma in the world which, at the time of its arising, brings great benefit and great happiness to many sentient beings;
it draws forth the great assemblies of gods and humans from all worlds, accomplishing great purpose and profit, and inducing the fruit of great bliss.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"When a single dharma arises in the world, it can give rise to immeasurable merit;
namely, the harmony of the Saṃgha, which those with wisdom and benefit rejoice in."
"To bring harmony to the Saṅgha is joy; to reconcile a divided assembly is also joy.
To restore peace where the Saṅgha was broken leads one to enjoy celestial bliss for an eon.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One these words:
“Bhikṣus, you should know!
When a single fetter is severed among sentient beings in the world, all remaining fetters are also severed accordingly.
What is this one fetter?
This is called the conceit of "I am. Why is this so?
All fetters, whether subtle, middling, or coarse, are entirely rooted in the conceit of "I am"; they arise from the conceit of "I am" and are nourished by the conceit of "I am."
Therefore, when the single fetter of pride (*māna*) is severed, all other fetters are likewise severed along with it.
It is like the central pillar of a worldly multi-storied pavilion, which serves as the support for all its parts; if the central pillar collapses, the rest follow in collapse as well.
In this way, the conceit "I am" is the basis for all fetters; if the conceit "I am" is severed, the others are also extinguished accordingly.
If a bhikṣu has already severed the conceit "I am," it should be known that he has thereby severed the remaining fetters.

If any bhikṣus have severed the remaining fetters, you should know that they have reached the end of suffering, have cultivated right knowledge, and are well-liberated in mind and well-liberated in wisdom, with no further existence hereafter.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Just as the central pillar of a multi-storied pavilion is that upon which all parts depend,
if the central pillar collapses, all other parts fall down as well."
Such is the fetter of self-conceit, the basis upon which all fetters depend;
when the fetter of self-conceit is severed, all other fetters are extinguished accordingly.
When a bhikṣu has severed self-conceit, all remaining fetters are likewise severed.
Once all other fetters have been severed, one immediately attains the end of suffering.
Having attained the end of suffering, one is said to have cultivated right knowledge;
with mind and wisdom well-liberated, there is ultimately no further existence.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that there is one dharma in the world which, if well-cultivated and extensively practiced, brings both benefits to fulfillment: [the benefit for oneself and the benefit for others]."
That is to say: bringing the benefits of the present life to fulfillment, and bringing the benefits of future lives to fulfillment;

being able to accomplish benefit and happiness in the present life, being able to accomplish benefit and happiness in future lives, and being able to accomplish benefit and happiness in both the present and future lives.
What is this one dharma?
It is the cultivation of heedfulness among all the wholesome dharmas that are practiced. Why is this so?

If, among the various wholesome dharmas one cultivates, one is able to skillfully practice and extensively cultivate heedfulness, one will then be able to grasp and maintain two kinds of benefits until they reach fulfillment, as explained at length, even unto the point of accomplishing benefit and happiness in both the present and the future.

This is called the one dharma; if it is well-cultivated and extensively practiced, it will encompass both benefits for oneself and others, and, as explained at length, will even be able to accomplish benefit, peace, and happiness in both the present and the future.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more,
spoke in verse: “Those who possess much learning, Who can renounce wealth and status,
And diligently practice without negligence, Realize the eternal bliss of Nirvana.”
The wise person is free from negligence and is able to maintain both types of benefit—
namely, those of the present life and the future— causing both to reach fulfillment.
All such wholesome qualities that can be accomplished bring benefit and happiness in both the present and the hereafter.
“The multitude of sages and saints of the past and future are all called wise men.
To summarize the preceding sutra, the uddāna says:
Obscurations, fetters, eons, two minds, Karma, two intentions, and prior conduct.
The schism of the Saṃgha and the reconciliation of the Saṃgha; the severing of pride and the cultivation of diligence.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!..."
"If sentient beings were to permanently sever a single dharma, I would certify that they will certainly attain the fruit of non-returning.
What is this one dharma? It is craving."
Why is this? Because all sentient beings, due to the defilement of craving, repeatedly return to fall into the various evil destinies and undergo the suffering of birth and death.
If one can forever sever this single dharma, I testify that they will certainly attain the fruit of non-returning and will no longer return to be born in this world.
"Therefore, I say:
if any sentient beings permanently sever one dharma, I certify that they will certainly attain the fruit of non-returning.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“I observe that sentient beings, defiled by craving,
return again to fall into the evil destinies and undergo the cycle of birth and death.
If one can correctly understand and forever sever this craving, [one will escape].”
"Having attained the fruit of non-returning, he will not come back to this world.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:

if any sentient beings permanently sever a single dharma, I certify that they will certainly attain the fruit of a non-returner.

"He has certainly attained the fruit of non-returning; he shall not come back to be born in this world.

Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One these words:
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

If there is one who has not known attachment as it truly is, has not correctly and fully understood it, and has not been able to permanently abandon it, then because they have not yet become free from attachment within their own mind, they cannot penetrate it, cannot fully understand it, cannot awaken to it equally, cannot attain nirvāṇa, and cannot realize unsurpassed peace and happiness.”

If there is one who has known attachment as it truly is, has fully understood it, and has been able to abandon it forever, then because they have already become detached from attachment within their own mind, they are able to penetrate it, are able to fully comprehend it, are able to awaken to it equally, are able to attain nirvana, and are able to realize unsurpassed peace and happiness.

"Therefore, one should understand indulgence as it truly is, one should fully comprehend it, and one should seek its permanent abandonment; within the Buddha’s Dharma, one should practice the holy life.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing the foregoing meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one does not know indulgence, One is far from Nirvāṇa."
For one who has understood the nature of attachment, nirvana is not far away.
I observe that all sentient beings, defiled by attachment,
return once more to fall into the evil destinies and undergo the cycle of birth and death.
"If one can correctly understand and forever sever this craving,
one attains the supreme fruit of asceticism and will ultimately not undergo further birth.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One these words:
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

If one has not known conceit as it truly is, has not correctly and fully understood it, and has not been able to permanently abandon it, then because that person has not yet become free from conceit within their own mind, they will be unable to penetrate it, unable to fully understand it, unable to awaken to it equally, unable to attain nirvāṇa, and unable to realize unsurpassed peace and happiness.”

If there is one who has known conceit as it truly is, has fully understood it correctly, and has been able to eradicate it forever, then because they have already become free from conceit within their own mind, they are able to penetrate it, are able to comprehend it thoroughly, are able to awaken to it equally, are able to attain nirvana, and are able to realize unsurpassed peace and happiness.
"Therefore, one should know conceit as it truly is, should fully and correctly understand it, and should seek its permanent abandonment; within the Buddha’s Dharma, one should practice the holy life.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing the preceding meaning, spoke in verse:
"If one does not know conceit, One is far from nirvāṇa."
Those who have understood conceit are not far from Nirvana.
I observe all sentient beings who, defiled by conceit,
return again to fall into the evil realms and undergo the cycle of birth and death.
"If one can correctly understand and forever sever this conceit,
one attains the supreme fruit of the śramaṇa and will ultimately never again undergo birth.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One these words.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

If one has not known harm as it truly is, has not correctly and fully understood it, and has not permanently abandoned it, then because that person has not yet become free from harm within their own mind, they cannot penetrate it, cannot fully understand it, cannot awaken to it equally, cannot attain nirvāṇa, and cannot realize unsurpassed peace and happiness.”

If one has known violence as it truly is, has fully understood it, and has been able to permanently abandon it, then because one’s own mind is already free from violence, one is able to penetrate it, is able to fully know it, is able to awaken to it equally, is able to attain nirvana, and is able to realize unsurpassed peace and happiness.
"Therefore, one should know harm as it truly is, should fully and correctly understand it, and should seek its permanent abandonment; within the Buddha's Dharma, one should practice the holy life.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing the above meaning, spoke in verse:
"If one does not know harm as it is, One is far removed from Nirvāṇa."
For one who has brought an end to harming, Nirvāṇa is not far away.
I observe all sentient beings: defiled by harming, they return to fall into the evil destinies and undergo the cycle of birth and death.
"If one can correctly understand and forever sever this harm,
one will attain the supreme fruit of the śramaṇa and ultimately never undergo rebirth.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

If one has not known all things as they truly are, has not correctly and fully understood them, and has not permanently abandoned them, then because one has not yet become free from all [defilements] within one’s own mind, one cannot penetrate them, cannot fully understand them, cannot awaken to them equally, cannot attain nirvāṇa, and cannot realize unsurpassed peace and bliss.”

If one has already known all things as they truly are, has already fully and correctly understood them, and has already been able to permanently sever them, then because one’s own mind is already free from all [defilements], one is able to penetrate them, is able to understand them completely, is able to awaken equally to them, is able to attain nirvana, and is able to realize unsurpassed peace and happiness.

"Therefore, regarding all things, one should know them as they truly are, one should fully and correctly comprehend them, and one should seek their permanent abandonment; within the Buddha’s Dharma, one should cultivate the holy life.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"If one does not know all things, One is far from Nirvana."
All those who have full knowledge are not far from Nirvana.
I observe all sentient beings, defiled by everything,
returning again to fall into evil realms and undergoing the cycle of birth and death.
To summarize the preceding sutra, the uddāna says:
Greed, hatred, and delusion; Concealment, vexation, anger, resentment, envy, stinginess, and attachment;
Pride, harmfulness, and all [the remaining afflictions].
I have heard these words from the World-Honored One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that among all practices for cultivating meritorious deeds, the liberation of the mind through loving-kindness (*maitrī-vimokṣa*) is the foremost."
Why is this so? Because the majestic power of the liberation of loving-kindness is so blazingly intense that it eclipses all other meritorious deeds.
Compared to the liberation of loving-kindness thus cultivated, the majesty of all those other deeds does not equal even one-sixteenth part of it.
"O Bhikṣus, you should know!
Just as, among all kings, great and small, the Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) is the foremost. Why is this so?"
The majestic power and splendor of a Wheel-Turning Sage King are so blazing and intense that they eclipse all other kings, both small and great.
When the majesty and power possessed by those various kings are compared to that of a Wheel-Turning King, they do not equal even a sixteenth part of it.
All other meritorious deeds are likewise so; compared to the liberation through the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta-vimokṣa*) that one has cultivated, they do not equal even a sixteenth part.
It is also like how, among all the stars, both small and large, the full moon disk is the foremost.
Why is this so? Because the majestic radiance of this full moon disk is so intensely blazing that it eclipses all the stars, both small and large.
When compared to the full moon disk, the entire radiance of those stars does not equal even a sixteenth part of it.
"All such meritorious deeds are likewise; compared to the liberation through the mind of loving-kindness that has been cultivated, they do not equal even one-sixteenth part.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"All meritorious deeds, Compared to the liberation of the loving mind, [Do not equal even one-sixteenth part]."
Even among sixteen parts, it could not approach even one.
If one can cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward a single sentient being, that merit is already boundless; how much more so for all!
Whatever great kings there are who, with their majesty, subdue the entire earth,
perform all manner of worldly sacrificial offerings and assemblies;
yet the merit of such sacrifices and gifts cannot compare to the loving-kindness one has cultivated.
Among sixteen parts, it cannot equal even one.
Like a Wheel-Turning Sage King, whose majestic virtue eclipses all other kings;
or like the full orb of the moon, whose radiance outshines all the stars.
Thus, all such practices and every deed of merit are encompassed by a heart of loving-kindness and are covered by its majestic power.
Through the cultivation of the liberation of the mind through loving-kindness, whether they be humans or non-humans, [they are all protected].
"No sentient beings whatsoever shall be able to cause them harm.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"

I observe that there is no other single thing in the world that serves as an external, powerful condition for those in training who have not yet attained their goal, when they seek the fruit of unsurpassed peace and happiness, like a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).

Why is this so? Because those sentient beings, by means of spiritual friends, have all their aspirations fulfilled—namely, the severing of all evils, the cultivation of all virtues, and the attainment of a truly pure body free from defilement.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to summarize this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"In my observation of all the worlds, there is no other single dharma such that for one who has not yet attained the mind through training, when seeking the unsurpassed fruit,"
Acting as an external supporting condition, like that spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), one should draw near to the spiritual friend;
whatever one seeks will not fail to be accomplished.
Receiving their instructions with reverence, one should practice them without negligence.
"Quickly realize nirvāṇa, Free from fear and always at peace.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"

I observe that there is no other single dharma in the world that serves as such a powerful internal condition for those in training who have not yet attained their goal, when they seek the fruit of unsurpassed peace and happiness, as does right attention (*samyak-manasikāra*).

Why is this so? Because those sentient beings, through correct mental attention (*samyak-manasikāra*), have all their aspirations fulfilled; that is to say, by abandoning all evils and cultivating all virtues, they attain a body that is truly pure and free from defilement.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to summarize this meaning once more,
spoke in verse: "As I observe all the worlds, there is no other single dharma that,
for one who has not yet attained the mind through training, aids in the quest for the unsurpassed fruit."
To create internal strengthening conditions, as one does with right attention (samyak-manasikāra).
By cultivating right attention, there is nothing sought that will not be accomplished;
through investigation according to reality and practicing without negligence.
"Swiftly realize nirvāṇa, free from fear and always at peace.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"

If all sentient beings were able to clearly perceive before them the fruits of giving as I perceive them, their minds would certainly not be entangled by the defilement of stinginess; even if they possessed only a single morsel of food, they would surely share it with others before eating it themselves.

Because of this ignorance, their minds are entangled and defiled by various forms of stinginess; thus, although they possess immeasurable food, drink, wealth, and treasures, they do not give them to others, consuming them for themselves alone.
"Why is this so? Because the fruit of giving is rebirth among humans and devas, where one experiences various pleasures through immeasurable cycles of coming and going.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"If all sentient beings in the world Could understand that giving brings about great rewards,
And perceive clearly as if before the Tathāgata;
Their minds would certainly not be Ensnared and defiled by stinginess."
Though eating but a single morsel, he was still able to share it with others.
Because they do not know the fruit of giving, even those who clearly see one resembling a Tathāgata remain stingy and cannot relinquish their abundant food and wealth.
"If one gives with a joyful mind at the three times to the field of ordinary beings or the field of the noble ones,
one will receive the retribution of the realms of humans and devas, wandering back and forth in measureless abundance.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One these words.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

If sentient beings were to clearly perceive before them the karmic retribution resulting from violating the precepts, just as I perceive it, they would find no peace whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; they would have no thought for speech, laughter, food, or drink; their minds would be terrified and deranged, they would vomit blood, and their bodies would wither like mown reeds.”
Because they do not know this, they remain at ease and without fear. Why is this?
Because the offenses of violating the precepts can induce rebirth in the evil realms and result in the ripening of intense and powerful suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“If sentient beings in the world Can understand that violating the precepts Brings about the retribution of suffering, They will see clearly as if before the Tathāgata.”
The four modes of deportment were uneasy; he could not think of speaking or smiling.
His heart was terrified and he vomited blood; his body withered like cut reeds.
Because he did not know that violating the precepts could induce the suffering of the evil realms, [he fell into them].
Seeing clearly as if before the Tathāgata, one remains serene and free from fear.
Those who violate the precepts will certainly fall into the evil realms,
where they will undergo intense and sharp suffering with boundless karmic retribution.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!

If sentient beings were to clearly perceive before them the karmic results produced by the observance of ethical discipline, just as I perceive them, they would develop a profound sense of weary detachment toward their own bodies and would joyfully embrace and firmly maintain the prohibitions and precepts for the sake of the future."
Because of this ignorance, they take pleasure in and become attached to their own bodies, thereby violating the prohibitive precepts. Why is this?
For the merit of observing the precepts can induce rebirth in the happy realms and result in superior, intense, and powerful fruits of happiness.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"When sentient beings in the world Fully understand that upholding the precepts Can bring about the fruition of happiness,
They see clearly as if before the Tathāgata."
Thus, regarding this impure body, one can deeply give rise to weary detachment;
seeking the superior fruits of the future, one firmly maintains pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Because of not knowing that maintaining discipline can induce the happiness of the happy realms, [one fails to do so].
Seeing what appears to be a Tathāgata, they thus violate the pure precepts.
Those who uphold the precepts will be born in the happy realms,
enjoy the various sublime pleasures of the heavens, and realize unsurpassed nirvāṇa.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!

If sentient beings speak falsely with full knowledge, being without shame, without remorse, and without a mind of repentance, I say that there is no evil or unwholesome deed they are incapable of committing."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to summarize this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Those sentient beings who knowingly speak falsehoods, Lacking shame, remorse, or a sense of regret— There is no evil they will not commit."
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that if sentient beings speak falsely while knowing the truth, yet give rise to deep shame and remorse with a mind intent on reform, I say that there is no pure, wholesome dharma they are incapable of accomplishing."
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse: "Those sentient beings who,
though knowing the truth, deliberately speak falsehoods, yet possess a sense of shame, remorse, and repentance—
there is no wholesome deed they will not perform."
"Exerting oneself with diligence and without negligence, practicing correctly as taught,
one attains unsurpassed nirvana and is forever freed from all fears.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One these words.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!
There is one most excellent person; if he does not appear in the world, immeasurable sentient beings will fall away from noble wisdom.”
What is the one person?
It is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Why is that?

If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not appear in the world, there is no one able to proclaim the dharma for cultivating noble wisdom; consequently, all sentient beings fall away from noble wisdom.
"O bhikṣus, you should know this!
To lose one's friends, wealth, and status is called a minor loss;
to lose noble wisdom is called a great loss."

Why is this so? Because if sentient beings fall away from noble wisdom, they will experience much sorrow and suffering in the present life, lacking abiding joy and bliss; they will be beset by calamities, afflictions, vexations, and burning anguish, and will undergo suffering throughout the long night of the future, as well as various intense and violent misfortunes. They increase the drops of blood [of rebirth], constantly wander the paths of death, repeatedly fall into the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras, and repeatedly undergo the sorrows and sufferings of birth and death among gods and humans.

Why is this so? Because those sentient beings have not yet awakened to, nor fully realized, that noble wisdom; therefore, they transmigrate through the cycle of birth and death within the six realms of existence.
If sentient beings attain noble wisdom, they are able to transcend and reach the very end of the exhaustion of suffering.
Therefore, you should train yourselves in this way:
"How may we cultivate noble wisdom so that it does not decline or perish?"
"How should I realize and penetrate the noble wisdom?
You, bhikṣus, should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"When the Tathāgata does not appear, all sentient beings in the world have no protector and no refuge; they all fall away from noble wisdom.
To lose friends, wealth, and status is called a minor loss."
If one loses the sublime noble wisdom, this is called a great loss.
I observe all those in the world who, having lost the unsurpassed noble wisdom,
revolve in birth and death and undergo various bodies of name-and-form.
In this present life, there is suffering and no supreme bliss;
in the long night of the future, one will wander for a long time in the cycle of birth and death.
If you wish to seek noble wisdom and rightly bring an end to all suffering, [you must practice].
"May all Tathāgatas appear repeatedly in the world.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
There is one most excellent person (*pudgala*); if he appears in the world, immeasurable sentient beings will increase their noble wisdom (*ārya-prajñā*).
Who is this one person?
This refers to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Why is this so?

Because when the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas appear in the world, they are able to proclaim the Dharma for cultivating noble wisdom, thereby causing all sentient beings to increase their noble wisdom.
"O bhikṣus, you should know this!
That which increases one's friends, kin, wealth, and status is called 'minor increase';
that which increases noble wisdom is called 'great increase'."

Why is this so? Because if sentient beings increase their noble wisdom, they will experience much joy and happiness in the present life, dwelling without sorrow or suffering, free from calamity, affliction, distress, and burning anguish; they will not suffer for a long night in the future, nor undergo various sharp and violent misfortunes; their drops of blood will not increase, they will not wander the path of death, and they will not fall into the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, or asuras, nor will they undergo the sorrow and suffering of birth and death among humans or devas.

Why is this? Because those sentient beings have already been able to awaken to and have already fully realized that noble wisdom; they no longer wander in the cycle of birth and death within the six realms of existence.
If sentient beings have not increased their noble wisdom, they will be unable to transcend [suffering] and reach the ultimate end of its exhaustion.
Therefore, you should train yourselves in this way:
"How may we cultivate noble wisdom so that it increases?"
"How should I realize and penetrate the noble wisdom?
You, bhikṣus, should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"When a Tathāgata appears in the world, all sentient beings have rescue and refuge, and their noble wisdom increases.
To obtain friends, wealth, and status is called 'minor increase.'"
If one attains true noble wisdom, this is called "great increase.
I observe all the worlds: having attained unsurpassed noble wisdom, they no longer transmigrate through birth and death, but will certainly attain nirvana.
In this present life, he is free from suffering and always at peace;
in the long night of the future, he will be free from the cycle of birth and death.
If one desires to increase noble wisdom and rightly reach the end of all suffering, [one should practice thus].
"May the Buddha, the World-Honored One, long remain in the world.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"

There is one dharma in the world which, at the time of its growth, causes the delusion of sentient beings to increase, their perversion to become firm, their defilements to proliferate, and the miserable realms to be filled; it brings harm and lack of peace to many beings, and causes the great multitudes of gods and humans in the world to be without meaning or benefit, increasing only sorrow and suffering.
What is this one dharma?
It is namely wrong view. Why is that?

Due to wrong view, it causes sentient beings to increase their delusion, solidify their perversions, augment their defilements, and fulfill their rebirths in evil destinies; it brings harm and lack of peace to many beings, and causes the great multitudes of humans and devas in the world to be without meaning or benefit, increasing their sorrow and suffering.

This is called the one dharma that exists in the world which, at the time of its growth, causes the increase of delusion in all sentient beings; as it is explained in detail, it leads the great assemblies of humans and devas in the world to what is meaningless and disadvantageous, increasing their sorrow and suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"When false views grow and flourish, They cause delusion to increase,
As well as making inversions firm, And all defilements follow suit."
"It brings about the fulfillment of all evil realms and serves as no benefit or happiness;
wrong view harms the foolish man just as fire consumes all things.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One these words.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

There is one dharma in the world which, when it arises and grows, causes the delusion of sentient beings to diminish, their inversions to be extinguished, and pure dharmas to increase accordingly; it delivers them from the evil realms, fulfills the good realms, acts as a great benefit and a great happiness for many beings, and brings purpose, profit, and the increase of joy and bliss to the multitudes of gods and humans in all worlds.”
What is this one dharma? It is right view. Why is that?

By means of right view, it causes the ignorance of sentient beings to diminish, their perversions to be extinguished, and pure dharmas to increase accordingly; it brings liberation from the evil realms and the fulfillment of the happy realms, acting as a source of great benefit and great peace for many sentient beings, and bringing purpose, profit, and increasing joy to the multitudes of gods and humans throughout the world.

This is called the one dharma that exists in the world which, at the time of its growth, causes the delusion of all sentient beings to diminish, and so forth, until it brings benefit and purpose to the great assembly of humans and devas in the world, increasing their joy and happiness.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to summarize this meaning once more,
spoke in verse: "When right view grows and develops, It causes ignorance to diminish,
And the perversions to be eradicated, While all pure dharmas increase accordingly."
"Released from evil and filled with the happy realms, For the sake of benefit and happiness, etc.,
When right view is present before one, One swiftly realizes the bliss of Nirvāṇa.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
“Bhikṣus, you should know!
When I observe the world, I see no other single phenomenon that changes as rapidly as the mind. Why is this so?
This mind turns swiftly toward its objects; there is nothing in the mundane or supramundane realms that can serve as a metaphor for it. You should grasp the characteristics of this mind.
Having grasped these characteristics well, you should reflect upon them well;
having reflected upon them well, you should examine them well.
Having observed well, you should dwell securely;
having dwelt securely, if you do not perceive the presence of internal sensual desire that has enveloped you, you should further examine with precision:
"Do I now have internal sensual desire enveloping me, yet fail to perceive it?"
"Am I now not aware because I am entangled by internal sensual desire?
Having examined this thoroughly, one should further bring to mind and contemplate the mental image of any single desirable object.

When one attends to and contemplates any such attractive sign in this manner, if the mind follows, inclines toward, and finds delight in that attractive object, it should be understood that this mind conforms to sensual desires and opposes renunciation.
At that time, you should realize for yourselves:
"I still possess internal fetters of sensual desire which I have not yet awakened to; it is not that they do not exist.
I have not yet severed the fetters of craving for the five desires, and what I have realized is no different from before."
I have not yet realized the fruit of my practice.

It is like a person who, on a swift current, pulls a heavy boat or raft upstream; at that time, this person must exert great effort, for if they momentarily relax their diligence, the vessel will drift downstream with the current.

In this way, when you contemplate any one of these attractive signs, if the mind follows, inclines toward, and finds delight in that attractive object, you should know that this mind conforms to the various desires and opposes renunciation.
At that time, you should realize for yourselves:
"I still possess internal fetters of sensual desire which I have not yet awakened to; it is not that they do not exist at all.
I have not yet severed the fetters of craving for the five desires, and what I have realized is no different from before."
"I have not yet realized the fruit of my practice.

When you direct your attention toward any single attractive object, if your mind inclines toward, pursues, and finds delight in the signs of renunciation, you should know that this mind is oriented toward renunciation and is opposed to all sensual desires."
At that time, you should realize for yourselves:
"I now have no internal entanglement of sensual desire; it is not that such still exists within me but I am unaware of it.
I have now severed the entanglements of craving for the five desires, and what I have realized is already different from before."
I have now been able to realize the fruit of my cultivation.
Just as when sinew or feathers are cast into a fire, they immediately curl and shrivel rather than remaining relaxed, so it is with you:

whenever you contemplate any single attractive mark, if your mind follows and inclines toward the mark of joy and renunciation, you should know that this mind is conforming to renunciation and opposing all desires.
At that time, you should realize for yourselves:
"I now have no internal fetters of sensual desire; it is not that they still exist within me but I am unaware of them.
I have now severed the fetters of craving for the five desires, and what I have realized is already different from before."
I have now been able to realize the fruit of my practice.
Therefore, you should train yourselves in this way:
"How may I skillfully transform my own mind so that it becomes subdued, turns away from all desires, and accords with renunciation?"
"O bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the Blessed One, wishing to summarize this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"There is no other single dharma That is as volatile in nature as the mind."
Difficult to tame and difficult to guard— so it has been taught by the Great Sage.
Just as a wise man, using fire and various other tools,
straightens a sharp arrow so that it may strike its distant mark.
"In this way, all bhikṣus should skillfully train in expedient means,
straightening the nature of the mind so that nirvāṇa may be swiftly realized.
The summary verse (*uddāna*) of the preceding sutra says:
Cultivating loving-kindness, cultivating the two conditions; giving, violating precepts, and observing precepts;
the two delusions, the two noble wisdoms; wrong view and right view.
*Cittaviparyāsa-sūtra*, Fascicle Two.
*Sūtra on Past Lives*, Volume Three, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Two: On the Two Dharmas (3–5). Part One of Chapter Two: On the Two Dharmas.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!

If a bhikṣu is possessed of two factors, he will experience much sorrow and suffering in this present life, lacking joyful abiding; he will be beset by calamity and affliction, by vexation and burning, by guilt and reproach, and will be censured and reviled by his fellow practitioners of the holy life. At the dissolution of the body after death, he will be reborn in the woeful realms."
What are these two?
First, being unable to guard the doors of the sense faculties;
second, not knowing the proper measure in eating and drinking.

Any bhikṣu who possesses these two [qualities] will experience much sorrow and suffering in this present life, and will not dwell in joy and happiness; he will be beset by calamities and afflictions, by vexations and burning anguish, by guilt and reproach, and will be censured and reviled by wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life; at the breaking up of the body after death, he will be reborn in the evil destinies.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"If one cannot guard the gates of the six sense organs, such as the eyes,
if one does not know moderation in eating and drinking, one will become faithless and indolent."
In this present life, they experience much suffering of body and mind;
they encounter calamities and afflictions, distress and burning anguish;
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, and whether awake or dreaming, [they suffer].
Due to those two causes and conditions, one will always be subject to guilt and reproach.
Whether dwelling in a village or a secluded place, whether among the assembly or in solitude,
the wise will constantly censure such a person, who shall be reborn in the evil realms.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:

“Bhikṣus, you should know that if a bhikṣu accomplishes two factors, he will experience much joy and happiness in this present life, dwelling free from sorrow and suffering, free from calamity and affliction, free from vexation and burning, free from fault and reproach; he will be praised by wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life, and at the breaking up of the body after death, he will be reborn in the happy realms.”
What are the two?
First, being able to guard the doors of the sense faculties oneself;
second, being able to know the proper measure regarding food and drink.

Any bhikṣu who accomplishes these two will, in this present life, experience much joy and happiness, dwelling free from sorrow and suffering, free from calamity and affliction, free from vexation and burning, free from fault and reproach; he will be praised by wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life, and at the breaking up of the body after death, he will be reborn in the happy realms.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“If one can guard for oneself The gates of the six faculties, such as the eyes,
Knows the proper measure in eating and drinking, And accomplishes faith and diligence.”
In this present life, his body and mind experience much happiness;
free from calamity and affliction, without distress or burning anguish;
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, and whether awake or dreaming—
By virtue of these two causes and conditions, one is forever free from fault and reproach.
Whether dwelling in a village or a secluded place, amidst the assembly or in solitude,
the wise will always praise such a person, and they shall be reborn in the higher realms.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there are two kinds of dharmas that give rise to burning affliction."
What are these two?

There is a certain class of person who does nothing but commit various evils, acts only with violence and madness, and gives rise only to impurity; they do not cultivate various virtues, do not practice gentleness and flexibility, and do not rescue others from fear. At a later time, their body is stricken by a grave illness, and throughout their entire frame there arise intense, sharp, and piercing painful sensations; the agony is so extreme that death is imminent and it can no longer be treated.
While undergoing this suffering, they groan and lament with resentment, thinking to themselves:

"From the past until now, I have done nothing but commit various evils, act only with wild recklessness, and give rise only to impurities; I have not cultivated various virtues, practiced gentleness and flexibility, nor have I rescued those in fear."

If there are sentient beings who do nothing but commit various evils, act only with ferocity and madness, and give rise only to impurity; who do not cultivate various virtues, do not practice gentleness and flexibility, and do not rescue those in fear—whichever destination they go to, that is where I shall certainly go as well.

"Because he has committed only various evils and so forth, his mind gives rise to burning affliction; and because he has failed to cultivate various virtues and so forth, his mind gives rise to burning affliction.
These are called the two kinds of dharmas that can produce burning affliction."
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"There are two things that cause the foolish to suffer mental anguish:
namely, performing only sinful deeds and failing to cultivate the causes of merit."
Later, when one encounters the suffering of illness, one groans and laments in resentment;
hating that one has committed sins and lacks merit, the mind is consumed by remorse and anguish.
For those who have sinned and lack merit, they will be reborn in the various evil realms.
"I too shall follow along; there is certainly no doubt about this.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!..."
There are two kinds of dharmas by which the mind is not tormented or distressed.
What are these two? They are as follows:

suppose there is a certain type of person (pudgala) who practices only various virtues, cultivates only gentleness and flexibility, and only rescues those in fear; they do not commit various evils, do not act with violence or madness, and do not give rise to impurities. At a later time, that person is afflicted by a grave illness, and throughout their entire body there arise intense, sharp, and piercing painful sensations, so agonizing that death is imminent and no medical treatment can save them.
When undergoing this suffering, although there may be groans, there is no resentment or lamentation; one forms this thought:

"From the past until now, I have cultivated only various virtues, practiced only gentleness and flexibility, and sought only to save those in fear; I have not committed any evils, nor acted with violence or madness, nor given rise to any impurities."

If there are sentient beings who cultivate only various virtues, practice only gentleness and flexibility, and rescue others from fear; who do not commit various evils, do not act with violence or madness, and do not give rise to impurity—whichever destination they go to, that is where I shall certainly go as well.

Because he practices only various wholesome deeds and so forth, his mind is not scorched by affliction; and because he does not commit various unwholesome deeds and so forth, his mind is not scorched by affliction.
These are called the two kinds of dharmas by which the mind is not scorched by affliction.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"There are two things that can cause the wise to rejoice in their hearts:
namely, cultivating only meritorious deeds, and refraining from the causes of transgression."
When later encountering the suffering of illness, one groans without resentment or lamentation;
rejoicing that there is merit and no fault, one feels no regret, distress, or burning anguish.
For the person who possesses merit and is free from fault, wherever they are born in the various happy realms, they shall dwell in bliss.
"I too shall follow along; there is no doubt about it.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
I shall briefly explain for you the two paths of swift progress.
What are these two?
The first is the path of ease.
Second is the path of painful practice (*duḥkhā pratipad*).
This refers to the realization of swift super-knowledge (*kṣiprābhijñā*) through pleasant practice, as well as the realization of swift super-knowledge through painful practice.

Because the preparatory application (*prayoga*) cultivated therein is free from harshness and difficulty, and because the faculties (*indriya*) attained therein are all sharp and keen, this is called the "pleasant and swift path" (*sukhā kṣiprābhijñā-pratipad*).
Because the preparatory application practiced therein is harsh and difficult, yet the faculties attained are all sharp and keen, this is called the "path of swift progress with difficulty.
This is a brief explanation of the two paths of swift progress.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"I have now briefly explained for you The two types of swift paths:
Namely, the pleasant practice and the painful practice; By means of these, one realizes swift penetration."
There is the practice that is difficult and arduous, yet possesses sharp faculties;
for this reason, the Great Sage is called the One Who Travels by the Path of Joyful and Swift Progression.
There is also the practice that is difficult and arduous, yet possesses sharp faculties.
"For this reason, the Great Seer is named 'The Path of Swift Progress through Suffering.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
I shall briefly explain for you the two types of practice with sluggish progress.
What are these two? The first is pleasant practice; [the second is painful practice].

The second is the path of painful practice with slow superknowledge (*duḥkhā pratipat dhandhābhijñā*). This refers to realizing that superknowledge through pleasant practice, yet doing so slowly, and realizing that superknowledge through painful practice, yet doing so slowly.

Because the preparatory application (*prayoga*) lacks any harshness or difficulty, yet the faculties (*indriya*) obtained are all weak and dull, this is called the path of pleasant practice with slow superknowledge.

Because the preparatory practices (prayoga) cultivated therein are harsh and difficult, and because the faculties (indriya) attained are all weak and dull, this is called the "difficult path of slow progress" (duḥkhā pratipad dhandhābhijñā).
This is a brief explanation of the two paths of slow progress.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"I have now briefly explained for you the two kinds of slow progress:
namely, pleasant practice and painful practice; it is by means of these that one realizes slow progress."
There is practice that is without difficulty or hardship, yet possesses weak and dull faculties;
for this reason, the Great Sage is called one who possesses the "pleasant and slow" progress.
There is practice that involves difficulty and hardship, yet possesses weak and dull faculties.
"For this reason, the Great Sage is named 'the One Who Practices the Path with Difficulty and Slow Progression.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
If there is a certain class of person who possesses two qualities, they are unable to give rise to pure and wholesome dharmas;
even if they have already given rise to them, they cannot become certain;
and even if they have already become certain, they cannot bring them to fulfillment.

These act as obstacles to such pure and wholesome dharmas, cause their decline, and give rise to remorse; when the body breaks up at the end of life, like casting off a heavy burden, one falls into hell and undergoes various intense sufferings.
What are the two?
First, immoral conduct;
second, wrong views.
Any class of individuals who possess these two aforementioned qualities will certainly be unable to give rise to pure and wholesome dharmas;

even if they have already arisen, they will not remain stable. To speak at length, until the breaking up of the body and the end of life, they will cast off their burden like a heavy load and fall into hell, where they shall undergo various intense sufferings.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"If one accomplishes two things— namely, evil conduct and evil views—
that person will ultimately be unable to give rise to pure and wholesome dharmas."
Though born, one is not settled; lacking complete determination, one is able to cause the decline and obstruction of pure and wholesome dharmas.
When such a person approaches the end of life, they will experience anxiety, regret, and grief.
"Like one who has cast off a heavy burden, he will certainly be born in hell.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
If there is a certain class of person who accomplishes two dharmas, they will certainly be able to give rise to pure and wholesome dharmas;
if these have already arisen, they can make them certain;
and if they have already become certain, they can bring them to fulfillment.

Because he does not create obstacles for such pure and wholesome dharmas, nor cause their decline, nor give rise to regret, at the breaking up of the body after death, like casting off a heavy burden, he is reborn in the heavenly realms to experience various pleasures.
What are the two? First is virtuous conduct;
second is right view.
Any class of individuals who accomplish these two aforementioned qualities will certainly be able to give rise to pure and wholesome dharmas;

if they have already arisen, they will cause them to become certain, and so on at length until, upon the breaking up of the body and the end of life, like casting off a heavy burden, they are reborn in the heavenly realms to experience various pleasures.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"If one accomplishes two dharmas— namely, virtuous precepts and right view—
that person will certainly, in the end, be able to give rise to pure and wholesome dharmas."
If one is resolute from birth, and that resolve is surely fulfilled,
then regarding pure and wholesome dharmas, there will be no decline or hindrance.
When such a person approaches the end of life, they will be free from sorrow, regret, and distress.
"Like one who has cast off a heavy burden, he will certainly be reborn in the heavenly realms.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"

If there is a certain type of person who possesses two qualities, at the time of death they will give rise to grief and regret; when the body breaks up and life ends, they will fall into the evil destinies and be born in hell.
What are the two? They are "action" and "non-action. What is action?
That is to say, misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind—these are called "doing.
What is "not doing"? That is to say, good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind—these are called "not doing."

There are certain individuals who, having accomplished these two aforementioned qualities, give rise to sorrow and regret at the time of death; when their body breaks up and life ends, they fall into the evil destinies and are born in the hells.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“Those foolish people who commit three kinds of unwholesome conduct, And fail to practice the three kinds of sublime conduct,
Draw forth further faults and cause them to arise.”
"When they approach the end of life, they will certainly experience grief and regret;
upon death, they will fall into the various evil realms and be born within the hells.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One these words.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

If there is a certain type of person who accomplishes two qualities, at the time of death they will not give rise to sorrow or regret; when the body breaks up and life ends, they will ascend to a happy destination and be born in the heavenly realms.”
What are the two? They are:
that which is done and that which is not done. What is meant by "that which is done"?
That is to say, wholesome conduct of body, wholesome conduct of speech, and wholesome conduct of mind—these are called "doing.
What is "not doing"? That is to say, unwholesome conduct of body, unwholesome conduct of speech, and unwholesome conduct of mind—these are called "not doing."

Any class of individuals who accomplishes these two aforementioned qualities will not give rise to sorrow or regret at the time of death; when their body breaks up and life ends, they will ascend to a happy destination and be reborn in the heavenly realms.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“Those who possess wisdom perform three kinds of sublime conduct and refrain from the three unwholesome actions,
thereby drawing forth the arising of further virtues.”
"When they approach the end of life, they will certainly be free from grief and regret;
upon death, they shall ascend to the various happy realms and be born within the celestial worlds.
Thus have I heard these words from the World-Honored One.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that there are two sublime knowledges that ought to be cultivated so as to arise;

they enable one to attain what has not yet been attained, to touch what has not yet been touched, and to realize what has not yet been realized; they enable one to transcend sorrow and lamentation, to extinguish grief and suffering, to accord with the true principle, to obtain the nectar of immortality, and to realize nirvāṇa.”
What are the two? First is the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna);
second is subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
When the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) arises, one is then able to know conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) thoroughly and without error.
Having thoroughly known conditioned phenomena, one is then able to prevent the causes that induce future existence from arising, increasing, or expanding.
When subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) arises, one is able to eliminate ignorance (*avidyā*) as it truly is;
because ignorance is eliminated, there is no conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);
because there is no conceptual proliferation, there is no discursive thought (*vitarka*) or investigation (*vicāra*).
Because there is no applied thought or sustained thought, there is no desire;
because there is no desire, there is no love or hatred;
because there is no love or hatred, there is no stinginess or envy.

Because there is no stinginess or envy, there is no grasping for various weapons such as swords and staves, nor any harmful conflict, mutual abuse, untruthful speech, divisive speech, frivolous chatter, or other immeasurable evil and unwholesome dharmas.
Because those evil and unwholesome dharmas are absent, the karma that brings about future existence does not increase.
Because the karma that brings about future existence does not increase, all karmas are extinguished.
Because karma is extinguished, all suffering is extinguished;
because suffering is extinguished, the path of birth and death is cut off.
Once this path is severed, one then knows for oneself:
“Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence after this.
Thus, it is said that there are two sublime knowledges which should be cultivated so as to arise;

they enable one to attain what was not yet attained, to touch what was not yet touched, and to realize what was not yet realized; they enable one to transcend sorrow and lamentation, to extinguish grief and suffering, to accord with the true principle, to obtain the nectar of immortality, and to realize nirvana.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“There are two kinds of sublime knowledge that should be cultivated and brought forth;
they enable the attainment of what has not yet been attained, namely, the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).”
When the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) arises, one thoroughly understands all conditioned dharmas;
thus, the causes for future existence can neither arise nor increase.
When the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) arises, ignorance is then severed and extinguished.
By means of this successive dharma, one cuts off the cycle of birth and death.
Knowing for oneself that birth has been exhausted, that the holy life is established,
and that all that was to be done has been accomplished, one shall no longer undergo future existence.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there are two sublime forms of knowledge which should be correctly investigated, properly weighed, and carefully scrutinized."

One is able to attain what has not yet been attained, to touch what has not yet been touched, and to realize what has not yet been realized; one is able to transcend sorrow and lamentation, to extinguish grief and suffering, to accord with the true principle, to obtain the deathless nectar, and to realize nirvana.
What are these two?
They are mundane knowledge and supramundane knowledge.
"Mundane knowledge" refers to correctly understanding the aggregate of form as "this is the aggregate of form."
It is likewise with regard to the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
One correctly understands the earth element as the earth element;
and it is likewise with regard to the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.
Regarding the eye-element, one correctly understands it as the eye-element; the same applies to the form-element and the eye-consciousness-element.
Regarding the ear-element, one correctly understands it as the ear-element; the same applies to the sound-element and the ear-consciousness-element.
Regarding the nose-element, one correctly understands it as the nose-element; the same applies to the odor-element and the nose-consciousness-element.
Regarding the tongue element, one correctly understands it as the tongue element; the same applies to the taste element and the tongue-consciousness element.
Regarding the body element, one correctly understands it as the body element; the same applies to the tangible-object element and the body-consciousness element.
Regarding the mind element, one correctly understands it as the mind element; the same applies to the mental-phenomena element and the mind-consciousness element.

Within such conventional phenomena, to understand them as they truly are in this way and that way—through wisdom, vision, penetrating insight, clear realization, and perfect awakening, illuminating them completely—is called mundane knowledge (*loka-jñāna*).
“Noble disciples, regarding this worldly knowledge thus described, you should correctly investigate it, skillfully weigh it, and carefully examine it:
‘When this worldly knowledge is properly cultivated, is it able to cause sentient beings subject to birth to forever escape from birth?’”
Is it possible to cause those sentient beings subject to the nature of aging to be forever liberated from aging?
It is likewise for those subject to the natures of illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, despair, suffering, and lack of peace.
Having investigated thoroughly, he is able to understand correctly:
