"When this mundane wisdom is properly cultivated, it cannot cause sentient beings subject to birth to be forever liberated from birth; it cannot cause sentient beings subject to aging to be forever liberated from aging; and the same applies to those subject to illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, despair, suffering, and lack of peace."

Why is this so? This worldly knowledge is not the Dharma of the noble ones; it does not lead to permanent transcendence, nor does it tend toward Nirvana; it cannot bring about permanent weariness with the world, permanent detachment, permanent cessation, or permanent stillness. It is not true supernormal wisdom, nor is it perfect enlightenment; it does not realize Nirvana.
It is a dharma that brings about birth, a dharma that brings about aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and lack of peace.
When he thus investigates, weighs, and examines with careful scrutiny, he dwells with a sense of dread toward worldly phenomena and dwells with a sense of tranquility toward supramundane phenomena.
Because they give rise to fear toward the world, they have no grasping whatsoever;
because they have no grasping, craving does not arise;
and because there is no craving, they personally realize ultimate nirvana within themselves.
Having realized nirvana, he then knew for himself:
"Birth has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further existence."
This is what is called that which should be correctly investigated, properly weighed, and carefully examined within this mundane knowledge.

As for supramundane knowledge, it refers to the correct and thorough understanding of all aggregates, elements, and bases—that these phenomena are impermanent, suffering, like a disease, like an abscess, like an arrow, like an affliction, like harm, like terror, like a fever, like destruction, like cessation, like calamity, like adversity, like a pestilence, like something empty, like something false, like something hollow, like something deceptive, like something lacking a real self, and like something unreliable.

To understand these various natures of phenomena as they truly are, and to possess the wisdom of insight, the super-knowledge, the clear realization, and the perfect awakening that illuminates them all-pervasively—this is called supramundane knowledge.
The noble disciples, regarding this aforementioned supramundane wisdom, should correctly investigate, skillfully weigh, and minutely examine it:
"When this supramundane wisdom is being properly cultivated, is it able to cause those sentient beings subject to birth to be forever liberated from birth?"
Is it able to cause those sentient beings subject to the law of aging to be forever liberated from aging?
It is likewise for those subject to the laws of illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, despair, suffering, and lack of peace.
Having thus investigated, he is able to know correctly:

"When this supramundane knowledge is properly cultivated, it will certainly cause sentient beings subject to birth to be forever liberated from birth; it will certainly cause sentient beings subject to aging to be forever liberated from aging; and the same applies to those subject to illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, despair, suffering, and lack of peace."
Why is this so? This supramundane wisdom is the Dharma of the noble ones;

it is that which leads to definitive emergence, it is the path to Nirvāṇa, it is that which brings about definitive weariness [with saṃsāra], definitive detachment, definitive cessation, and definitive tranquility. It is true higher knowledge, it is perfect enlightenment, and it is capable of realizing Nirvāṇa.
It is not a phenomenon that brings about birth, nor a phenomenon that brings about aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, despair, suffering, or lack of peace.
When he thus investigates, weighs, and examines them, he conceives of supramundane phenomena as rare treasures and conceives of mundane phenomena as base and inferior.
Because one perceives the arising of rare jewels within the supramundane, joy is born;
because joy is born, the mind becomes tranquil and at ease;
because the mind is tranquil and at ease, the body attains pliancy.
Because the body is pliant, one experiences joy;
because one experiences joy, the mind attains tranquility and concentration;
because the mind is tranquil and concentrated, one is able to know and see reality as it truly is.
Because one knows and sees reality as it is, one is able to develop profound revulsion and turning away;
because one develops profound revulsion and turning away, one is able to correctly abandon desire;
because one correctly abandons desire, one is able to attain liberation.
Having attained liberation, he then realized for himself:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."
This is what is called that which should be correctly investigated, properly weighed, and carefully examined within this supramundane knowledge.
Thus, it is said that there are two sublime knowledges which should be correctly investigated, properly weighed, and carefully examined;

through them, one can attain what has not yet been attained, touch what has not yet been touched, and realize what has not yet been realized; one can transcend sorrow and lamentation, extinguish grief and suffering, accord with the true principle, obtain the nectar of immortality, and realize nirvana.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"There are two kinds of sublime wisdom, Which the knower should investigate:
Namely, the mundane and the supramundane, Which can rightly bring an end to all suffering."
One should contemplate mundane wisdom, Giving rise to the perception of dread;
Being entirely without grasping, One successively realizes nirvana.
One should contemplate supramundane wisdom, Giving rise to the perception of a precious jewel.
From this, joy arises, and one immediately attains physical pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
Because of pliancy, there is rapture; because of rapture, the mind becomes concentrated.
Through the concentration of the mind, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are able to arise.
"By contemplating the noble truths through the factors of awakening, one forever severs the web of doubts;
being without doubt and without grasping, one is eternally liberated from the limits of all suffering.
To summarize the preceding sutra, the uddāna says:
The two faculties, the two torments, the two practices, the two types of precepts and views,
the two acts of doing and not doing, and the two kinds of knowledge—
thus have I heard from the Blessed One.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

If there are bhikṣus who go forth from the household life for the sake of deceiving sentient beings, for the sake of seeking fame and renown heard afar, or for the sake of seeking gain and honor, they are not said to be truly practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) under the Tathāgata.”
If there are bhikṣus who have gone forth for the sake of thorough penetration and for the sake of complete knowledge, they are said to be truly practicing the holy life under the Tathāgata.

Why is this? Because these bhikṣus have gone forth for the sake of thorough penetration and for the sake of complete knowledge; they are thus able to penetrate that which is to be penetrated and know that which is to be known, exactly as it is.

Being able to penetrate that which is to be penetrated as it truly is and to know that which is to be fully known, one is then able to abandon that which is to be abandoned as it truly is, cultivate that which is to be cultivated, and realize that which is to be realized.
Having thus abandoned, cultivated, and realized according to reality, he then knows for himself:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."
Thus, if one has gone forth for the sake of penetrating and for the sake of fully knowing the conditioned, this is called truly practicing the holy life under the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"For the sake of deception and reputation, For gain, profit, and honor, One does not truly practice the holy life; This is a false renunciation."
"To attain thorough penetration and complete knowledge, and to swiftly realize the supreme meaning—this is the true cultivation of the holy life; it is not a false renunciation.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

If there is a bhikṣu who has gone forth for the sake of deceiving sentient beings, for the sake of seeking a reputation that is heard afar, or for the sake of seeking gain and honor, he is not said to be one who truly practices the holy life under the Tathāgata.”
If there is a bhikṣu who has gone forth for the sake of discipline and for the sake of right abandonment, he is called one who truly practices the holy life under the Tathāgata.

Why is this? Because these bhikṣus have gone forth for the sake of restraint and for the sake of right abandonment; they are thus able to guard the six sense faculties as they truly are, not to violate the prohibitions and precepts, and to swiftly realize the supreme right abandonment.

Being able to guard the six sense faculties as they truly are and not violate the prohibitions and precepts, and being able to swiftly realize the supreme right exertions, one is then able to, as they truly are, abandon what should be abandoned, cultivate what should be cultivated, and realize what should be realized.
Having thus abandoned, cultivated, and realized things as they truly are, he then knows for himself:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."
Thus, if one has gone forth for the sake of restraint and for the sake of right abandonment, this is called truly practicing the holy life under the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"For the sake of deception, fame, and reputation, For gain, profit, and honor, One does not truly practice the holy life; This is a false renunciation."
"By practicing the restraint of right abandonment, one swiftly realizes the supreme goal;
this is the true cultivation of the holy life, not a hollow renunciation.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

If there are bhikṣus who go forth from the household life for the sake of deceiving sentient beings, for the sake of seeking fame and renown heard afar, or for the sake of seeking gain and honor, they are not said to be practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) in its true sense under the Tathāgata.”
If there is a bhikṣu who has gone forth seeking revulsion and seeking dispassion, he is said to be truly practicing the holy life under the Tathāgata.

Why is this? Because these bhikṣus have gone forth for the sake of revulsion and for the sake of detachment from desire, they are thus able to revile and become detached from desire in accordance with reality.
Having become free from desire, one attains liberation.
Having attained liberation, one knows for oneself:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."

Thus, if one has gone forth out of weariness with and aversion toward conditioned existence, and for the sake of detachment from desire, this is called truly practicing the holy life under the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"For the sake of deception, fame, and reputation, For gain, offerings, and respect, One does not truly practice the holy life; This is a false renunciation."
"To cultivate revulsion for and turn away from desire, and to swiftly realize the supreme goal—this is the true cultivation of the holy life; it is not a hollow renunciation.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One these words.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!
The Dharma gates taught by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are, in brief, of two kinds.
What are these two?
First, one should correctly understand what is unwholesome;
second, one should develop deep revulsion toward and turn away from what is unwholesome.
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas briefly teach these two types of Dharma-gates.
Why is this? All practitioners should correctly understand all unwholesome phenomena;
having correctly understood these unwholesome phenomena, they are then able to feel weary of them and turn away from them.
Once they have become weary of and turned away from it, they are able to become free from desire;
once they are free from desire, they attain liberation.
Having attained liberation, they know for themselves:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence.
For one who practices in this way, all cravings and fetters are forever severed; through unerring realization, they rightly reach the end of suffering."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to summarize this meaning once more,
spoke in verse: "You should know that all Tathāgatas, The Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas,
Out of compassion for sentient beings, Have taught two kinds of Dharma gates."
"Having right knowledge of all evils, and through weariness, turning away, and dispassion, the mind is liberated and autonomous;
thus one rightly reaches the end of all suffering.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One these words:
“Bhikṣus, you should know that there are two kinds of dharmas; if they are cultivated, practiced, or frequently cultivated, they can sever two other dharmas.
What are these two dharmas which, when cultivated, practiced, or frequently cultivated, can sever two other dharmas?”
This refers to the contemplation of impurity and the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion, which are able to sever both greed and hatred. Why is this so?
Because all past greed, present greed, and future greed arise from the mental attention directed toward signs of purity.
All instances of past, present, and future hatred arise from the mental attention directed toward the signs of enmity.
All instances of past, present, and future craving that have been, are being, or will be severed arise from the mental attention cultivated through the meditation on impurity.
All hatred that has been severed, is being severed, or will be severed, arises from the cultivation of the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion through mental attention.
Whether one cultivates, practices, or frequently practices the contemplation of impurity, it is certain that one will sever all sensual desire.
If one cultivates, practices, or repeatedly develops the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion, one will certainly be able to sever all ill-will.
If one wishes to decisively sever sensual desire, one should diligently apply oneself to the cultivation of the contemplation of impurity.
If one wishes to decisively sever hatred and anger, one should diligently apply oneself to the cultivation of the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion.
As for the cultivation of the contemplation of impurity, there is no craving that cannot be severed by it.
By cultivating the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion, there is no ill will that cannot be severed.
Thus, it is said that there are two dharmas which, if cultivated, practiced, or frequently cultivated, can sever these two dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“By practicing and cultivating extensively these two dharmas, one abandons two other dharmas:
Namely, through impurity and loving-kindness and compassion, One abandons sensual desire and ill will.”
Therefore, the wise person, seeking their own benefit,
should practice the contemplation of impurity and loving-kindness and compassion, thereby severing greed and hatred.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that the realm of nirvāṇa is, in brief, of two kinds."
What are these two?
First is the realm of nirvana with remainder;
second is the realm of nirvana without remainder.
What is called the realm of nirvana with remainder?

It refers to those bhikṣus who have attained arhatship; their outflows are exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, the heavy burden is laid down, their own goal is realized, the fetters of existence are ended, they have attained perfect understanding, their minds are well-liberated, and they have attained full knowledge.

With past karma as the condition, the various sense faculties that have been induced continue to abide; although these faculties are formed, one is able to feel detachment toward the various pleasant and unpleasant objects encountered in the present, remaining free from attachment and having one’s mind unentangled by craving or aversion, for all fetters such as craving and aversion have been permanently severed.
"When he seeks to see various forms, although he observes those forms with his eyes, he does not give rise to greed, hatred, delusion, or the like."
Although he possesses eyes and encounters both beautiful and ugly forms, he is without desire and without hatred.
Why is this? Because the fetters of craving, hatred, and so forth have been forever severed.
When he desires to hear various sounds, although he listens to those sounds with his ears, he does not give rise to greed, hatred, delusion, or the like.
Although they possess ears and encounter pleasant or unpleasant sounds, they have neither craving nor aversion.
Why is this? Because all fetters such as craving and aversion have been eternally severed.
When he desires to smell various fragrances, although he uses his nose to smell them, he does not give rise to greed, hatred, delusion, or the like.
Although they possess a nose and encounter pleasant or unpleasant odors, they harbor neither greed nor hatred.
Why is this? Because all fetters such as craving and aversion have been eternally severed.
When seeking to taste various flavors, although he uses his tongue to taste them, he does not give rise to greed, hatred, delusion, or the like.
Although he possesses a tongue and encounters both pleasant and unpleasant tastes, he has neither craving nor aversion. Why is this?
Because all fetters such as attachment and hatred have been eternally severed.
When he seeks the perception of desire regarding various contacts, although he perceives those contacts with his body, he does not give rise to greed, hatred, delusion, or the like.
Although he possesses a body and encounters pleasant or unpleasant tactile sensations, he has neither craving nor aversion. Why is this?
Because all fetters such as attachment and hatred have been eternally severed.
When seeking to understand all phenomena, although he may cognitively comprehend them with his mind, he does not give rise to greed, hatred, delusion, or the like.
Free from all craving, he realizes ultimate, quiescent *nirvāṇa*.
He reflects thus:

"For the sake of those who fear the *ālayavijñāna* of all existences (*bhava*) and are constantly bound by the view of annihilationism, the World-Honored One has taught the True Dharma so that they may know that the fruits of karma are never lost or destroyed. This Dharma is directly perceptible, timely, easy to see, beneficial, to be personally realized by the wise, and a true antidote for the entire world; it is able to eliminate pride and thirst, destroy the *ālayavijñāna*, sever all pathways, realize the nature of true emptiness, become free from all craving, and attain ultimate, quiescent *nirvāṇa*."
This is called the correct observation of one who possesses the eye of wisdom.

Thus, it is said that due to these two types of entanglements, among gods and humans—one class being timid and inferior, and the other class being courageous and vigorous—the one who possesses the eye of wisdom is able to observe correctly.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Bound by two kinds of fetters, the hosts of devas and humans are made such that some are timid and inferior, while others are courageous and resolute."
The Śrāvaka who possesses the eye of wisdom is able to observe things as they truly are;
being able to eliminate pride and cultivate weary detachment, they ultimately realize Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, they understand with perfect accuracy the True Dharma taught by the Buddha.
Able to extinguish the views of eternalism and nihilism, And the two types of craving without remainder;
The Dragon King with the Eye of Wisdom Is able to rain down the Dharma everywhere,
Extinguishing the flames of all afflictions And causing one to realize great, pure coolness.

**Postscript to the Collation of the Third Scroll of the *Mūlaparivarta-sūtra*** Regarding this single scroll of the sūtra, the Song and the Xiang editions are identical; both contain forty-three sections, whereas the Dan edition contains only eighteen.
Regarding these various discrepancies in wording and meaning, which differ significantly from beginning to end, how should one decide what to adopt and what to reject?
Now, upon examining the Song and Xiang editions of the sutra, four major errors are found; furthermore, two points in the Dan edition reveal its correctness.
Why is this? Since the title of this fascicle refers to "two dharmas," it should consistently expound only these two dharmas from beginning to end;
yet in the Song and Xiang editions of the sutra, all forty-three sections consist of only one dharma. Thus, the name and the content do not correspond, which is the first error.

Furthermore, the first two sections and the first six lines of the third section of the Song and Xiang editions constitute only one twelve-line passage from the *Cittārtha-sūtra* on the third folio of the initial fascicle in all other versions.
The Song edition rewrites this section three times over; this is the second error.

From "a class of sentient beings" onwards in the third paragraph constitutes only seventeen lines of a single passage from the *Bhikṣu-saṃghabheda-sūtra* on the seventh fascicle of the first volume in all other editions.
In the Song edition, this was transcribed repeatedly, eventually reaching forty-one layers; this constitutes the third error. The verse at the end of that scroll reads:

"Greed, hatred, and delusion, concealment, vexation, and anger, lack of remorse, envy, and stinginess, indulgence, pride, and harm. This is actually the concluding verse of the ninth fascicle of the second volume in various editions, which correctly states: "Greed, hatred, and folly, concealment, vexation, anger, and resentment, envy, stinginess, and craving, pride, and harm—all these. The former is merely a minor corruption and variation of the latter.
In the Song dynasty, it was transcribed again here with care, yet there were four errors; thus one knows they were indeed major mistakes.

Now, these eighteen sections of the present edition of the *Dan* (Red) manuscript begin from the "Two Parts of Accomplishment" and end with the "Two Fruits and Two Bonds," all of which pertain to the two dharmas; this corresponds precisely to the titles and meanings of the chapters, and is thus the first correction.

Furthermore, according to various editions, on the seventh folio of the fourth fascicle there is a concluding verse which reads: "In order to master the discipline, to loathe and know the fruit of impurity, to awaken from the fetters through meditative seclusion, and to seek with shame for what has been done. This concludes the twelve sūtras as a single verse.
The five sutras following "Its Awakening" (其覺悟已下) are the same five sutras found at the beginning of the fourth fascicle in various editions.
The seven sutras beginning with "The Sutra on Entanglements" (其纏經) and "The Sutra on Fruits" (果經) are simply the seven sutras at the end of this fascicle in the Dan edition (丹本).
Thus, the arrangement and the associated [commentary] are correct; these two versions are authentic.
Other editions are incorrect, and therefore we now adopt this Dan edition as the standard. It says:
"Although there may be mental states and phenomena of beauty or ugliness, there is neither greed nor hatred."
Why is this so? Because the fetters such as craving and aversion have all been eternally severed.

As long as his physical continuity remains in the world and he has not yet entered parinirvāṇa, he is constantly gazed upon, venerated, honored, and offered to by devas and humans; this is called the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder.
"What is called the realm of nirvana without remainder?

It refers to those bhikṣus who have attained arhatship, whose outflows are exhausted, whose holy life is established, whose task is accomplished, who have laid down the heavy burden, who have realized their own goal, who have exhausted the fetters of existence, who have attained perfect understanding, who are well-liberated, and who have attained complete knowledge."

At this time, because there is no longer any causal impetus for any that is experienced, he no longer harbors expectations; all has become eternally extinguished, ultimately quiescent, and finally cooled. It has vanished and does not appear, existing solely as a pure essence free from conceptual proliferation.

Such a pure essence, free from conceptual proliferation, cannot be said to exist, nor can it be said not to exist; it cannot be said to both exist and not exist, nor can it be said to neither exist nor not exist. It can only be described as the ultimate nirvana, which is beyond all designation.
This is called the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Bhikṣus, you should know that,
in brief, there are these two kinds of realms of nirvana.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"With outflows extinguished and the mind liberated, sustaining the final body,
this is called nirvana with remainder, wherein all conditioned phenomena still continue."
All that is experienced has ceased; it is tranquil and eternally cool.
This is called nirvāṇa without remainder, wherein all conceptual proliferations have subsided.
These two realms of nirvāṇa are supreme and beyond compare.
"Meaning that in this present life and in the future, one shall be tranquil and forever at peace.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
Due to these two entanglements, among gods and humans, one class becomes timid and inferior, while another class becomes courageous and vigorous.
Those who possess the eye of wisdom are able to observe this correctly.
What are the two entanglements?
That is to say: there is the fetter of the view of existence, and there is the fetter of the view of non-existence.
Why is it that a certain class of devas and humans is timid and inferior?

It refers to those gods and humans who love existence, delight in existence, rejoice in existence, and take pleasure in existence; when the True Dharma is preached for the sake of extinguishing existence, they are unable to listen with reverence and attentive ears, nor can they abide in a mind intent on following the teaching, nor can they practice accordingly to realize reality as it is.
Instead, they give rise only to timidity and inferiority, retreating in terror and alarm, thinking: "What shall we have at that time?"
"What shall we become at that time?
Thus do some classes of devas and humans feel timid and inferior.
How is it that some classes of devas and humans are courageous?

It refers to certain devas and humans who, fearing existence, wearying of existence, and longing for non-existence because they are oppressed by various painful phenomena, embrace and adhere to such and such wrong views, thinking:
"If I were to be severed, destroyed, vanish, and cease to appear, only then would it be called peace and subtlety."
"Thus, there is a class of gods and humans who are fierce and powerful.
How is it that those who possess the eye of wisdom are able to observe correctly?
It refers to the noble śrāvakas observing according to reality."

Having observed this, one does not give rise to conceit regarding reality as it is, does not rely on reality as it is to give rise to conceit, does not cause conceit by means of reality as it is, and does not take pride in reality as it is to give rise to conceit.
Having seen things as they truly are, one gives rise to revulsion;
having become repelled, one is able to become free from desire;
having become free from desire, one attains liberation.
Having attained liberation, he then knew for himself:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."
He reflects thus:

"The World-Honored One, for the sake of those who delight in the various realms of existence (*bhava*) and the *ālayavijñāna*, and who are constantly bound by the view of permanence, has taught the True Dharma in order to cause them to extinguish existence. This Dharma is subtle and profound, difficult to see and difficult to realize, tranquil, sublime, and beyond the sphere of discursive thought; it is realized by those of discerning wisdom and serves as the true antidote to all worlds—namely, that which can eliminate pride and craving, destroy the *ālaya*, sever all paths [to rebirth], and realize the nature of true emptiness."
The Sutra of Past Lives, Volume Four,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Second Part of the Second Chapter on the Two Dharmas.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!..."

If there is a bhikṣu who diminishes sleep, possesses mindfulness and clear comprehension, and whose mind constantly dwells in joy and purity, he will skillfully observe the proper timing for all wholesome dharmas and practice them correctly.

In this way, the bhikṣu diminishes sleep, possesses mindfulness and clear comprehension, and his mind constantly dwells in joy and purity. He skillfully observes the proper timing for all wholesome dharmas and practices them correctly; among the two fruits, he realizes one accordingly—either the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder in this very life, or the fruit of non-returning.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"One who awakens and is able to hear the Dharma Practices it and attains the supreme fruit;
But one who is addicted to sleep Attains nothing at all."
One who diminishes sleep, possessing right mindfulness and clear comprehension,
dwelling well-composed in mind, and always joyful and pure—
knowing the proper time among all wholesome dharmas, one should practice cultivation accordingly.
One can ultimately transcend the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Therefore, one should diligently practice the method of reducing sleep;
by constantly and attentively contemplating tranquility, one will undoubtedly attain the two fruits.
"Either severing the lower fetters, one realizes the fruit of non-return;
or severing the higher fetters, one transcends birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

If there is a bhikṣu who, dwelling in a secluded place, always delights in sitting in meditation, diligently cultivates the internal samatha-concentration, does not depart from dhyāna, achieves clear and pure vipaśyanā, guards his own mind so that it is not distracted, and tirelessly practices and accumulates all wholesome dharmas—[he is one who has attained the fruit of the path].”

In this way, for such a bhikṣu among these two fruits, I declare that he will certainly realize one or the other: namely, either the attainment of the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder in this very life, or the fruit of non-returning.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Delighting in seclusion and sitting in meditation, Possessing right mindfulness and clear comprehension,
Skillfully abiding the mind, One is free from false conceptualization."
Skillfully guarding one’s own mind, Swiftly severing the darkness of ignorance,
As well as all desires and afflictions, One returns to the truth without sorrow or regret.
Always tranquilizing the mind in meditative concentration, Possessing right mindfulness and dhyāna.
Liberated through non-attachment, one forever exhausts all craving for existence.
Constantly delighting in heedfulness and perceiving heedlessness as a source of fear,
one can eternally sever all views and swiftly realize parinirvāṇa.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!

If there is a bhikṣu who is without shame and without remorse, that person will certainly be unable to penetrate, unable to fully understand, will not realize equal enlightenment, will not realize nirvāṇa, and will be unable to attain unsurpassed peace and happiness."

If there is a bhikṣu who possesses a sense of shame and a sense of dread, that person will certainly be able to attain penetration, attain thorough knowledge, realize equal enlightenment, realize nirvāṇa, and realize the ultimate, unsurpassed peace and happiness.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“Those who lack shame and dread of blame, Who are indolent and lack diligence,
And who are full of lethargy and sleep— For them, the exhaustion of the fetters is far away.”
Those who possess a sense of shame and dread of blame are ever free from negligence;
delighting in quietude and profound meditative concentration, they are not far from Nirvana.
They are able to sever all fetters, as well as birth, old age, sickness, and death.
"Swiftly realize perfect enlightenment and attain unsurpassed peace and bliss.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
For those who have gone forth, there are briefly two kinds of duties that ought to be performed.

If one can perform them correctly, one will attain what has not yet been attained, reach what has not yet been reached, and realize what has not yet been realized; one will be able to transcend sorrow and lamentation, extinguish grief and suffering, touch the reality of things as they are, attain the deathless nectar, and realize nirvana.
What are the two?
First, meditative concentration;
second, listening to and expounding the Dharma.
What is meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)?

It refers to when monks, secluded from sensual desires and unwholesome states, possessing directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and experiencing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, fully abide in the first *dhyāna*.

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is internal serenity and one-pointedness, free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and filled with joy and bliss.
Free from joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing bliss with the body;
he enters and dwells in the third dhyāna, of which the noble ones declare: "He dwells in bliss who has equanimity and mindfulness."
With the abandoning of suffering and the abandoning of pleasure, and with the prior disappearance of sorrow and joy,
he dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness, having fully attained it.
What is meant by "listening to the Dharma"?

It refers to when the bhikṣus, regarding the teachings spoken by the Buddha—which are excellent in the beginning, middle, and end; skillful in their phrasing and meaning; pure, complete, and pristine in their holy conduct—namely the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, jātakas, vaipulyas, and adbhutadharmas—receive, recite, listen to, and study these teachings until they have mastered them, and then proclaim and explain them. This is called listening to the Dharma.
Thus, it is said that for those who have gone forth, there are briefly two kinds of duties to be performed.

If one can perform them correctly, one will attain what has not yet been attained, contact what has not yet been contacted, and realize what has not yet been realized; one will be able to transcend sorrow and lamentation, extinguish grief and suffering, contact the reality of things as they are, attain the deathless nectar, and realize nirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"There are two kinds of duties for those who have gone forth, Which are precisely what ought to be done:
namely, meditative concentration and listening to the Dharma, By which one swiftly realizes nirvana."
With meditative concentration as the cause for wisdom, and wisdom necessarily arising from meditative concentration, one who possesses both concentration and wisdom will swiftly realize nirvana.
There are hundreds of thousands of monks who are like mute sheep; though they practice meditative concentration, they lack wisdom.
Even if one were to pass a hundred thousand years, not a single person would attain Nirvana.
But those who diligently cultivate wisdom, who delight in hearing and preaching the Dharma,
and who concentrate their minds for even a brief moment, can swiftly realize Nirvana.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there are two kinds of seeking; there is no third."
What are the two?
They are noble seeking and non-noble seeking.
What is called non-noble seeking?
That is to say, there is a certain class of persons who, already subject to the nature of aging, seek out what is subject to aging;
who, already subject to the nature of illness, seek out what is subject to illness;
and who, already subject to the nature of death, seek out what is subject to death.
There already exists the phenomenon of sorrow, and one seeks the phenomenon of sorrow;
there already exists the phenomenon of defilement, and one seeks the phenomenon of defilement.
What is the phenomenon of aging?
What are called wife and children, slaves and servants; elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, chickens, pigs; fields and houses; gold, silver, wealth, and grain—these are termed the law of old age.
Such is the nature of aging; it is the root of the suffering of birth and death for all sentient beings.
Foolish worldlings guard it with defiled craving and attachment; because of this, they cannot be liberated from birth and death, and therefore it is called the "dharma of aging."
What is the nature of illness?

It refers to wives, children, slaves, and servants; to speak more extensively, it includes everything up to the point that because of these things one cannot be liberated from birth and death. Therefore, they are called the nature of illness.
What are the phenomena subject to death?

They are one's wife, children, slaves, and servants; as explained at length, because these things prevent one from attaining liberation from birth and death, they are called phenomena subject to death.
What are the phenomena of sorrow?

They refer to wives, children, slaves, and servants; explained at length, they include everything up to the fact that because of these things one cannot be liberated from birth and death. Therefore, they are called the phenomena of sorrow.
What are defiled phenomena? They are as follows:

wives and children, male and female slaves, servants and laborers; elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, chickens, and pigs; fields and houses; gold, silver, wealth, and grain—these are called defiled phenomena.
Such defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) are the root of the suffering of birth and death for all sentient beings.

Foolish worldlings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*) guard, crave, and become attached to them; because of this, they are unable to liberate themselves from birth and death, and are therefore called "defiled phenomena."
If there is any seeking out of this with craving and delight, know that it is called non-noble seeking;
such seeking the Tathāgata never praises or extols, but only exhorts others to recognize it and abandon it.
For what reason does the Tathāgata never praise or extol such un-noble seeking, but only exhorts others to know how to abandon it? Because this seeking is not the dharma of the noble ones;

it is not capable of leading to transcendence, nor does it lead toward nirvāṇa; it is not characterized by disenchantment, nor by detachment, nor by cessation, nor by peace; it does not result in the attainment of supernormal powers, nor in the realization of perfect enlightenment, nor in the witness of nirvāṇa.
By means of this seeking, one brings about all phenomena of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and various fevers of affliction.
Therefore, such un-noble seeking is never praised or extolled by the Tathāgata; rather, he only exhorts and guides others so that they may know how to abandon it.
What is called noble seeking?

It refers to a certain class of persons who, already subject to the nature of aging, are able to recognize for themselves that they possess this nature of aging; they are able to know, as it truly is, the defects and perils of aging, and they seek the ultimate, unsurpassed peace and happiness of *nirvāṇa*, which is free from aging.

Since there exists the nature of illness, one is able to know for oneself that one possesses this nature of illness; one is able to know, as it truly is, the perilous consequences of the nature of illness, and seeks the ultimate, illness-free, unsurpassed peace and bliss of Nirvana.

Since there is the nature of death, one is able to know for oneself that "I have the nature of death," and is able to know, as it truly is, the perilous faults of the nature of death, thereby seeking the ultimate, deathless, unsurpassed peace and bliss of Nirvana.

Since there exists the phenomenon of sorrow, one is able to know for oneself that "I have the phenomenon of sorrow," and is able to know the faults and perils of the phenomenon of sorrow as they truly are, seeking the ultimate, sorrowless, unsurpassed peace and happiness of *nirvāṇa*.

When there is a defiled state, one is able to know for oneself that "I have a defiled state," and is able to know the faults and perils of the defiled state as they truly are, thereby seeking the ultimate, stainless, unsurpassed peace and bliss of Nirvana.
This is called the noble seeking.
Such seeking is praised and extolled by all Tathāgatas.
For what reason is this noble seeking praised and extolled by all Tathāgatas?

By seeking through this, one attains the noble and holy Dharma, which can lead to eternal transcendence, can lead toward Nirvana, can produce weariness with and detachment from [suffering], can bring about cessation and tranquility, can attain supernormal knowledge, can accomplish perfect enlightenment, and can realize Nirvana.
By means of this seeking, one is able to transcend all birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and the feverish afflictions of saṃsāra.
Therefore, such is the noble seeking, which all Tathāgatas praise and extol.
Thus it is said that there are two kinds of seeking, and no third.
Therefore, you should train yourselves in this way:
"How may we abandon such un-noble seeking and practice such noble seeking?"
"O bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to summarize this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"All classes of sentient beings Have two kinds of seeking."
There is no third category, namely, the noble and the non-noble.
Not knowing the suffering of old age, sickness, and death, nor the faults and afflictions of the phenomena of grief and defilement,
yet yearning for them with deep attachment— this is called "non-noble seeking."
This increases manifold sufferings, and liberation remains far off;
from birth to birth again, one wanders through high and low realms.
One who well understands the faults of old age, sickness, death, and the defilements of sorrow—
To seek that cessation is called the true noble quest;
it diminishes all suffering and swiftly realizes nirvāṇa—
eternal peace, bliss, and coolness, forever untainted and fearless.
That is the seeking of the non-noble, censured and reviled by all Buddhas;
it is the root of birth and death, which the wise should keep far from.
This is the true seeking of the noble, praised by all Buddhas.
"This is the path leading to nirvāṇa; those with wisdom should cultivate it.
A summary verse (udāna) for the preceding sūtra says:
"For thorough penetration, restraint, revulsion, knowledge, impurity, and the elements."
Envelopments, Awakening, and Seated Meditation; Shame, What Is Done, and Seeking.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know this!"
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of pure and wholesome dharmas that can protect the world.
What are these two? They are shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*).

If these two pure and wholesome dharmas did not exist, sentient beings in the world would all become defiled and impure, just like cattle, sheep, chickens, pigs, dogs, and the like; they would fail to recognize their parents, brothers, and sisters, nor would they recognize their preceptors, teachers, instructors, or those who resemble instructors.

Due to these two pure and wholesome dharmas, sentient beings in the world are free from all defilement and impurity; they are not like cattle, sheep, chickens, pigs, dogs, and the like, but rather clearly recognize their parents, brothers, and sisters, as well as their preceptors, teachers, instructors, and those who resemble instructors.
Therefore, you should train yourselves in this way:
"How may we accomplish these two kinds of supreme, foremost, pure, and wholesome dharmas of shame and dread?"
“O bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“The two pure and wholesome dharmas Are able to protect all worlds.”
To ensure one does not lose the status of a human or a deva, there must be a sense of shame (*hrī*) and a dread of blame (*apatrāpya*).
If these two qualities are absent, one fails to recognize the distinction between the noble and the base;
such a person is defiled and impure like cattle, sheep, chickens, pigs, dogs, and the like.
Because these two qualities exist, one is able to distinguish between the noble and the base;
unlike cattle or sheep, one does not engage in various defiled and impure deeds.
All wise people who have accomplished these two pure dharmas [are thus distinguished].
"Always guarding the realms of humans and devas, one shall never fall into the three miserable states.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
When I was a bodhisattva dwelling in the stage prior to my awakening as a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, I for the most part dwelt in two kinds of reflection.
What are these two?
First, when the Tathāgata dwells in the stage of a bodhisattva, he for the most part abides in the joyful delight of non-harming mental exploration (*avihiṃsā-vitarka*).
To thus abide in the joyful delight of non-harming mental exploration is called the first "predominant mental exploration."
By abiding in such a path of cultivation, one causes no harm whatsoever to sentient beings; through this contemplation, one realizes the immeasurable and perfect Brahma-abodes.
Second, when the Tathāgata dwells in the stage of a bodhisattva, he for the most part abides in the joy and delight of having permanently severed discursive thought (*vitarka*).
To thus abide in the joy and delight of having permanently severed discursive thought is called the second "predominance of discursive thought."

By abiding in such a path of cultivation, one is able to correctly and permanently sever unwholesome dharmas; through this investigation, one realizes the supreme path that brings the roots of virtue to perfection.

At that time, abiding in these two kinds of investigation, I applied myself with fierce diligence until all the blood and flesh of my own body were completely exhausted, leaving only the bones, sinews, and skin wrapped together; yet I remained without negligence, never slackening in my fierce diligence while I remained vigilant until I had known, seen, attained, understood, and realized those dharmas which ought to be known, seen, attained, understood, and realized.

Through heedfulness, by being diligent, courageous, and untiring, one swiftly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; swiftly realizes unsurpassed, cool nirvāṇa; and swiftly realizes unsurpassed omniscient vision.
Therefore, you should train yourselves in this way:
"How shall we dwell with frequent reflection on the joy and delight of non-harming, and dwell with frequent reflection on the joy and delight of perpetual abandonment?"
“Monks, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the Blessed One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
“When the Buddha was a bodhisattva, He frequently dwelt in two dharmas.
It is said: Non-harming and perpetual abandonment, The volition of joy and delight.
Not harming any sentient beings, Cultivating loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, One realizes the immeasurable Brahma-abodes; To bring them to perfection is not difficult.
Forever severing unwholesome dharmas and all entanglements of affliction,
Realizing all roots of goodness and perfecting the sublime path,
Always diligent and valiant, dwelling without negligence—
"Realizing unsurpassed bodhi, attaining the coolness of nirvana, and so forth.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"

Many brahmins, householders, lay devotees, kṣatriyas, and others have performed many deeds for you, namely, providing you with clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine for the treatment of illness, and dwellings and requisites in accordance with the Dharma.

"O bhikṣus, you have much to do, namely, to proclaim for them the True Dharma—excellent in its beginning, middle, and end; skillful in its words and meaning; a pure, complete, and pristine way of holy conduct (brahmacarya)."
By means of this, both are able to be liberated from the phenomena of birth, aging, sickness, and death; from the phenomena of sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and feverish affliction.

You and they, possessing the wheel of power and the wheel of Dharma, shall rely upon one another and diligently cultivate the holy life under the Tathāgata, swiftly reaching the city of unsurpassed parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"The life of renunciation and the life of the household Depend upon one another;
By means of the two wheels of power and Dharma, One swiftly reaches the bliss of Nirvana."
The ordained rely on the laity to obtain requisites in accordance with the Dharma;
the laity rely on the ordained to attain the subtle and sublime True Dharma.
When these two assemblies rely upon one another, they enjoy the happiness of humans and devas.
"Having crossed over birth, old age, sickness, and death, one reaches the cool state of nirvāṇa.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
Abiding in and relying upon ethical discipline (śīla), one is able to cultivate two dharmas.
What are these two? They are śamatha and vipaśyanā.

It means that a practitioner, relying on and abiding in ethical discipline (*śīla*), cultivates calm abiding (*śamatha*); having cultivated such calm abiding, they cultivate the mind to bring it to fulfillment.
For what purpose do they cultivate the mind?
Those who cultivate the mind do so for the sake of severing craving.
All practitioners, relying upon and abiding in ethical discipline (*śīla*), diligently cultivate vipaśyanā; having thus cultivated vipaśyanā, they cultivate wisdom (*prajñā*) until it is fulfilled.
For what purpose does one cultivate wisdom?
One cultivates wisdom for the sake of abandoning delusion.
Greed defiles the mind and prevents it from attaining liberation; delusion defiles wisdom and prevents it from being luminous.
If one is forever free from greed, the mind is well-liberated;
if one is forever free from delusion, wisdom is well-liberated.

If, regarding these two kinds of liberation, one has been able to correctly know, see, attain, touch, and realize them, I declare that person to be one whose mind is well-liberated and whose wisdom is well-liberated—a solitary practitioner, a supreme among men.

When the noble disciples have thus directly realized liberation of mind, even when others revile, rebuke, mock, or humiliate them, they do not, on account of these conditions, give rise to various states of mind such as intolerance, lack of faith, malice, or resentment.
Why is this so? Because they are able to clearly perceive that when others revile them and the like, there is fault in the other but no harm to themselves.

When noble disciples have thus realized liberation of mind, even when others praise, honor, prostrate to, or make offerings to them, they do not give rise to various states of joy, exultation, or delight on account of such conditions.
Why is this? Because one is able to clearly perceive that when others offer praise and the like, there is merit for them but no benefit for oneself.
If one can act in this way, it is called attaining equanimity of mind regarding worldly dharmas; being without resentment and without elation, one dwells in peace and sovereign ease.
Therefore, you should train yourselves in this way:
"How shall we dwell in reliance upon ethical discipline (śīla) to cultivate serenity (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā)?
Monks, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Abiding in pure ethical discipline, Cultivating faultless tranquility and insight,
Thoroughly guarding the sense faculties and the mind, One realizes the nectar of Nirvana."
Cultivate *śamatha* to harmonize the mind; with a harmonized mind, one leaves behind craving.
Free from craving, one realizes liberation; realizing liberation, the mind becomes equanimous.
Cultivate *vipaśyanā* to clarify wisdom; with clarified wisdom, the darkness of delusion is extinguished.
Having extinguished darkness, one realizes liberation; having realized liberation, the mind attains equanimity.
Therefore, you bhikṣus, be diligent and do not be heedless;
always abide in reliance upon ethical discipline (śīla), and cultivate faultless calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā).
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there is a great benefit in training and practicing the holy life under the Tathāgata."
Wisdom is the foremost, liberation is firm, and mindfulness is most preeminent.
If one accomplishes the excellence of training and practices the holy life under the Tathāgata,
wisdom is the foremost, liberation is firm, and mindfulness is most preeminent.

He will never have his mind entangled by the craving that relishes and clings to forms, nor will he have his mind entangled by the craving that relishes and clings to sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.

Because the mind is not entangled or disturbed by greed, there is no consciousness that follows after attachment to the signs of forms; there is no consciousness that follows after attachment to the signs of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
"Among these two fruits, one will realize either fruit; that is, in this very life, one will realize the realm of parinirvāṇa with remainder, or the fruit of non-returning.
At that time, the Blessed One, summarizing this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The person who trains in the excellence of practice, Relies on the Buddha to cultivate the holy life,"
Wisdom is the foremost, and liberation is firm;
mindfulness dwells in the most exalted state. One realizes one of two fruits:
namely, nirvana in the present life, or the fruit of non-returning forever.
With wisdom as the foremost, greed does not disturb the mind;
there is no consciousness arising from signs produced by conditions such as form.
Through the perfection of training in the benefits [of dharma], one gives rise to supreme meditative concentration and superior wisdom.
Having reached the end of birth, old age, and death, you shall realize the realm of the remaining substratum.
Therefore, O bhikṣus, you should diligently cultivate ethical discipline and meditative concentration,
and give rise to subtle and supreme wisdom, so as to exhaust birth, old age, sickness, and death.
"Those who abide within my Dharma and Vinaya, And are able to remain free from negligence,
Will surely destroy the power of Māra’s army And forever reach the end of all suffering.
Thus have I heard these words from the World-Honored One:
“Bhikṣus, you should know!
All evil and unwholesome phenomena in the world grow and develop with ignorance as their precursor;
they are sustained without diminution by the assistance of shamelessness and lack of dread.”

Why is this so? All states of existence within the various realms of rebirth—including birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and mental distress—all arise and grow with ignorance as their root.
Once they have grown, based upon them, one is further able to give rise to all manner of evil and unwholesome dharmas.
Once these evil dharmas have arisen, due to a lack of shame and remorse, there is no repentance or transformation whatsoever.
Because they are free from regret and transformation, they do not diminish.
All wholesome and pure dharmas of the world grow and flourish with the light of wisdom as their precursor;
they do not diminish because they have a sense of shame and dread of blame as their subsequent support.

Why is this? With the fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) before them and a sense of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*) as their guide, they are able to forever sever and extinguish the cycle of rebirth across all realms of existence—including birth, aging, sickness, and death—and are able to transcend all states of sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and feverish affliction. They are able to touch the reality of things as they are, attain the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*), and realize *nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, you should train yourselves in this way:

"How may we forever sever ignorance and give rise to the light of wisdom; forever sever all rebirths within the various realms of existence, including birth, old age, sickness, and death; forever transcend all states of sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and distress; and thereby touch the reality of things as they are, attain the nectar of immortality, and realize nirvana?"
“O bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the Blessed One, wishing to summarize this meaning, spoke these verses:
“In this world and in future lives, birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth...”
Afflictions such as craving and the rest all have ignorance as their root.
Ignorance is a great delusion that causes one to dwell long in birth and death,
wandering back and forth through high and low realms in this world and the next.
In the beginning there is ignorance, and at the end there is shamelessness and lack of remorse;
these give rise to all unwholesome dharmas, causing one to fall into the various evil realms.
Therefore, one should apply oneself with diligent vigor, abandoning craving, attachment, and delusion.
"Arising the light of wisdom, one cuts off the root of the suffering of birth and death.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas arise in the world out of compassion for the world, desiring to forever sever and abandon these two dharmas, and thus turn the unsurpassed wheel of the Dharma of the noble ones.
In all the world, among all śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, devas, māras, brahmās, and others, none have ever been able to turn it in accordance with the Dharma.
What are the two dharmas?
First, ignorance;
second, craving for existence.

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas appear in the world out of compassion for the world, solely for the sake of eternally severing and abandoning these two, and turning the unsurpassed Dharma-wheel of the noble ones—a wheel that, as has been extensively explained, no one has ever before been able to turn in accordance with the Dharma.

If one can forever sever and relinquish all ignorance and craving for existence, bringing them to complete exhaustion without remainder, one will then be able to forever sever all afflictions and all phenomena of defilement.

This is what is called emerging from all pits and moats, leaping over all walls, breaking all bolts and latches, and crushing the *iṣīkā* reed; these are the true noble ones (*ārya*), the banner of the True Dharma, the great śramaṇas, the brāhmaṇas, the truly wise, the truly purified, the truly intelligent, and the truly disciplined who have reached the stage of perfect discipline; they are called the field of merit for the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“The Unsurpassed Perfectly Enlightened One, The Caravan Leader, Honored One of the World,
The Great Hero, the Great Man, Who has extracted the poisonous arrows of the multitudes.”
Out of compassion for all the world, in order to sever two things—namely, ignorance and craving for existence—he turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma:
"This is suffering; this is the cause of suffering; this is the eternal cessation of all suffering."
This is the Noble Eightfold Path, leading to the extinction of suffering and Nirvana.
When the wise hear this Dharma, their faith, understanding, and so forth become firm;
they penetrate the true reality of all phenomena and sever ignorance and craving for existence.
"When ignorance and craving for existence are removed, all defilements are extinguished;
having reached the stage of sublime discipline, one is called a worthy field of merit for the world.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that there are two painful matters most difficult to endure:
first, shaving off the hair and beard;”
2. Constant begging. Why is this?
Those in the world who harbor resentment and cast curses make this vow, saying:
"May that poor man shave off his hair and beard, don worn-out and tattered robes, and holding an earthenware bowl in his hand, go from house to house begging for alms to sustain himself."

"Any sons of good family with pure faith who, having received and upheld this Dharma, go forth into homelessness, do not do so because they are oppressed by the terrors of kings, thieves, or creditors, nor out of fear for their livelihood; rather, it is solely to transcend birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and feverish distress, and to utterly extinguish this entire mass of suffering."
My disciples, seeking such matters as these, leave the household life with right faith to benefit themselves and others, and receive and uphold this Dharma.

Yet, there may be some who, having thus left the household life, soon thereafter become lax and negligent, indolent and inferior in their diligence; they lose right mindfulness and lack right awareness, their minds are distracted and unsettled, and they allow their sense faculties to run wild. Possessing much desire and attachment, harboring anger and resentment, they are dull-witted and ignorant, becoming immersed in various desires and false reflections, thereby violating the prohibitions and precepts.

They are not truly śramaṇas though they claim to be śramaṇas; they do not truly practice the holy life (brahmacarya) though they claim to practice the holy life. Rotten within and flowing with the current like a filthy snail, they have the voice of a conch but the conduct of a dog; concealing their own evils, they falsely manifest themselves as virtuous, having accomplished various kinds of evil and unwholesome dharmas.
For example, it is as if someone were to go from darkness into darkness, fall from one pit into another, or go from one enemy to another; I say that such a foolish renunciant is exactly like this.
Furthermore, it is like a piece of wood with fire burning at both ends and excrement smeared in the middle; whether it is in a village or in a secluded place, it has no further use.

I say that such a foolish renunciant is just like this: having lost the dharma of a householder, yet not being a śramaṇa either, he possesses no excellence whatsoever, whether in the worldly or the world-transcending realm.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"To leave the home life and yet break the precepts— Neither of these two achieves anything;
It means losing the decorum of a householder And destroying the Dharma of a śramaṇa."
It would be better to swallow a hot iron ball and have molten copper poured into one's mouth than to accept the faithful offerings of others while violating the precepts (śīla).
As for those who violate the precepts without remorse and without shame, [they fall into ruin].
One who receives many offerings of faith from others will certainly be reborn in hell.
All wise people should firmly uphold the pure precepts;
do not accept the offerings of faith while violating the *śīla*.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there are two types of persons in the world who embrace and increase the evil, unwholesome dharmas of the miserable realms and the hells."
What are the two kinds of *pudgalas*? First, there is a certain class of *pudgala* who violates pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).

In reality they are not śramaṇas, yet they call themselves śramaṇas; in reality they do not practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*), yet they call themselves practitioners of the holy life. Rotten within and flowing with defilements, they are like filthy snails or conches; they have the voice of a conch but the conduct of a dog. They conceal their own evils and falsely manifest themselves as virtuous. Like a dilapidated staircase, they are no longer of any use and only increase rebirth in the evil destinies.

Second, there is a certain class of individuals who, with groundless charges of unchaste conduct, slander and humiliate virtuous bhikṣus who possess pure ethical discipline, refrain from all transgressions, and diligently practice the stainless holy life, thereby causing them to lose their majestic splendor.
"These two types of persons embrace and increase the evil, unwholesome dharmas of the miserable realms and hells.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"The two types of persons generate and grow karma for the miserable realms."
Those who violate pure precepts and those who slander the virtuous—
these two kinds of people are both called base and lowly;
they are despised by others in the present and shall suffer in the future.
"Therefore, O bhikṣus, you should always be heedful,
uphold the pure precepts, and do not slander others.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One these words:
“Bhikṣus, you should know that there are two kinds of persons in the world whose kindness is profound and difficult to repay.
What are these two?
This refers to one's father and mother.

Suppose there were someone who carried their father on one shoulder and their mother on the other, never setting them down for even a moment throughout the entirety of their lifespan, providing them with clothing, food, and various necessities such as medicine for the occasion of illness; even so, they would still be unable to repay the profound kindness of their parents.
Why is this so? Because the kindness of parents toward their children is exceedingly profound and heavy.

That is to say, they bring them forth, nourish them with milk out of a compassionate heart, wash and care for them to ensure they grow up, provide them with all manner of necessities for sustaining life, and instruct them in all worldly rites and ceremonies. Their hearts constantly desire that their children be free from suffering and attain happiness, never abandoning them for even a moment, following them like a shadow follows a form.
Since parents possess such profound kindness toward their children as has been described, how should they be repaid?

If those parents lack pure faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, the child should employ skillful means to demonstrate, exhort, encourage, and comfort them, so that they may give rise to pure faith.
If those parents lack pure precepts, the child employs skillful means to demonstrate, exhort, encourage, and comfort them, causing them to receive and uphold pure prohibitory precepts.
If those parents lack extensive learning, the child employs skillful means to demonstrate, exhort, encourage, and console them, causing them to hear the true Dharma of the Buddhas.

If those parents are by nature stingy and greedy, taking no pleasure in giving, the son employs skillful means to demonstrate, exhort, encourage, and console them, leading them to practice generosity.
If those parents are by nature dull-witted and lack superior wisdom, the child employs skillful means to demonstrate, exhort, encourage, and comfort them, causing them to cultivate superior wisdom.
"When a son acts in this manner, he is said to truly repay the kindness of his parents.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to summarize this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Two types of persons possess a profound and heavy kindness that is difficult to repay:"
What are called father and mother are those who can give birth to and raise one in this world;
even if one were to carry them on both shoulders for the rest of one's life,
constantly providing offerings and showing reverence, one would still not have repaid their kindness.
In this world, parents are able to give birth and provide instruction;
with a compassionate heart, they seek one's benefit and happiness, following one like a shadow follows a form.
If one’s parents were previously lacking in faith, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, and wisdom, [one must cultivate them].
To command them to practice is called repaying kindness in truth;
to respectfully provide what they require brings only peace and happiness in this present life,
while leading them to cultivate faith, precepts, and so forth, so that they may ultimately realize nirvana.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there are two kinds of non-deceptive phenomena in the world."
What are these two?
They are karma and wisdom.
If sentient beings have already accumulated various karmas, their ripening fruits will never be exhausted or extinguished as long as they have not yet manifested before them.
If sentient beings have already given rise to various forms of knowledge, they will never abandon it as long as all afflictions have not been permanently eliminated.
These two are called the non-deceptive phenomena that exist in the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"The two things that cannot deceive Are what all Buddhas together proclaim:
Namely, the karma already accumulated and already produced, And all forms of wisdom."
As long as the ripening fruit has not arisen, karmas will never cease;
As long as afflictions are not exhausted, wisdom will never abandon them.
Karma is the cause of birth and death; wisdom is the root for extinguishing delusions.
"Therefore, one should cultivate wisdom, to bring all suffering to its ultimate end.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"

In this world, there are two kinds of persons whom one should deeply respect, prostrate to, and make offerings to, and with a heart of reverence and affection, draw near to and dwell in their presence.
What are these two?
They are the father and the mother.
If sentient beings deeply respect, prostrate to, and make offerings to their parents, and dwell in close proximity to them with a heart of reverence and love, they will generate immeasurable merit.

All wise people praise them in unison, their reputation is heard everywhere, they dwell among the multitude without fear, they suffer no burning distress later on, and they pass away without regret; after the dissolution of the body at death, they ascend to the various happy realms and are reborn among the devas.
For what reason should sentient beings deeply respect, prostrate to, and make offerings to their parents, and dwell in close proximity to them with a heart of reverence and affection?

Parents have profound and heavy kindness toward their children; that is to say, they give birth to them, nourish them with milk out of a compassionate heart, wash and cleanse them, and nurture them until they grow up. They provide various necessities for sustaining the body, instruct them in all worldly rites and ceremonies, and constantly desire to free them from suffering and enable them to attain happiness, never abandoning them for even a moment, like a shadow following a form.
Therefore, parents should be deeply revered, honored with prostrations, and supported with offerings; one should dwell in close proximity to them with a heart of reverence and affection.
If sentient beings revere and love their parents and dwell in close proximity to them, [they will likewise receive such benefits].

Out of deep compassion for them, their parents eliminate what is unbeneficial and bestow what is beneficial; they restrain them from various evils and encourage the cultivation of various virtues; they arrange for them to marry virtuous and excellent spouses, and at times bestow upon them rare jewels, wealth, and grain.
The gods and humans of the world all join in praising them, honoring and making offerings to them, and drawing near to provide protection, so that they may be free from decline and affliction.
Therefore, sentient beings should deeply respect their parents, prostrating to and making offerings to them, and dwelling near them with a heart of reverence and love.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“Those who delight in merit should honor their parents, Prostrating to them and practicing offerings;
With reverence and affection, they should dwell in close proximity.”
The wise people of the world Revere their parents,
constantly practicing offerings And always giving rise to a joyful heart.
In this world, the kindness of parents Is profound and heavy, difficult to repay.
Restraining evil that is unbeneficial, Bestowing benefit and encouraging the practice of good,
Providing a wife, household, and wealth, And always protecting with a heart of compassion—
For these reasons, by practicing such offerings, An immeasurable mass of merit arises.
In this life one attains supreme renown, All offer worship and respect;
At death, one is born in the celestial realms, Experiencing infinite sublime bliss.
If you wish to be born among gods or humans, And enjoy the sublime pleasures of the five desires,
"Just as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, Should make offerings to his parents.
The summary verse (*uddāna*) of the preceding sutra states:
"Wholesome, investigation, the wheel, precepts, training, Ignorance, wisdom, and abandonment."
