Chapter Two: The Two Dharmas, Part Three.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One:
“Bhikṣus, you should know that there are two kinds of giving.
What are these two?
The first is the gift of material wealth;
the second is the gift of the Dharma.
What is the gift of material wealth?

It refers to a certain class of individuals who are able to give various kinds of exquisite food and drink, perfumes and garlands, clothing, vehicles, dwellings, bedding, property, lamps, and medicinal requisites for the sick; by relinquishing such things and distributing them as gifts to others, it is called the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*).
What is the gift of Dharma?

It refers to extensively proclaiming the true Dharma for others—excellent in the beginning, middle, and end; skillful in its phrasing and meaning; a pure, full, and pristine practice of the holy life—thereby enabling sentient beings, upon hearing it, to be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and all afflictions of feverish distress. This is called the gift of Dharma.
Among these two kinds of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—the gift of the Dharma is the most supreme, excellent, and foremost.
It is like this world: from the cow comes milk; from milk comes curd; from curd comes fresh butter; from fresh butter comes clarified butter; and from clarified butter comes the finest cream (mṛdvī).
Among all the various flavors derived from cattle, clarified butter (ghṛta) is the most supreme, excellent, and foremost.
Likewise, between the two kinds of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—the gift of the Dharma is the most supreme, excellent, and foremost.

Among those who bestow the gift of Dharma, it is only the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Hero, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the Bhagavān, who is able to bestow the gift of Dharma without error.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Between the two kinds of giving, The gift of Dharma is supreme.
One who can practice the gift of Dharma Is most honored among the Sugatas."
Among those who receive material gifts, the Tathāgata is foremost;
while the practice of giving material gifts is not fixed, it is for the sake of sentient beings receiving the gift of Dharma.
Material gifts cause sentient beings to obtain worldly peace and happiness;
"Through the gift of Dharma, one causes the recipient to ultimately realize Nirvana.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
There are two kinds of sacrificial offerings.
What are the two? First, the sacrifice of material wealth; [second, the sacrifice of dharma].
2. The Sacrifice of Dharma.

As for the sacrifice of material wealth (*āmiṣa-yajña*), it refers to a certain class of individuals who offer various kinds of exquisite food and drink, perfumes and garlands, clothing, vehicles, dwellings, bedding, assets, lamps, and so forth; such categories are called the sacrifice of material wealth.

The "sacrifice of the Dharma" refers to being able to perform sacrifice through the discourses (*sūtra*), verses (*geya*), prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), stanzas (*gāthā*), spontaneous utterances (*udāna*), past events (*itivṛttaka*), birth stories (*jātaka*), extensive teachings (*vaipulya*), and marvelous qualities (*adbhutadharma*); by means of immeasurable gateways, it is called the sacrifice of the Dharma because it is proclaimed according to principle, established, and analytically revealed.
Between these two types of sacrifice—the sacrifice of material wealth and the sacrifice of the Dharma—the sacrifice of the Dharma is the most supreme, excellent, and foremost.

For example, in the world, from a cow comes milk; from milk comes curd; from curd comes fresh butter; from fresh butter comes clarified butter; and from clarified butter comes the finest essence, *sarpis* (ghee). Among all these various products derived from the cow, *sarpis* is the most supreme, excellent, and foremost.
Thus, between these two types of sacrifice—the material and the Dharma—the Dharma-sacrifice is the most supreme, excellent, and foremost.

Within the Dharma-sacrifice, the one capable of performing the Dharma-sacrifice without error is none other than the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the One Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Worthy One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the Bhagavat.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Between the two kinds of offerings, the Dharma-offering is supreme;
he who is able to practice the Dharma-offering is most honored among the Sugatas."
Among those who receive offerings of material wealth, the Tathāgata is foremost;
while the practice of material sacrifice is uncertain, the offering of the Dharma is received by all sentient beings.
The sacrifice of material wealth enables sentient beings to attain worldly peace and happiness; [but the sacrifice of the Dharma leads them to transcendental bliss].
"The Dharma-sacrifice causes those who receive it to ultimately realize nirvāṇa.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
When practitioners assemble together, they should perform two activities:
first, discourse on the Dharma;
second, maintain silent meditation.
Because of their words regarding the Dharma, one comes to know with certainty that they possess virtue;
because one knows with certainty their virtue, one develops deep respect and faith;
because of this deep respect and faith, one proceeds to visit them.
Because he goes to visit him, he draws near and serves him;
because he draws near and serves him, he seeks to hear the True Dharma;
because he seeks to hear the Dharma, he lends an attentive ear without distraction.
Because the ears are not distracted, one hears the true Dharma;
because one hears the true Dharma, one becomes proficient in the Dharma;
because one is proficient in the Dharma, one is able to retain and uphold it.
Because one retains the Dharma in mind, one is able to investigate its meaning;
when investigating the meaning, one is capable of reflecting with precision upon the Dharma;
and when one is capable of reflecting with precision upon the Dharma, a desire for it arises.
Having given rise to the desire for joy, one then attains power;
having attained power, one is then able to weigh and measure;
by means of weighing and measuring, one is then able to make a definitive discernment.
Because he is capable of discernment, he awakens to the truths and thereby knows for himself:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."

"Through the practice of meditative seclusion, the mind becomes tranquil and concentrated; it is pure, bright, and free from blemish. Being detached from secondary afflictions, it is pliant, serviceable, stable, and immovable, and is capable of being brought forth.
Because it can be brought forth, one understands things as they truly are;
because one knows them as they truly are, one is able to cultivate weary detachment."
Because one is able to feel revulsion and turn away from them, one is then able to become free from desire;
having become free from desire, one attains liberation;
having attained liberation, one then knows for oneself:
"I have attained liberation; my births are exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence.
You, bhikṣus, should proclaim the supreme Dharma and you should realize the supreme Dharma."
If one can act in this way, then one is truly said to uphold the banner of the sages.
It is not through the frivolous speech of congregations that one can correctly understand the true nature of all phenomena, sever all outflows, and realize nirvana.
"I always assemble and proclaim the supreme Dharma, and I fully realize the supreme Dharma; therefore, I am called the 'Foremost One Who Upholds the Banner of the Sages.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"When practitioners assemble, They should perform two tasks: [The first is to listen to the Dharma, And the second is to practice it.]”
That is to say: remaining in tranquil silence, and speaking the words of the True Dharma.
By means of speaking the words of the True Dharma and by remaining in tranquil silence, one knows the true reality of all phenomena and ultimately realizes nirvana.
"You monks, if you expound this supreme Dharma,
you shall be called true and shall uphold the banner of the Great Sage.
Constantly dwelling amidst the assembly, I proclaim the Dharma that brings clear illumination."
For this reason, it is called the foremost, upholding the banner of the Great Sage.
If one relies upon the banner of the True Dharma, being able both to preach and to practice it,
one will certainly and swiftly escape birth and death, reaching ultimate nirvana.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!

If bhikṣus, at the time of speech, engage in improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), giving rise to thoughts of sensual desire (*kāma-vitarka*), thoughts of ill will (*vyāpāda-vitarka*), and thoughts of harmfulness (*vihiṃsā-vitarka*), such bhikṣus are called those who are full of evil and those whose conduct is lax."

Because they are intent upon engaging in manifold evils as their means, they abandon the yoke of virtue through renunciation and detachment; they are negligent and indolent, possessing inferior diligence; they lose right mindfulness and lack clear comprehension; their minds are undisciplined and distracted, leaving their faculties unrestrained; they lack the vision of transcendence and do not know transcendence through authentic, correct wisdom; they incline toward evil Māras and evil, unwholesome dharmas, and being overwhelmed by those evil Māras and evil, unwholesome dharmas, they cause all evil and unwholesome dharmas to increase.
If any bhikṣus, while in a state of silent seclusion, engage in improper mental attention— and as has been explained at length— thereby increase all evil and unwholesome dharmas,
such bhikṣus will be censured and reviled by their wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life, and I too shall never praise them.
"Thus, although such a bhikṣu has gone forth and received full ordination, he is called a person of evil wisdom who delights in existence and is deluded.
Therefore, you all should train yourselves in this way:
'By what means shall we abandon and eliminate improper mental attention (ayoniśomanasikāra), and by what means shall we cultivate and practice proper mental attention (yoniśomanasikāra)?"
"O bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the Blessed One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"When speaking or remaining silent, if one allows the sense faculties to commit evil,"
Those who do not practice my teaching are foolish and deluded people.
Therefore, you bhikṣus, should cultivate heedfulness,
abandon improper attention, and reflect according to reason.
"If you all apply yourselves with right diligence, remaining heedful whether speaking or silent,
before long you shall cross over birth and death and realize unsurpassed Nirvana.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

If bhikṣus attend to their speech with correct mental attention—engaging in thoughts of renunciation, thoughts of non-ill will, and thoughts of non-harming—such bhikṣus are called those who possess much goodness and are free from laxity.”

Because he is oriented toward the cultivation of much wholesome merit as his means, he does not relinquish the noble yoke regarding abandonment and detachment; free from all negligence, he is courageous and energetic, possessing right mindfulness and clear comprehension, with a mind concentrated and undisturbed, and closely guarding the sense faculties. Possessing the vision of renunciation, he is able to know renunciation through suchness and right wisdom; he turns his back on Māra and evil, unwholesome dharmas, subdues Māra and evil, unwholesome dharmas, and diminishes all evil, unwholesome dharmas.
If bhikṣus, during their time of silent seclusion, attend to the mind correctly, and so forth, up to the point that they diminish all evil and unwholesome dharmas—
such bhikṣus are praised by wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life, and I too shall always praise them.
Such a bhikṣu is called one who has truly gone forth and received full ordination; possessing great wisdom, he does not delight in any forms of existence and is called a person free from delusion.
Therefore, you should train yourselves in this way:
"By what skillful means shall I cultivate appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) and by what skillful means shall I abandon inappropriate mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*)?"
"O bhikṣus, you should train yourselves thus.
At that time, the Blessed One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"In speech and in silence, do not allow the senses to commit evil."
One who is able to carry out my teaching is a wise and intelligent person.
Cultivating thoughts of renunciation, as well as non-ill will and non-harming,
possessing the right view of renunciation, they are able to know things as they truly are.
One can subdue the evil Māras and all unwholesome, non-virtuous dharmas;
by forever severing all afflictions, one realizes ultimate nirvāṇa.
Therefore, you bhikṣus, should cultivate heedfulness.
One should attend to things as they truly are, abandoning improper reflection.
If you apply yourselves with right effort, remaining heedful whether speaking or silent,
before long you shall cross over birth and death and realize unsurpassed Nirvana.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there are two kinds of power for a bhikṣu in training."
What are these two?
They are the power of discernment and the power of cultivation.
What is a bhikṣu who possesses the power of discernment?

This refers to a certain class of bhikṣus in training who, when utilizing various robes, food and drink, dwellings, bedding, and medicinal requisites for the treatment of illness, always employ them with careful discernment and never without such discernment.
Regarding the requisites for life—clothing, food and drink, housing, bedding, and medicinal provisions for the sick—that have not yet been obtained, one does not intensely crave them;
regarding those clothing, food and drink, housing, bedding, and medicinal provisions for the sick that have already been obtained, one does not deeply indulge in attachment to them.

He is capable of enduring cold and heat, hunger and thirst, the touch of wind, sun, mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, scorpions, and the like; he is capable of enduring the words of others, such as slander and insults; he is capable of enduring the intense, piercing, agonizing, and unbearable pains arising within his own body—those life-threatening, terminal, and incurable sufferings at the point of death—and he is capable of enduring all the most difficult things in the world that are hard to bear.

They are able to skillfully discern the three types of misconduct—of body, speech, and mind—and are able to illuminate the undesirable and painful results of karmic maturation in the present life, the life to come, and subsequent lives.
He reflects thus:
"I shall now certainly abandon the three types of unwholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind; I shall now certainly cultivate the three types of sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind."

One is able to correctly understand all the faults and afflictions inherent in the three types of unwholesome conduct, and furthermore, correctly understands all the merits inherent in the three types of wholesome conduct.

Having gained this correct knowledge, one diligently abandons unwholesome conduct and diligently cultivates wholesome conduct; thus refining oneself to make it pure and remaining free from all unwholesome dharmas.
This is called the first power of discernment belonging to a bhikṣu in training.
What is the power of cultivation belonging to a bhikṣu?

It refers to a certain class of bhikṣus in training whose attained mindfulness is entirely concordant with the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and not discordant with them; and whose attained investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya), diligence (vīrya), joy (prīti), pliancy (praśrabdhi), concentration (samādhi), and equanimity (upekṣā) are all entirely concordant with the factors of enlightenment and not discordant with them.

One cultivates the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, all of which relies upon disenchantment, relies upon detachment, and relies upon cessation, and is dedicated toward relinquishment; one cultivates the factors of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, all of which rely upon disenchantment, rely upon detachment, and rely upon cessation, and are dedicated toward relinquishment.
"This is called the power of subsequent cultivation of a bhikṣu in training;
this is called the two powers of a bhikṣu in training.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“Monks in training possess, in brief, two kinds of power:
the power of discernment and the power of cultivation; these enable them to subdue the armies of Māra.
Seeing faults, they are able to sever them; knowing sublime virtues, they are able to cultivate them.”
The ability to endure and reflect is called the power of investigation.
Relying on disenchantment, cessation, and dedication toward equanimity, one cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment; this is called the power of cultivation.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that death occurs through the exhaustion of two things."
What are the two dharmas?
First, karma;
second, life-span.
Due to the exhaustion of karma and the exhaustion of lifespan, death is certain.
When there is karma, at that time there is lifespan;
when there is lifespan, at that time there is karma.
Why is this? Because these two dharmas are eternally in union and never not in union; these two dharmas cannot be conceptually designated as being analyzed or separated.
At this time there is karma, and at that time there is life;
at this time there is life, and at that time there is karma.
If there is that karma, then there is that life.
If there is lifespan, there is karma;
if there is no karma, there is no lifespan;
if there is no lifespan, there is no karma.
It is like lighting a lamp: it produces flames and emits light;
if there are flames, there is light, and if there is light, there are flames.
If there is no flame, there is no light;
if there is no light, there is no flame.
It is the same with karma and lifespan.
If there is karma, there is life;
if there is life, there is karma.
If there is no karma, there is no life.
"If there were no life-span, there would be no karma.
Because these two dharmas are both exhausted and extinguished, there is death.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Two things always follow one another: namely, karma and life-span.
Where there is karma, there is also life-span; where there is no karma, there is no life-span.
As long as life-span and karma have not been extinguished, sentient beings will never die."
"When the karma of longevity is exhausted and ceases, there is no doubt that sentient beings will die.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!..."
There are two kinds of actions that all worldly beings collectively perform. What are these two?
The first is action that brings about a short lifespan.
The second is the conduct that can bring about long life.
What is the conduct that can bring about short life?

It refers to a certain class of *pudgala* who constantly delights in taking life; they are by nature fierce and violent, their hands are stained with blood, they harm the lives of beings, and they possess neither shame nor remorse. They constantly practice killing toward all sentient beings, even down to killing a legless ant; this is called the conduct that can bring about short life.
What is the conduct that brings about a long life?

It refers to a certain class of individuals who distance themselves from taking life, relinquish the instruments of killing, and, out of a sense of shame, modesty, compassion, and pity, never harm any sentient being—even down to a crippled ant. This is called the conduct that brings about a long life.
"Thus, it is said that there are two kinds of conduct, which all worldly sentient beings collectively engage in.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to summarize this meaning, spoke these verses:
"All sentient beings in the world Briefly have two kinds of conduct."
Due to the distinction between these two types of conduct, the lifespan experienced is either short or long.
Specifically, those who constantly delight in killing, who are fierce and violent with blood-stained hands,
and who lack shame, modesty, and compassion, will undoubtedly experience a short life.

"Always delighting in abstaining from taking life, Having cast aside all instruments of killing, Possessing a sense of shame, modesty, and compassion— One will attain long life; of this there is no doubt.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One these words:
“Bhikṣus, you should know that one apprehends the characteristics of the mind through two modes of practice. What are these two?
The first is called the aspect of the object of focus;
the second is called the aspect of mental attention.
All mental aspects that have been grasped, are being grasped, or will be grasped, arise solely through these two kinds of aspects.
"O bhikṣus, by means of two modes of practice, you should diligently and correctly grasp the characteristics of the mind;
having grasped the characteristics of the mind, you should apply correct attention;
having applied correct attention, you should engage in thorough investigation."
Having observed well, one should dwell securely;

having dwelled securely, one should, like the earth element, diligently practice the immeasurable and the undiminishing, and likewise, like the water element, the fire element, and the wind element, diligently practice the immeasurable and the undiminishing.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

It is like the element of earth: if one places within it excrement, filth, nasal mucus, saliva, pus, blood, or other such pure and impure things, although these are placed therein, that element of earth never experiences aversion or attraction, joy or grief, nor does it become elevated or depressed.
In this way, one should settle the mind so that it is equal to the earth element, practicing with right effort immeasurably and without impairment.

Having thus settled the mind in equality with the earth element and practiced with right effort immeasurably and without impairment, even when encountering various favorable or adverse conditions, the mind remains entirely free from conceptual discrimination or attachment; its state never fluctuates upward or downward due to these diverse causes and conditions.

Furthermore, it is like the water element, the fire element, and the wind element: even if one places within them such things as excrement, filth, nasal mucus, saliva, pus, or blood—whether pure or impure substances—even though these are placed therein, the water, fire, and wind elements never experience compliance or opposition, joy or grief, nor do they undergo any increase or decrease.
In this way, one should settle the mind so that it is like the element of water, the element of fire, and the element of wind, practicing with right diligence, immeasurably and without impairment.

Having practiced with right diligence, immeasurably and without impairment—like the elements of water, fire, and wind—even when encountering various favorable or adverse conditions, the mind remains entirely free from conceptual discrimination or attachment; its state never rises or falls on account of such diverse causes and conditions.

“By means of this concentration, within the conscious body and among all external objects of perception, the grasping at ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ as well as views, pride, and underlying tendencies, are thoroughly subdued and completely severed.”
His mind transcends those two types [of concentration], free from all signs, tranquil and blissful, attaining excellent liberation.

All that constitutes the excellent liberation of mind and the excellent liberation of wisdom—in all of these, the grasping at "I" and "mine," views, conceit, and underlying tendencies are well-subdued and thoroughly severed.
Regarding those two types, their minds transcend them, free from all signs, tranquil and secure, attaining excellent liberation.
Their minds do not rejoice in the gain, honor, praise, and pleasure they obtain;
nor do their minds feel dejection when encountering loss, defamation, disparagement, or suffering. This is called transcending the eight worldly dharmas.
"His mind is equanimous, just like the earth, water, fire, and wind of the world, which cannot be defiled by the eight worldly dharmas.

At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse: "The mind, difficult to tame and restless, travels far and has no second; It wanders through the three realms, following after objects of perception.
If one can subdue it, one attains peace; If not subdued, one suffers calamity. Therefore, the wise person always restrains the mind, For the mind is the root of all dharmas."
One who can correctly and diligently grasp the signs is called wise in the world.
Having properly grasped the characteristics of the mind, one further applies mental attention to observe it;
dwelling the mind in right mindfulness, one diligently cultivates it as being identical to the four elements.
Abiding correctly in this way, one is able to renounce all desires;
among the eight worldly concerns, such a person is called skillful and undefiled.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that there are two kinds of phenomena which, though mutually opposed and never in harmony, are nonetheless without deficiency or interruption.
What are these two?
This refers to birth and death.
For example, just as light and shadow in the world are mutually opposed and never coexist, yet between them there is no gap and no interval.
When the radiance appears, the shadows and darkness vanish;
when the shadows and darkness arise, the radiance fades away.
Birth and death are likewise: they are perpetually at odds and never in harmony, yet within this process there is neither deficiency nor interruption.
"When the time for the phenomenon of birth arrives, the phenomenon of death vanishes;
when the time for the phenomenon of death arrives, the phenomenon of birth passes away.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Just as light and shadow, though they are always mutually opposed,
yet between these two phenomena, there has never been a moment of separation."
Birth and death are likewise: though they are constantly at odds with one another, there has never been an interval or gap between these two states.
Born from the root of ignorance and nourished by the water of craving, [they continue to arise].
"As soon as death occurs, birth immediately follows; there is no interval or gap between them.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!..."
There are two kinds of death. What are the two?
The first is untamed death;
The second is death through subjugation.
What is meant by "death without subjugation"?

It refers to those foolish, unlearned worldlings who have not been able to attend upon virtuous persons of right view, nor have they been able to understand the Dharma of such virtuous persons; they have not themselves brought their minds into harmony with the Dharma of virtuous persons.
He contemplates and sees:
"Form is self; form belongs to me; form is within me; I am within form.
He contemplates and sees:
"Feeling is my self; feeling belongs to me; feeling is within me; I am within feeling.
He observes accordingly: "Perception is my self; perception belongs to me; perception is within me; I am within perception."
He contemplates and sees:
"Volitional formations are my self; volitional formations belong to me; volitional formations are within me; I am within volitional formations.
He contemplates and sees:
Consciousness is the self; consciousness belongs to the self; consciousness is within the self; the self is within consciousness.
Having seen a form with the eye, one grasps its signs and grasps its secondary characteristics.

Due to these causes and conditions, one fails to dwell with right mindfulness in guarding the faculty of the eye; craving and sorrow arise, and then immeasurable evil and unwholesome states flow out following the mind, impossible to dam or block.
Failing to guard the faculty of the eye, one allows the eye faculty to run wild among its objects, becoming greedily attached to the flavors of forms and entangling the mind.

Due to this craving, one undergoes suffering for a long night, undergoes fierce and sharp suffering, and undergoes the suffering of deprivation. One increases the number of bodies cast into boiling blood cauldrons and increases the distance traveled on desolate paths; wandering back and forth immeasurably, one is born within the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, humans, and devas, experiencing various intense sufferings—all because the eye faculty has not been subdued.

In this way, at times, having heard sounds with the ear, smelled odors with the nose, tasted flavors with the tongue, felt tangibles with the body, or cognized mental phenomena with the mind, one grasps at their signs and grasps at their secondary characteristics.

Due to these causes and conditions, one is unable to dwell with right mindfulness guarding the faculty of the mind; consequently, craving and sorrow arise, and immeasurable evil and unwholesome states flow forth following the mind, impossible to dam or block.
Failing to guard the faculty of the mind, one allows the mind to run wild among its objects, becoming greedily attached to the flavor of phenomena which entangles and disturbs the heart.

Because of this craving, one undergoes suffering for a long night, undergoes fierce and sharp suffering, and undergoes the suffering of deprivation. One increases the number of bodies in the cauldrons of blood and increases the distance traveled on desolate paths, wandering back and forth countless times through the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, humans, and devas, experiencing various intense sufferings—all of which result from the failure to subdue the faculty of the mind.
This is called dying unsubdued. What is meant by dying subdued?

It refers to the noble disciples who are well-versed in the teachings, who have been able to personally attend upon virtuous persons of right view, who have been able to understand the Dharma of such virtuous persons, and who have themselves become disciplined and compliant within that Dharma of virtuous persons.
One does not contemplate or perceive:
"Form is self," "form belongs to me," "form is within me," or "I am within form.
One does not contemplate or perceive:
"One regards feeling as self, feeling as belonging to self, feeling as being within self, or self as being within feeling.
One does not contemplate and see:
perception as self, perception as belonging to self, perception as being within self, or self as being within perception."
One does not contemplate and see:
"Volitional formations are my self; volitional formations belong to me; volitional formations are within me; I am within volitional formations.
One does not contemplate and see:
Consciousness is the self; consciousness belongs to the self; consciousness is within the self; the self is within consciousness.
Having seen forms with the eye, one does not grasp at their signs nor grasp at their secondary characteristics.

By this cause and condition, one dwells with the faculty of the eye well-guarded through right mindfulness; thus, neither greed nor sorrow arises, and all the immeasurable evil and unwholesome states that would otherwise flow and leak out following the mind are effectively dammed up.
One is well able to guard the faculty of the eye, not allowing the eye faculty to roam among its objects, nor becoming greedily attached to the flavors of forms so as to entangle the mind.

By not taking this greed as a condition, one does not undergo suffering for a long night, nor undergo fierce and sharp suffering, nor undergo the suffering of deprivation; one does not increase the number of bodies in the cauldrons of blood, nor increase the distance on the desolate paths, nor again travel back and forth through rebirth in the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, humans, and devas to undergo various intense sufferings—all because the faculty of the eye has been well subdued.

In this way, at times, having heard sounds with the ear, smelled odors with the nose, tasted flavors with the tongue, felt tangibles with the body, or cognized mental objects with the mind, one does not grasp at their signs nor grasp at their secondary characteristics.

By this cause and condition, he dwells with the faculty of mind well-guarded through right mindfulness; he does not give rise to desire or distress, and is able to dam up all the immeasurable evil and unwholesome states that would otherwise flow out along with the mind.
He is well able to guard his faculty of mind, not allowing the faculty of mind to roam among its objects, nor permitting himself to crave the flavor of phenomena to entangle his mind.

Because he does not rely on this craving, he does not undergo suffering for a long night, nor undergo fierce and sharp suffering, nor undergo the suffering of deprivation; he does not increase the number of bodies in the cauldrons of blood, nor increase the length of desolate paths, nor again go back and forth through birth in the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, humans, and gods to undergo various intense sufferings—all because his faculty of mind has been well subdued.
This is called dying having been tamed.
"Bhikṣus, you should know!

"Dying through subduing [defilements], one transcends the immeasurable ocean of suffering of birth and death.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to summarize this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"To speak briefly, there are two kinds of death for all sentient beings:

All phenomena are briefly of two kinds.

For one whose mind is agitated, turbid, and defiled, it is impossible that they can correctly understand matters of their own benefit and happiness, the benefit and happiness of others, or the benefit and happiness of both;

Why is this so? It is because the mind is agitated, turbid, and defiled.

"For example, in the world, if the central roof of a pavilion is not properly covered, then the rafters, beams, and walls will all be drenched by leaks; and because the rafters, beams, and walls are drenched by these leaks, they will all fall into ruin."

it is impossible that they can correctly understand the meaning of well-spoken words or the meaning of ill-spoken words;
and it is likewise impossible that they can realize the noble knowledge and vision of the truly holy ones regarding all superior human states.
Why is this? Because the mind is subject to agitation, turbidity, and defilement.

For one whose mind is free from agitation, turbidity, and defilement, it is possible that they will correctly understand matters of their own benefit and happiness, the benefit and happiness of others, and the benefit and happiness of both;

and it is possible that they will realize the true noble knowledge and vision of all the supreme human dharmas.
Why is this? Because the mind is free from agitation, turbidity, and defilement.

Why is this? Because water is free from agitation, turbidity, and impurities.

because these actions are not corrupted, the mind is free from agitation, turbidity, and defilement.

it is possible that they will correctly understand the meaning of well-spoken words and the meaning of ill-spoken words;
and it is possible that they will realize the true noble wisdom and vision of all the supreme human states.
Why is this? Because the mind is free from agitation, turbidity, and defilement.
"Bhikṣus, you should know this!"
Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled;
because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure.
Therefore, both the phenomena of defilement and purity depend upon the mind and arise from the mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more,
spoke in verse: "If one does not guard the mind, But follows after all desires,
Constantly racing about in heedlessness, There is nothing one will not do."
If one well guards the mind, does not follow after various desires,
and is without distraction or negligence, then everything is protected.
The wise person in this world is able to guard body, speech, and mind.
"One who refrains from committing all evils is called a truly valiant man.

"Bhikṣus, you should know!"

There are certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who embrace the view of non-existence, cultivate the view of non-existence, and cling to the view of non-existence; they are in constant opposition with those who delight in the views of existence, mutually harming one another, and they praise the view of non-existence as being supreme.

If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, regarding these two views, do not understand their origin, cessation, gratification, danger, and escape as they truly are with right wisdom, I say that such persons are called "lacking knowledge and vision.

If there be any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who, regarding these two views, can understand through right wisdom as they truly are their origin, cessation, gratification, peril, and the escape from them, I say that such a person is called one possessed of knowledge and vision;

free from greed, hatred, and delusion, without hostility or malice, possessing wisdom and clarity, he will certainly be liberated from birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, and will certainly be liberated from the great suffering of saṃsāra.

"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
There are two right views that should be thoroughly investigated, weighed, and examined.

If one thoroughly investigates, weighs, and examines them, one will be able to attain what has not yet been attained, touch what has not yet been touched, realize what has not yet been realized; one will be able to transcend sorrow and lamentation, extinguish grief and suffering, attain accordance with reality, touch the deathless nectar, and realize nirvana.
What are these two?
They are mundane right view and supramundane right view.
What is called mundane right view?
It refers to a certain class of people who give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine:

"There definitely exists giving, there exist recipients and sacrificial offerings, there exist wholesome and unwholesome karmas, and there exist their maturation fruits; there is this world and there is that world; there is a father and there is a mother; there exist in this world various types of beings born by transformation; and there exist śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who have attained rightness and practiced rightly, who have spontaneously realized and personally experienced [the truth] regarding this world and that world."
This is called mundane right view.
Regarding this mundane right view thus described, the noble disciples should thoroughly investigate, weigh, and examine it:

"Can this mundane right view, as here described, bring about the ultimate liberation of sentient beings from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and mental distress?"
Having observed this thoroughly, he correctly understood:

"Based on this aforementioned worldly right view, one does not bring about the ultimate liberation of sentient beings from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and the feverish afflictions."

Why is this so? Such worldly right view as has been described is not the true noble vision, nor is it the vision of renunciation; it is not the vision capable of ultimately realizing nirvāṇa. It does not involve disenchantment, nor detachment; it does not lead to cessation or tranquility. It does not realize the superknowledges (abhijñā), nor does it bring about perfect awakening (samyak-saṃbodhi) or the attainment of nirvāṇa; rather, it brings about the phenomena of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and despair.
Having understood this, one conceives a sense of dread toward worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*) and a sense of peace and tranquility toward supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*).
Because one conceives a sense of dread toward the world, there is no grasping whatsoever;
because there is no grasping, there is nothing to be sought after.
Because of being free from longing, he realizes ultimate *nirvāṇa* within himself.
Having realized this, he knows for himself:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."
In this way, you should thoroughly investigate, weigh, and examine this worldly right view that has been explained.
"What is called supramundane right view?"

That is to say, the knowledge that knows suffering, the knowledge that knows the origin of suffering, the knowledge that knows the cessation of suffering, and the knowledge that knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering; these are called supramundane right view.
"The noble disciples should thoroughly investigate, weigh, and examine this aforementioned supramundane right view:

'Does this aforementioned supramundane right view enable sentient beings to achieve ultimate liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and mental distress?'"
Having observed this thoroughly, he correctly understood:

"By relying on this aforementioned supramundane right view, sentient beings can achieve ultimate liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and mental distress."

Why is this so? This aforementioned supramundane right view is the true noble vision, the vision of transcendence, and the vision capable of ultimately realizing *nirvāṇa*. It can engender disenchantment, it can lead to detachment; it can bring about cessation and tranquility; it can realize supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), accomplish perfect awakening (*sambodhi*), and attain *nirvāṇa*. It enables one to transcend all phenomena such as birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and feverish affliction.
Having understood this, one conceives of supramundane dharmas as rare jewels and conceives of mundane dharmas as base and lowly.
Because one conceives of supramundane dharmas as rare jewels, joy arises;
because joy arises, the mind becomes peaceful and at ease.
Because the mind is at ease, the body attains pliancy;
because the body is pliant, one experiences joy;
because one experiences joy, the mind attains tranquility and concentration.
Because the mind is tranquil and concentrated, one is able to know and see reality as it is;
because one knows and sees reality as it is, one is able to develop profound revulsion and renunciation;
because one develops profound revulsion and renunciation, one is able to correctly abandon desire.
Because he is rightly detached from desire, he is able to attain liberation.
Having attained liberation, he then knows for himself:
"Birth has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence."
In this way, you should carefully investigate, weigh, and examine this supramundane right view that has been taught.
"These are called the two kinds of right view; they should be carefully investigated, weighed, and examined.

They can lead to what has not yet been attained, bring contact with what has not yet been touched, and realize what has not yet been realized; they can transcend sorrow and lamentation, extinguish grief and suffering, attain the state of accordance with reality, touch the nectar of immortality, and realize nirvana."
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"There are two kinds of right view: The mundane and the supramundane.
When the wise investigate them with discernment, They are able to rightly exhaust all suffering."
Contemplating the world with discernment, one gives rise to the thought of fear;
through non-appropriation and the like, one ultimately realizes nirvana.
Contemplating that which transcends the world with discernment, one gives rise to the thought of it being a precious treasure.
With a joyful mind, one attains composure; from this, one gains pliancy.
Because of pliancy, one experiences happiness; because of happiness, the mind becomes tranquil and settled.
From a settled mind, the factors of enlightenment arise, leading to the knowledge and vision of the four truths as they truly are.
"Seeing reality, one cuts through all doubts; with doubt removed, there is nothing to grasp.
One is liberated from all suffering and realizes unsurpassed nirvāṇa.
