You bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"Through three causes and conditions, the pursuit of various gains destroys manifold virtues and leads to the loss of both human and celestial states.
Any person of intelligence who encounters such decline in gain,"
His mind is well-stabilized, immovable like the king of mountains;
always tranquil in meditative concentration, he correctly contemplates the meaning of all phenomena.
Cultivating profound and subtle wisdom and insight, he realizes the Nirvana of eternal bliss.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that there are, in brief, three types of superior births within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Although one may accumulate a vast mass of merit therein while experiencing various sensual pleasures, one is unable to escape the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*)."
Why is this? Because that superior place of rebirth is the sphere of activity for desire.
What are the three?
First, the superior rebirths within the desire realm of the gods who dwell in desire;
second, the superior rebirths within the desire realm of the gods who delight in emanation;
third, the superior rebirths within the desire realm of the gods who control the emanations of others.

Although these three types of superior births in the desire realm result in the accumulation of immense merit, one still experiences various sensual desires and is unable to escape the cycle of birth and death.
Why is this so? Because those superior states of rebirth are the objective domains where desire operates.

My noble disciples, by observing these three types of superior rebirths within the desire realm as they truly are—including their various defects and afflictions—give rise to a profound sense of revulsion and turning away from the desire realm.
Because they give rise to revulsion and detachment, they are able to correctly abandon desire;
because they correctly abandon desire, they are able to attain liberation.
Having attained liberation, they then know for themselves:
“Birth for me has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; I shall not undergo further existence.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“The three superior births in the desire realm Constantly experience all manner of sensual pleasures.”
That is to say, those who dwell in the Heaven of the Gods Who Control Others' Emanations, the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, and the Heaven of the Gods Who Control Others' Emanations—
though they attain great merit by being born in these three places,
they remain within the cycle of birth and death and cannot be reborn in the higher realms.
"Among these various desires, if one can recognize their faults and perils,
one will abandon the realms of humans and devas and realize unsurpassed nirvana.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
“Bhikṣus, you should know!
There is a class of evil bhikṣus in the world who, having accomplished three dharmas, resemble the braying of a donkey.
What are these three?
It refers to a certain class of wicked bhikṣus who lack respect and deference, lack a sense of shame and dread of blame, and are indolent and forgetful.
Such a class of wicked bhikṣus, being fully possessed of these three qualities, resembles the braying of a donkey.
This refers to those who, while actually devoid of virtue, follow the assembly of monks and proclaim these words:
"Venerable ones, you should know that I too am a true śramaṇa, a son of the Śākya.

Yet this class of evil bhikṣus lacks the superior training in ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom; they merely follow the assembly of monks like other pure and true bhikṣu-saṃghas and proclaim these words.
"Venerable sir, you should know that I, too, am a true śramaṇa and a son of the Śākya.
It is like a donkey following behind a herd of oxen in the world, loudly proclaiming:
"I, too, am an ox; we should look after one another."
"However, although this donkey’s body, head, ears, hooves, snout, coat, color, and voice are all distinct from those of an ox, it follows behind the ox and cries out in a loud voice:
'I am also an ox; we should look after one another.'"
"In this way, a certain class of evil bhikṣus, though truly devoid of virtue, follow along with the Saṃgha and proclaim these words:
'Venerable ones, you should know that I, too, am a true śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas.'"

"However, this class of wicked bhikṣus dwells in dependence upon villages, cities, and market towns. During the first part of the day, they adjust their robes and take up their bowls and robes to enter the villages, cities, and market towns for alms. Being unable to guard their actions of body, speech, and mind, they do not abide in right mindfulness nor restrain their sense faculties. They go to the homes of faithful donors and, for the sake of gain and offerings, take a lower seat themselves while preaching the Dharma to laypeople seated on higher seats."
"I say that all the speech of such evil bhikṣus is like the braying of a donkey.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Shaved heads and dyed robes, Holding alms-bowls in hand— [Yet they do not practice the true Dharma. "
In truth, they possess neither precepts, concentration, nor wisdom, yet they call themselves śramaṇas.
They are like donkeys in this world, whose physical forms differ from those of oxen;
yet they follow behind a herd of oxen and claim for themselves that they are true oxen.
"Such evil bhikṣus, having established qualities such as lack of respect and so forth,
though they constantly sit among the pure assembly, shall not realize bodhi.
Thus I heard these words from the World-Honored One.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that there are three trainings.

If one can remain free from negligence therein, exerting oneself day and night, severing all worldly entanglements, dwelling alone in seclusion, and practicing the training without error, then the outflows not yet arisen shall never arise, and the outflows already arisen shall be forever extinguished.”
What are the three?
First, the training in higher ethical discipline;
second, the training in higher mental cultivation; [and third, the training in higher wisdom].
Third is the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).
What is called the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*)?

It refers to those bhikṣus who possess pure morality (*śīla*), who abide in and guard the prātimokṣa vows, whose conduct and deportment are entirely perfect, who perceive great dread even in minor transgressions, who are fully capable of undertaking and training in the precepts they ought to learn, and who achieve purity in the two karmas of body and speech, achieve purity of livelihood, and achieve pure view. This is called the training in higher ethical discipline.
What is called the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*)?

It refers to those bhikṣus who are able to correctly distance themselves from sensual desires and unwholesome, evil states; possessing applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, joyful and blissful, they fully abide in the first dhyāna, and so on in detail until they fully abide in the fourth dhyāna. This is called the training in higher mind.
What is called the training in higher wisdom?
It refers to when monks understand as it truly is:

the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering; this is called the training in higher wisdom.

Regarding these three trainings, if one can remain free from all negligence therein, practicing with diligence day and night, severing all worldly entanglements, dwelling alone in seclusion, and training without error, then those taints (*āsrava*) not yet arisen shall never arise, and those taints already arisen shall be forever extinguished.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"The wise should train in the three— The training in morality, mind, and wisdom.
Diligent and ever-peaceful in their exertion, They guard the sense faculties with secret restraint."
Dwelling in solitude day and night, having severed all worldly ties and affairs, one should diligently cultivate precepts, mind, and wisdom as if extinguishing a fire on one's own head.
This is called training in the noble training; reaching the ultimate limit of what is to be learned, one attains the goal.
Having liberated all that was to be liberated without exception, he has perfected pure and wondrous wisdom;
having attained immovable liberation and forever severed all outflows,
he has reached the end of the suffering of birth and death, such that no further existence shall arise.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there are three kinds of training.
If one practices them diligently, they will not be in vain or fruitless; they will lead inevitably to the ultimate goal, enabling one to attain the Deathless and realize Nirvāṇa."
What are the three?
First, the training in higher ethical discipline;
second, the training in higher mental cultivation; [and third, the training in higher wisdom].
Third is the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).
What is called the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*)?
It refers to those bhikṣus who revere the precepts (*śīla*), for whom ethical discipline is paramount.
If they do not value meditative concentration (*samādhi*), concentration will not be predominant;
if they do not value wisdom (*prajñā*), wisdom will not be predominant.
Regarding the minor precepts they have studied, they are able to emerge from even the slightest transgression.

Why is that? I say that such a person will never violate the training rules as they have been prescribed, nor will they fail to feel deep shame and remorse; they will certainly be able to accord with the pure holy life and certainly be able to accomplish the pure holy life, abiding in ethical discipline (*śīla*) regarding all the training rules and dwelling in what is to be learned.

That person will certainly be able to exhaust the three fetters forever, realize the fruit of stream-entry, attain the state of no longer falling back, and be certain to proceed toward enlightenment; at most, after seven more往返 (transmigrations) between the human and celestial realms, they will reach the end of all suffering. This is called the training in higher morality.
"What is called the training in higher mind?
It refers to those bhikṣus who revere ethical discipline (*śīla*), taking precepts as paramount;
and who revere meditative concentration (*samādhi*), taking stabilization as paramount."
Not esteeming prajñā, their wisdom does not become predominant.
Regarding the minor precepts they have studied, they are able to emerge from even slight transgressions. Why is this so?

I say that such a person will never transgress the training rules prescribed for them without profound shame and remorse; they will certainly be able to accord with the pure brahmacarya and certainly be able to accomplish the pure brahmacarya, abiding in meditative equipoise regarding all the training rules and dwelling within what is to be learned.

He will certainly be able to exhaust the five lower fetters, realize the fruit of non-returning, attain the state of a non-returner, receive a mind-made birth, and attain parinirvāṇa in that very world; this is called the training in higher mind.
"What is called the training in higher wisdom?
It refers to those bhikṣus who revere ethical discipline, taking ethical discipline as supreme;
who revere meditative concentration, taking meditative concentration as supreme;"
Respecting prajñā and taking wisdom as supreme, they are able to emerge from even the slightest transgression of the minor precepts they have studied. Why is this so?

I say that such a person will never violate the training rules prescribed for them without deep shame and remorse; they will certainly be able to accord with pure brahmacarya and certainly be able to accomplish pure brahmacarya, abiding in wisdom regarding all the training rules and dwelling in what is to be learned.

That person will certainly be able to bring all outflows to an eternal end, attaining true outflowlessness, with mind well-liberated and wisdom well-liberated; dwelling fully established in the present life, they will personally realize higher knowledge and be able to know for themselves:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
This is called the training in higher wisdom.

"If there are those who diligently practice these three trainings as they have been taught, I declare that their effort will certainly not be in vain or fruitless; it will surely reach the ultimate goal, enabling them to attain the Deathless and realize Nirvana."

Thus, these are called the three kinds of training; if one practices them diligently, they will not be in vain or fruitless, but will certainly lead to the ultimate goal, enabling one to attain the Deathless and to attain Nirvana.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to summarize this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“Diligently cultivate the higher training in ethical discipline;
Abiding in the precepts and the trainings, one can forever exhaust the three fetters And certainly realize the fruit of stream-entry.”
Diligently cultivating the higher mind, abiding in the training of concentration,
one can exhaust the five lower fetters and will certainly realize the fruit of non-returning.
Diligently cultivating higher wisdom, abiding in the training of wisdom...
Able to exhaust all fetters, one will certainly realize the fruit of non-arising.
The three trainings are not in vain; one will surely realize the ultimate truth.
Therefore, by honoring the three trainings, one attains the nature of phenomena without doubt.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there are three kinds of training:
if one practices them to a small degree, one attains a small fruit; if one practices them to perfection, one attains a perfect fruit."
What are the three?
First, the training in higher ethical discipline;
second, the training in higher mental cultivation; [and third, the training in higher wisdom].
Third is the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).
What is called the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*)?
It refers to those bhikṣus who revere the *śīla* (precepts), taking ethical discipline as supreme.
If one does not value meditative concentration (*samādhi*), concentration will not be predominant;
if one does not value wisdom (*prajñā*), wisdom will not be predominant.
Regarding the minor precepts they have studied, even if they slightly transgress them, they are able to emerge from that transgression.

Why is that? I say that such a person will never transgress the training rules prescribed, nor will they fail to feel deep shame and remorse; they will certainly be able to accord with the pure holy life and certainly be able to accomplish the pure holy life. Regarding all the training rules, they will be able to abide in ethical discipline (śīla) and abide in what is to be learned.

That person will certainly be able to exhaust the three fetters forever, realize the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), and attain the state of no-falling-back; they are destined for enlightenment, returning at most seven times between the human and celestial realms before reaching the end of all suffering.

Alternatively, there may be those who can cause their greed and anger toward the desire realm to become attenuated, realizing the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*); they will return to this world once more before reaching the end of all suffering.
This is called the training in higher ethics.
What is called the training in higher mind?
It refers to those bhikṣus who revere ethical discipline (śīla) and take ethical discipline as supreme.
They revere meditative concentration (*samādhi*), making it predominant;
they do not revere wisdom (*prajñā*), so that wisdom is not predominant.
Regarding even the minor precepts they have studied, they are able to emerge from any slight transgression.

Why is that? I say that such a person will never transgress the training rules (śikṣāpada) as they have been prescribed, nor will they fail to feel deep shame and remorse; they will certainly be able to conform to the pure holy life (brahmacarya), certainly be able to accomplish the pure holy life, and regarding all the training rules, they will be able to abide in meditative composure (samādhi) and abide in what is to be learned.

He will certainly be able to exhaust the five lower fetters, realize the fruit of non-returning, attain the state of a non-returner, receive a mind-made birth, and attain parinirvāṇa in that very world; this is called the training in higher mind.
"What is called the training in higher wisdom?
It refers to those bhikṣus who revere ethical discipline, taking ethical discipline as supreme;
who revere meditative concentration, taking meditative concentration as supreme; [and who revere wisdom, taking wisdom as supreme]."
Respecting prajñā, wisdom becomes predominant.
Regarding the minor precepts they have studied, they are able to emerge from even the slightest transgression. Why is this so?

I say that such a person will never transgress the training rules prescribed for them without profound shame and remorse; they will certainly be able to accord with pure brahmacarya and certainly be able to accomplish pure brahmacarya; regarding all the training rules, they will be able to abide in wisdom and abide in what is to be learned.

That person will certainly be able to exhaust all outflows forever, attaining true non-outflow; their mind will be well-liberated and their wisdom well-liberated, dwelling fully established in the present life, having personally realized higher knowledge, and being able to know for themselves:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."
This is called the training in higher wisdom.
Thus, it is said that there are three kinds of training: if one practices to a small degree, one attains a small result; if one practices to perfection, one attains a perfect result.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Those who dwell frequently in the respect for precepts Are said to practice only a small portion;
If they are always diligent and ardent, They will obtain only a small portion of fruit."
One who frequently dwells in concentration with a sense of reverence is said to practice partially;
though they are constantly diligent and ardent, they obtain only a partial fruit.
One who frequently dwells in wisdom with a sense of reverence is said to practice fully.
Through constant and fervent diligence, one attains the fruit of perfection.
By practicing even a small portion of perfection, one obtains a corresponding result.
Knowing such distinctions between superior and inferior, one should abandon partial practice and strive for perfection.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there are three kinds of training; if practiced correctly, they cause sentient beings to achieve the distinctions of inferior, middling, and superior noble ones."
What are the three?
First, the training in higher ethical discipline;
second, the training in higher mental cultivation; [and third, the training in higher wisdom].
Third is the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).
What is called the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*)?
It refers to those bhikṣus who revere the precepts (*śīla*), taking ethical discipline as supreme.
If they do not value meditative concentration, their samādhi will not be predominant;
if they do not value wisdom, their prajñā will not be predominant.
Regarding the minor precepts they have studied, even if they slightly transgress them, they are immediately able to emerge from that lapse.

Why is that? I say that such a person will never transgress the training rules prescribed, nor will they fail to feel deep shame and remorse; they will certainly be able to accord with the pure holy life (*brahmacarya*) and certainly be able to accomplish the pure holy life. Regarding all the training rules, they are able to abide in ethical discipline (*śīla*) and are able to abide in what is to be learned.

That person will certainly be able to exhaust the three fetters forever, realize the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), and attain the state of no longer falling back; they are certain to progress toward enlightenment, limited to seven more returns between the human and celestial realms;
or they may become a "family-to-family" practitioner (*kulaṃkula*), or realize the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), or the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*) with one interval remaining.
This is called the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*).
What is called the training in higher mental cultivation (*adhicitta-śikṣā*)?
It refers to those bhikṣus who revere ethical discipline and take ethical discipline as supreme.
He respects meditative concentration, making it his primary focus;
he does not respect wisdom, so that wisdom is not his primary focus.
Regarding the minor precepts he has studied, he is able to emerge from even the slightest transgression.

Why is that? I say that such a person will never transgress the training rules (śikṣāpada) as they have been prescribed, nor will they fail to feel deep shame; they will certainly be able to accord with pure brahmacarya and certainly be able to accomplish pure brahmacarya. Regarding all the training rules, they will be able to abide in meditative equipoise (samādhi) and be able to dwell within what is to be learned.

He will certainly be able to exhaust the five lower fetters, realize the fruit of non-returning, and attain the state of a non-returner; he shall undergo miraculous birth and attain parinirvāṇa in that very world.

Alternatively, he may become one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, or one who attains it upon rebirth, or one who attains it with effort, or one who attains it without effort, or one who becomes an "upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas) proceeding to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, or proceeding to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception, and there attain parinirvāṇa.
This is called the training in higher mind (*adhi-citta-śikṣā*).
What is called the training in higher wisdom (*adhi-prajñā-śikṣā*)?
It refers to those bhikṣus who revere ethical discipline (*śīla*), for whom ethical discipline is paramount;
Respecting meditative concentration, one takes stabilization as predominant;
respecting wisdom, one takes insight as predominant.
Regarding even the minor precepts they have studied, they are able to emerge from any slight transgression.

Why is this? I say that such a person will never transgress the training rules (śikṣāpada) prescribed for them without profound shame and remorse; they will certainly be able to accord with pure brahmacarya and certainly be able to accomplish pure brahmacarya, abiding in wisdom regarding all the training rules and dwelling in what is to be learned.

That person will certainly be able to exhaust all outflows forever, attaining true non-outflow, with mind well-liberated and wisdom well-liberated; dwelling fully established in the present life, they will personally realize direct knowledge and be able to know for themselves:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."
This is called the training in higher wisdom.
Thus, there are these three types of training; if they are correctly cultivated, they cause sentient beings to become distinguished as inferior, middling, or superior noble ones.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"By the power of training in accordance [with the teachings], Always ardent and persevering,
Through cultivation of the lower, middle, and superior grades, One attains the corresponding distinctions of fruit."
That is to say, practicing with inferior diligence results in an inferior fruit;
practicing with middling diligence yields a middling fruit; and practicing with superior diligence is likewise.
Having understood these three grades of practice and the distinctions in the fruits obtained, [one should apply oneself accordingly].
"Therefore, one should abandon the middling and inferior, and it is fitting to follow the cultivation of the superior grade.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"

If there are bhikṣus who possess well-disciplined ethical conduct, possess well-disciplined qualities, and possess well-disciplined wisdom, they have already fully practiced within my Dharma and Vinaya and are called supreme persons.
What is meant by a bhikṣu who is endowed with well-trained ethical discipline?

It refers to those bhikṣus who possess pure śīla, who abide in and guard the prātimokṣa vows, whose conduct and observances are entirely perfect, who perceive great dread even in minor transgressions, who are fully capable of training in the precepts they ought to learn, who have accomplished the two actions of body and speech in their purity, who have accomplished a pure livelihood, and who have accomplished pure views. This is called a bhikṣu who is endowed with well-trained ethical discipline.
Having already fulfilled such well-trained ethical discipline, how does a bhikṣu fulfill the dharma of well-trained discipline?
It is said that when bhikṣus diligently cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment and abide fully therein, they are called bhikṣus who fulfill the dharma of well-trained discipline.
Having thus become endowed with such well-disciplined ethical conduct (*śīla*) and well-disciplined qualities, how does a bhikṣu become endowed with well-disciplined wisdom?

It means that those bhikṣus have forever exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), attained true outflowlessness, and are well-liberated in mind and well-liberated in wisdom. Abiding fully established in the present life, they personally realize higher knowledge and are able to know for themselves:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
This is called a bhikṣu who possesses well-trained wisdom.

Thus it is said: if a bhikṣu possesses well-trained ethical discipline, possesses well-trained qualities, and possesses well-trained wisdom, he has fully practiced within my Dharma and Vinaya and is called a supreme person.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse: "If one's actions of body, speech,
and mind Are free from all evil and unwholesome states,
One is said to possess the discipline of well-tamed virtue— Such is the bhikṣu who possesses shame and dread."
If one can skillfully practice the seven factors of enlightenment, they are said to possess the well-trained Dharma; such a bhikṣu has sublime concentration.
If one can correctly understand this, one will forever exhaust all outflows within oneself.
One who possesses well-trained wisdom is a true, stainless bhikṣu.
If one possesses the three types of well-trained discipline, their majestic power is inconceivable in this world;
if one has already perfected such practice, they are a most supreme and intelligent person.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!

Any bhikṣu who is endowed with three qualities should be known as one who has attained perfection in pure ethical discipline (śīla), has attained perfection in the ultimate state, and has attained perfection in the cultivation of the holy life (brahmacarya); he has been able to reach the very end of the holy life."
What are the three? They are as follows:

there is a bhikṣu who has perfected the aggregates of the precepts, concentration, and wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). This is called a bhikṣu who has accomplished the three parts; it should be known that such a person has attained perfection in pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), has attained perfection in the ultimate stage, and has attained perfection in the cultivation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), having been able to reach the very end of the holy life.

If any bhikṣus have attained perfection in pure ethical discipline, have attained perfection in the ultimate stage, and have attained perfection in the cultivation of the holy life, they have been able to reach the very end of the holy life.

It should be known that such a person will certainly not delight in dwelling in villages, cities, towns, houses, or lodgings; nor will they delight in living amidst the clamor and confusion of a common garden with the community of bhikṣus, the community of bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, śrāmaṇeras, and others.

It should be known that such a person has accomplished the foremost dharma of a tranquil mind; dwelling alone in seclusion, they abide by the four reliances, are free from all defilements, maintain internal truth, and have abandoned all seeking. Being without attachment or discrimination, they are not stained by worldly dharmas.
For example, just as the world’s *utpala*, *kumuda*, *padma*, and *pundarīka* flowers grow in water and flourish in water; though they emerge from the water, they are not defiled or adhered to by it.
"This person is also like this: born from the world and grown from the world, though appearing in the world, they are not defiled by worldly dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"The three parts of the stage of no-more-learning are perfected; This is the ultimate state of śīla (ethical discipline).
Having perfected the holy life and reached its ultimate limit,
such a community of bhikṣus attains the supreme yoga,
forever exhausting the bounds of all suffering and realizing unsurpassed peace and bliss.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!

If there is one who seeks the three kinds of happiness, they should maintain pure ethical discipline that is unimpaired, unperforated, untainted, and unmixed; regarding this pure śīla, they should give rise to the highest degree of desire, diligence, and vigor, never becoming lax or negligent."
What are the three?

First, for one who seeks the joy of reputation, they should maintain pure ethical discipline that is unimpaired, unpierced, unstained, and unadulterated; regarding this pure *śīla*, they should arouse the highest degree of desire, diligence, and vigor, never becoming lax or negligent.

Second, those who seek gain and pleasurable things should maintain pure ethical discipline—unimpaired, unpierced, unstained, and unadulterated—and should arouse the highest degree of desire, diligence, and vigor toward this pure *śīla*, never becoming lax or negligent.

Third, those who aspire to the blissful state of rebirth in heaven should ensure that their pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) is unimpaired, unpierced, unstained, and unadulterated; they should arouse the highest degree of desire, diligence, and vigor toward this pure morality, never allowing themselves to become lax or negligent.

This is called seeking the three kinds of happiness; one should remain flawless, unbroken, untainted, and unmixed in pure ethical discipline, and regarding this pure *śīla*, one should arouse the highest degree of desire, diligence, and vigor, never becoming indolent or negligent.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“Seeking three kinds of happiness, the wise protect their ethical discipline (*śīla*):
namely, worldly fame and reputation, gain and offerings, and the joy of rebirth in heaven.”
Contemplating such supreme happiness, the wise person guards their ethical discipline (śīla) and should distance themselves from evil associates as they would avoid a perilous and treacherous path;
though they commit no manifold evils themselves, they remain wary of associating with those who do.
It is like wrapping foul, rotting fish or meat in auspicious kusha grass;
associating with those one should not associate with, and becoming intimate with those one should not become intimate with,
is like taking a fresh, pure object and throwing it into a deep pit of excrement.
Just as people in the world who delight in purity are constantly afraid of being defiled by filth,
so too is the wise person deeply terrified of evil acquaintances.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that there are three kinds of fragrances that can only be wafted with the wind and cannot travel against it.
What are these three?
First, the fragrance of roots;
second, the fragrance of stems;
third, the fragrance of flowers.
These three kinds [of scents] can only be perfumed with the wind and cannot be perfumed against the wind.
You, bhikṣus, should not think that there is no other scent that can perfume either with the wind, against the wind, or both with and against the wind. All [scents] are indeed capable of perfuming.

Why is this? Within my Buddha-dharma there is a wondrous fragrance that can perfume with the wind, against the wind, and both with and against the wind; its sweet scent is perceived by those in the heavens and among humans alike, and there are no sages or worthies in the world who do not cherish it.

What is it that is called "the one exquisite fragrance within my Buddha-dharma," which can perfume with the wind, perfume against the wind, and perfume both with and against the wind; which is smelled by all in the heavens and among humans as a fragrant scent; and which all the worthy and holy ones of the world do not fail to cherish?
This is what is called the fragrance of morality.

By means of this fragrance of morality, one can perfume with it both with the wind and against the wind, and even both ways at once; its sweet scent is perceived throughout the heavens and among humanity, and there are no sages or worthies in the world who do not cherish it.

Thus it is said: Within my Buddha-dharma there is a sublime fragrance that can perfume with the wind, against the wind, and both with and against the wind; its sweet scent is perceived by all among gods and humans, and there are no sages or worthies in the world who do not cherish it.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Of all things existing in the world, The fragrances of roots, stalks, flowers, and the like,
None can waft against the wind, Because their power is so slight."
Only within my Buddha-dharma is there a wondrous kind of fragrance;
whether with the wind or against the wind, it pervades everywhere without exception.
Among gods and humans, and all the sages and saints of the world, [it reaches them all].
All things are cherished, yet that which is called the fragrance of pure precepts is most precious.
If one can abide in this fragrance without negligence,
giving rise to unerring concentration and wisdom, one shall forever reach the end of all suffering.
To summarize the preceding sūtra, the uddāna says:
The same realm, the production of future existence, Seeking profit, and the desire for birth;
Evil speech like the braying of a donkey, The four trainings, and the four precepts.
