Chapter Three: On the Three Dharmas, Part Two.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!

In this world, there are three kinds of sons. What are the three? First, the equal son; [the second, the similar son; and the third, the dissimilar son]. What is the equal son? It refers to one who possesses the same lineage, the same family name, and the same clan as his father. This is called the equal son. What is the similar son? It refers to one who possesses a different lineage, a different family name, and a different clan from his father, yet possesses the same physical appearance, the same conduct, and the same deportment as his father. This is called the similar son. What is the dissimilar son? It refers to one who possesses a different lineage, a different family name, and a different clan from his father, and whose physical appearance, conduct, and deportment are all different from his father. This is called the dissimilar son. Furthermore, there are three kinds of sons: first, the son born of one's own body; second, the son purchased; and third, the son received through inheritance. What is the son born of one's own body? It refers to one who is born of the union of one's own parents. This is called the son born of one's own body. What is the son purchased? It refers to one who was originally the son of another person, but whom one has acquired through payment. This is called the son purchased. What is the son received through inheritance? It refers to one who was originally the son of another person, but whom one has received by virtue of being designated as an heir. This is called the son received through inheritance. Furthermore, there are three kinds of sons: first, the son who is given away; second, the son who is taken back; and third, the son who is abandoned. What is the son who is given away? It refers to one who was originally the son of another person, but whom that other person has given away to oneself. This is called the son who is given away. What is the son who is taken back? It refers to one who was originally the son of another person, but whom that other person has taken back from oneself. This is called the son who is taken back. What is the son who is abandoned? It refers to one who was originally the son of another person, but whom that other person has abandoned and who has come to oneself. This is called the son who is abandoned. Furthermore, there are three kinds of sons: first, the son who is born after the death of the father; second, the son who is born before the death of the father; and third, the son who is born while the father is still alive. What is the son born after the death of the father? It refers to one who is conceived in the mother’s womb after the father has passed away. This is called the son born after the death of the father. What is the son born before the death of the father? It refers to one who is conceived in the mother’s womb before the father has passed away. This is called the son born before the death of the father. What is the son born while the father is still alive? It refers to one who is conceived in the mother’s womb while the father is still living. This is called the son born while the father is still alive. Furthermore, there are three kinds of sons: first, the son who is born of a wife legally wedded; second, the son who is born of a concubine; and third, the son who is born of a slave woman. What is the son born of a wife legally wedded? It refers to one who is born of a wife who has been formally married according to the law. This is called the son born of a wife legally wedded. What is the son born of a concubine? It refers to one who is born of a secondary wife. This is called the son born of a concubine. What is the son born of a slave woman? It refers to one who is born of a female slave. This is called the son born of a slave woman. Furthermore, there are three kinds of sons: first, the son who performs services for the father; second, the son who does not perform services for the father; and third, the son who both performs and does not perform services for the father. What is the son who performs services for the father? It refers to one who, having been born, provides support and service to his father. This is called the son who performs services for the father. What is the son who does not perform services for the father? It refers to one who, having been born, does not provide support or service to his father. This is called the son who does not perform services for the father. What is the son who both performs and does not perform services for the father?

It refers to one who, at times, provides support and service to his father, and at other times, does not. This is called the son who both performs and does not perform services for the father. Furthermore, there are three kinds of sons: first, the son who is obedient; second, the son who is disobedient; and third, the son who is both obedient and disobedient. What is the son who is obedient? It refers to one who, having been born, is compliant and respectful toward his father. This is called the son who is obedient. What is the son who is disobedient? It refers to one who, having been born, is contrary and disrespectful toward his father. This is called the son who is disobedient. What is the son who is both obedient and disobedient? It refers to one who, at times, is compliant and respectful toward his father, and at other times, is contrary and disrespectful. This is called the son who is both obedient and disobedient. Furthermore, there are three kinds of sons: first, the son who is virtuous; second, the son who is unvirtuous; and third, the son who is both virtuous and unvirtuous. What is the son who is virtuous? It refers to one who, having been born, possesses moral integrity and is endowed with wholesome qualities. This is called the son who is virtuous. What is the son who is unvirtuous? It refers to one who, having been born, lacks moral integrity and is devoid of wholesome qualities. This is called the son who is unvirtuous. What is the son who is both virtuous and unvirtuous? It refers to one who, at times, possesses moral integrity and is endowed with wholesome qualities, and at other times, lacks moral integrity and is devoid of wholesome qualities. This is called the son who is both virtuous and unvirtuous. Furthermore, there are three kinds of sons: first, the son who is learned; second, the son who is ignorant; and third, the son who is both learned and ignorant. What is the son who is learned? It refers to one who, having been born, has studied extensively and is well-versed in the teachings. This is called the son who is learned. What is the son who is ignorant? It refers to one who, having been born, has not studied much and is not well-versed in the teachings. This is called the son who is ignorant. What is the son who is both learned and ignorant? It refers to one who, at times, has studied extensively and is well-versed in the teachings, and at other times, has not studied much and is not well-versed in the teachings. This is called the son who is both learned and ignorant. Furthermore, there are three kinds of sons: first, the son who is wealthy; second, the son who is poor; and third, the son who is both wealthy and poor. What is the son who is wealthy? It refers to one who, having been born, possesses great wealth and property. This is called the son who is wealthy. What is the son who is poor? It refers to one who, having been born, possesses little wealth and property. This is called the son who is poor. What is the son who is both wealthy and poor? It refers to one who, at times, possesses great wealth and property, and at other times, possesses little wealth and property. This is called the son who is both wealthy and poor. Furthermore, there are three kinds of sons: first, the son who is long-lived; second, the son who is short-lived; and third, the son who is both long-lived and short-lived. What is the son who is long-lived? It refers to one who, having been born, lives for a long duration. This is called the son who is long-lived. What is the son who is short-lived? It refers to one who, having been born, lives for only a short time. This is called the son who is short-lived. What is the son who is both long-lived and short-lived? It refers to one who, at times, lives for a long duration, and at other times, lives for only a short time. This is called the son who is both long-lived and short-lived. Furthermore, there are three kinds of sons: first, the son who is handsome; second, the son who is ugly; and third, the son who is both handsome and ugly. What is the son who is handsome? It refers to one who, having been born, possesses a beautiful appearance and pleasing features. This is called the son who is handsome. What is the son who is ugly? It refers to one who, having been born, possesses an unattractive appearance and unpleasant features. This is called the son who is ugly. What is the son who is both handsome and ugly? It refers to one who, at times, possesses a beautiful appearance and pleasing features, and at other times, possesses an unattractive appearance and unpleasant features. This is called
Second, the superior son;
third, the inferior son.
What is meant by the "superior son"?

That is to say, there is a class of parents who possess the precepts, have accomplished the dharmas of discipline and goodness, and are able to abstain from taking life, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, and abstain from drinking intoxicants which lead to heedlessness.

If you, my son, also possess the precepts and have perfected the dharmas of discipline, being able to abstain from taking life, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, and abstain from drinking intoxicants which lead to heedlessness, then you are called an equal son.
What is a "superior son"?

It refers to a certain class of parents who violate the precepts, establish themselves in various unwholesome dharmas, and delight in committing killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants—the basis for heedlessness.

If you are able to uphold the precepts and accomplish the dharmas of discipline and goodness—being able to abstain from taking life, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, and abstain from drinking various intoxicants that lead to heedlessness—you are called a superior son.
What is meant by an inferior son?

It refers to a certain class of people whose parents are endowed with ethical discipline (*śīla*), have perfected the qualities of a well-trained person, and are able to abstain from taking life, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, and abstain from drinking intoxicants which are the basis for heedlessness.

If his son violates the precepts, brings about various unwholesome dharmas, and delights in committing killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants which lead to negligence, he is called an inferior son.
"Thus, it is said that in this world there are three kinds of sons.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"The wise person of the world Rejoices in sons who are equal or superior; ... [the rest of the verse follows]"
Do not take pleasure in inferior sons; do not bring ruin to your family line.
You should know that among three types of sons, one is inferior and two are superior;
thus has the Buddha, the Perfectly Awakened One, declared, and so too have all the noble sages.
Trusting in both [the Dharma and the Sangha], possessing ethical discipline, wise and free from stinginess—
like the full moon in a clear night, standing amidst the splendor of all the stars—
one should approach and make offerings to such a person; they are praised by all the Buddhas.
"Far removed from all defilements and dust, his conduct is free from fear.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
If there is a bhikṣu who respects the true Dharma, loves the true Dharma, delights in the joy of the true Dharma, practices with diligence, and takes pleasure in the practice of the Dharma.
In this way, a bhikṣu who recollects the True Dharma always delights in permanently severing the unwholesome root of greed and cultivates the wholesome root of non-greed until it is perfected;
he always delights in permanently severing the unwholesome root of hatred and cultivates the wholesome root of non-hatred until it is perfected;
he always delights in permanently severing the unwholesome root of delusion and cultivates the wholesome root of non-delusion until it is perfected.
Having brought the cultivation of the three roots of goodness to fulfillment, one also brings the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness to fulfillment.
Having brought the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness to fulfillment, one also brings the cultivation of the four right endeavors to fulfillment.
Having brought the four right endeavors to fulfillment through cultivation, one also brings the four bases of psychic power to fulfillment.
Having brought the four bases of psychic power to fulfillment through cultivation, one also brings the five faculties to fulfillment through cultivation.
Having brought the five faculties (pañcendriya) to perfection through cultivation, one also brings the five powers (pañcabala) to perfection through cultivation.
Having brought the five powers to perfection through cultivation, one also brings the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga) to perfection through cultivation.
Having cultivated the seven factors of enlightenment to fulfillment, one also brings the eightfold noble path to fulfillment.
Having cultivated the eightfold noble path to fulfillment, both knowledge and liberation are brought to fulfillment.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Revering the Dharma and delighting in the Dharma, Rejoicing in the Dharma and practicing the Dharma,
Constantly maintaining mindfulness of the Dharma, One is able to never retreat from the True Dharma."
One who cultivates wholesome deeds with mindfulness of the Dharma, and does not mindfully engage in unwholesome conduct,
will surely bring about happiness in this world and the next through the practice of the Dharma.
The Dharma protects the practitioner of the Dharma, just as a great umbrella protects one during the rain.
"By practicing the Dharma one obtains the benefits of the Dharma; one will certainly not fall into the three miserable realms.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"

Briefly, there are three kinds of discursive thoughts in the world that cause a trainee bhikṣu who has not yet attained the mind [of liberation] to fall away when he joyfully seeks the unsurpassed dharma of peace and happiness.
What are the three?
First, discursive thought associated with relatives;
second, discursive thought associated with gain and offerings.
Third is the discursive thought associated with envy toward excellence.

These three types of discursive thoughts, when briefly explained, cause a learned bhikṣu who has not yet attained the mind [of liberation] to fall away when he is joyfully seeking the unsurpassed dharma of peace and bliss.
Therefore, you should train yourselves in this way:
"How may we not give rise to thoughts associated with relatives?
How may we not give rise to thoughts associated with gain?"
"How can you not give rise to thoughts associated with envy toward those who excel?
You, bhikṣus, should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the Blessed One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"Based on the pursuit of sensual indulgence, there are briefly three kinds [of discursive thought] which,
for one seeking unsurpassed bliss, are undoubtedly obstacles. Those associated with kin,
those regarding gain and honor, and those arising from envy of others' excellence."
Departing from great pleasure and great purity, the exhaustion of fetters is exceedingly remote.
By abandoning kin, gain, and offerings, as well as envy and discursive thoughts,
and by diligently cultivating the integration of calm abiding and insight, one can swiftly bring an end to all suffering.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that there are briefly three things which cause a bhikṣu in training who has not yet attained the goal to fall away when he is joyfully seeking the unsurpassed dharma of peace and happiness."
What are the three?
First, a bhikṣu delights in worldly affairs, craves worldly affairs, and is attached to worldly affairs;
second, a bhikṣu delights in conversation, craves conversation, and is attached to conversation.
Third, there are bhikṣus who delight in sleep, crave sleep, and are attached to sleep.
These three qualities cause a bhikṣu in training who has not yet attained the mind [of liberation] to fall away when he seeks with joy the unsurpassed dharma of peace and bliss.
Therefore, you should train yourselves thus:
"How may we not delight in worldly affairs, not love worldly affairs, and not be attached to worldly affairs?
How may we not delight in idle talk, not love idle talk, and not be attached to idle talk?"
"How should I not delight in sleep, not love sleep, and not be attached to sleep?
You, bhikṣus, should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the Blessed One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"When seeking the unsurpassed fruit, there are three things that cause one to regress:
attachment to worldly affairs, idle chatter, and sleep.
For a bhikṣu in training, if he possesses these three qualities,"
In the end, one will be unable to realize The most supreme,
perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). If you wish to quickly realize The most supreme, perfect enlightenment,
You should minimize affairs, speech, and sleep, And diligently cultivate tranquility (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā).
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there are three factors which,
when combined and present, enable virtuous sons of noble family with pure faith to generate immeasurable merit."
What are the three?
First, the manifestation of the harmony of pure faith, which enables pure-faithed sons of good family to generate immeasurable merit.
Second, the manifestation of the harmony of the objects of giving, which enables pure-faithed sons of good family to generate immeasurable merit.
Third, when the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) is present through the convergence [of conditions], it enables pure-faithed sons of good family to generate immeasurable merit.
These are called the three factors that, when present through their convergence, enable pure-faithed sons of good family to generate immeasurable merit.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"When three factors come together and manifest before one, they can produce immeasurable merit:
namely, pure faith, the object of giving, and a truly pure field of merit."
Endowed with wisdom and endowed with ethical discipline, Well-subduing the three poisons and practicing the brahmacarya of a śramaṇa—
Such a one is called a truly pure field of merit.
Endowed with wisdom and endowed with pure faith, Holding wealth in accordance with the Dharma in their hands—
By making offerings to the excellent field of merit, one will surely obtain a great fruit.
Amidst the four modes of physical deportment, to be perfectly compliant with the Triple Gem and the Four Noble Truths,
free from all blemish— this is called pure faith.
"Among all forms of giving, the gift of Dharma is supreme;
to expound the True Dharma with a pure mind is what all Buddhas praise.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One:
“Bhikṣus, you should know!
Those who possess wisdom should trade the three kinds of non-durable things for the three durable things.
What are these three?
First, one should trade impermanent wealth for permanent wealth;
second, one should trade the impermanent body for the permanent body;
third, one should trade the impermanent life for the permanent life.
"How should one trade non-durable wealth for durable wealth?

It means that a son or daughter of good family who possesses pure faith, being diligent in accordance with the Dharma, exerts their hands and feet, toils until breaking sweat, and acquires precious wealth; they should use this to provide for themselves, offer it to their parents, and distribute it to their wives, children, slaves, servants, employees, friends, and kinsmen, gathering together day and night to enjoy joy and pleasure."

If one encounters a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa who is endowed with pure ethical discipline (śīla), has perfected the qualities of self-mastery, diligently cultivates the holy life (brahmacarya), has eliminated pride and negligence, is patient and gentle, treads the path of rectitude, has abandoned all wrong paths, and is heading toward the city of Nirvāṇa—one should, with pure faith, joy, and reverence, offer gifts at the appropriate time and in the proper manner. Whether seeking the unsurpassed peace and bliss of Nirvāṇa or hoping for the fruits of happiness among humans or devas in the future, this is called trading non-durable wealth for durable wealth.
"How should one trade this non-firm body for a firm body?

It means that there are sons or daughters of good family who possess pure faith and have accomplished right view; they are able to abstain from taking life, achieving ultimate perfection, being faultless and pure;
they abstain from taking what is not given, achieving ultimate perfection, being faultless and pure."
He is perfectly complete and pure in refraining from sexual misconduct, being entirely free from transgression;
he is perfectly complete and pure in refraining from false speech, being entirely free from transgression;
he is perfectly complete and pure in refraining from drinking intoxicants that lead to heedlessness, being entirely free from transgression.
Such categories as these are called "trading an unstable body for a stable body.
What is meant by "trading an unstable life for a stable life"?
That is to say, the noble disciples within my Dharma understand, as it truly is, that this is the truth of suffering;
they understand, as it truly is, that this is the truth of the origin of suffering;
they understand, as it truly is, that this is the truth of the cessation of suffering.
To understand as it truly is that this is the Noble Truth of the Path leading to the cessation of suffering—
this is called "trading an unstable life for a stable life.
Thus, it is said that those who possess wisdom should trade these three unstable things for the three stable things.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to summarize this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Just as a wise person in the world Exchanges what is base for what is precious, So too is it with one of right view:
They exchange the non-durable for the durable."
Knowing that these riches, body, and life are impure and unstable, one seeks what is pure and stable:
the happiness of this world and worlds beyond.
Wealth in the heavens, the body, and life—these are the pure and firm things of this world;
realizing the eternal bliss of Nirvana is the truly pure and firm Dharma.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that there are three kinds of faculties whose nature is profoundly deep and whose manifestation is profoundly deep; whose nature is difficult to see and whose manifestation is difficult to see."
What are the three?
First, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown";
second, the faculty of "knowing."
Third is the faculty of "knowing all" (*ājñātendriya*).
What is called the faculty of "knowing the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*)?

It refers to the noble disciples within my Dharma who, regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering not yet seen or known, generate a desire to see and know it, exert themselves with diligence, and collect and sustain their minds.

Regarding the Noble Truths of the Origin of Suffering (*duḥkhasamudaya-āryasatya*) that have not yet been seen or known, one generates the desire to see and know them, exerts oneself with diligence, and collects and sustains the mind.

Regarding the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (*duḥkhanirodha-āryasatya*) that has not yet been seen or known, one generates the desire to see and know it, exerts oneself with diligence, and collects and sustains the mind.

Regarding the Noble Truth of the Path leading to the cessation of suffering, which has not yet been seen or known, one generates the desire to see and know it, exerts oneself with diligence, and collects and sustains the mind; this is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñātāvyajñendriya).
"What is called the faculty of knowledge?
It refers to the noble disciples within my Dharma who, in accordance with reality, understand:

'This is the Noble Truth of Suffering; this is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering; this is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering; this is the Noble Truth of the True Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.'"
This is called the faculty of one who knows.
What is called the faculty of one who possesses complete knowledge?

It refers to the noble disciples within my Dharma whose outflows are already exhausted, who have attained true outflowlessness, whose minds are well-liberated and whose wisdom is well-liberated, and who are able to correctly understand:
“Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence.
This is called the faculty of one who possesses complete knowledge.

“Thus, these are the three kinds of faculties, whose nature is profoundly deep and whose manifestation is profoundly deep; whose nature is difficult to see and whose manifestation is difficult to see.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more,
spoke in verse: "Within my True Dharma, the noble disciple who is still in training,
Practicing in accordance with the straight path— This is called the foremost faculty."
Rightly knowing the Noble Truth of suffering, as well as the origin of suffering and the cessation of suffering,
and the path leading to the cessation of suffering— this is called the second faculty.
One should know that the third faculty is the permanent exhaustion of all taints.
Having realized true outflowlessness, with mind and wisdom well-liberated,
he knows: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life is established,
what was to be done has all been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."
"With body and mind ever tranquil, skillfully restraining and guarding the sense faculties,
sustaining this final body, he has subdued the emissaries of Māra.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One these words:
“Bhikṣus, you should know that there are,
in brief, three types of persons whom one should associate with for the sake of spiritual benefit.
What are these three?
First, there is a class of persons who possess inferior morality, inferior concentration, and inferior wisdom;
second, there is a class of persons who possess equal morality, equal concentration, and equal wisdom;
third, there is a class of persons who possess superior morality, superior concentration, and superior wisdom.
"There are certain individuals who possess inferior ethical discipline, inferior concentration, and inferior wisdom; for what purpose or benefit should they be approached?"
Regarding such individuals, one should have no expectations of personal gain, but out of deep compassion alone, urge them toward further progress;
for the sake of this benefit, one should attend upon them.
“Regarding those individuals who have accomplished equal morality, equal concentration, and equal wisdom—for what purpose and benefit should one associate with them?”
That is to say, regarding such a person, one reflects:
"He shall speak of counterfeit precepts to me, and I shall speak of counterfeit precepts to him."
They listen to one another so that their practice may continue and they may accomplish much.
They reflect thus:
"He shall explain to me a similar meditative concentration, and I shall explain a similar meditative concentration to him."
Listening to one another in turn, they enable their practice to continue uninterrupted and accomplish much.
They reflect thus:
"He shall speak of corresponding wisdom for my sake, and I shall speak of corresponding wisdom for his sake."
By listening to one another in turn, they enable [the teachings] to continue and accomplish much that is beneficial.
For the sake of this purpose and benefit, one should draw near.
"What is the purpose and benefit for which one should draw near to those individuals who have achieved superior ethical discipline, superior concentration, and superior wisdom?"
That is to say, regarding such a person (pudgala), one reflects thus:
"Depending upon him, I shall cultivate all the aggregates of ethical discipline (śīlaskandha) that are not yet perfected so that they become perfected;
and if they are already perfected, I shall inwardly collect right mindfulness and maintain them with firm stability."
He reflects thus:
"Depending upon that, regarding all the aggregates of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*) that are not yet perfected, I shall cultivate them until they are perfected;
if they are already perfected, I shall inwardly collect right mindfulness and maintain them with firm stability."
He reflects thus:
"Depending upon that, regarding the aggregate of wisdom, if it is not yet perfected, I shall cultivate it until it is perfected;
if it is already perfected, I shall inwardly collect right mindfulness and maintain it with firm resolve."
"One should associate with such individuals for the sake of this benefit and purpose.
Thus, it is said that there are briefly three kinds of persons whom one should associate with.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"To befriend the inferior is for the sake of compassion; to befriend the equal is for mutual benefit;
to befriend the superior is for one's own virtue, whether for its perfection or its steadfast maintenance.
Befriending those of the lesser vehicle results in inferior virtue; befriending those of the middling vehicle results in middling virtue."
"One should associate with superior persons whose virtue is supreme; therefore, one ought to associate with superior persons.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!
One should dwell upon the body with the contemplation of impurity;
one should dwell upon the breath with mindfulness of breathing;
and one should dwell upon all conditioned phenomena with the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
If one can abide in the contemplation of impurity regarding the body, one shall sever desire for the realm of purity.
If one can abide in mindfulness of breathing regarding the breaths, one will be able to sever the category of obstacles consisting of external discursive thoughts.
If one can maintain the contemplation of impermanence, suffering, and non-self while walking or standing, one will be able to sever craving for existence within all realms of being.
Because craving for existence is severed, one has nothing to grasp at in the world;
because there is no grasping, there is no fear.
Being free from fear, he personally realizes ultimate *nirvāṇa* within himself.
Having realized *nirvāṇa*, he knows for himself:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Contemplate the impurity of the body, Abide in mindfulness of the breath,
And contemplate all conditioned phenomena as impermanent, As well as suffering and non-self."
"Having realized that all conditioned phenomena are empty by nature, one attains the most supreme tranquility;
with craving exhausted and no further grasping, one realizes ultimate Nirvana.
Thus have I heard from the Blessed One these words.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!
The bodies of all sentient beings are constantly pursued and tormented by three types of valiant and fierce enemies.
What are these three?
First, the valiant enemy of old age;
second, the valiant enemy of illness;
third, the valiant enemy of impermanence.
These three kinds of valiant enemies and thieves constantly follow and inflict harm upon the bodies of all sentient beings.
Within the bodies of sentient beings, there are briefly three things:
first, life-span; [the other two being heat and consciousness].
Second is body heat;
third is consciousness.
When these three factors depart from the body, it is called death.
Foul and putrid corpses are cast away among the burial mounds, no longer of any use. Why is this so?
This body is illusory and composed of various dharmas; that which is supreme within it is life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Yet these phenomena arise dependent upon causes and conditions; they are impermanent, lacking strength, devoid of solidity, and powerless, swiftly decaying and perishing.
The thieves of old age, sickness, and death constantly follow them without ceasing, yet foolish worldlings, shrouded by ignorance, cherish and cling to them with insatiable attachment.

My noble disciples, being able to know and see, as it truly is, the many faults and afflictions within this body that is a mere composite of conditions, become deeply weary of and turn away from all internal and external bodies;
because they are deeply weary of and turn away from them, they are able to abandon craving;
because they abandon craving, they attain liberation.
Having attained liberation, he then realized for himself:
"Birth has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence."
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"The bodies of all sentient beings Are pursued and harmed by three enemies:
Namely, old age, sickness, and death, Which never for a moment leave them."
The body is a composite of many dharmas; it is deceptive and lacks any solid reality.
When life-force, warmth, and consciousness are abandoned, it is cast away among the graves.
The ignorant have no knowledge, yet they constantly treasure, cherish, and are addicted to [sensual desires];
the noble ones possess wisdom and insight, and loathe them as one would a pit of excrement.
By cultivating the untainted Noble Path, they sever the causes and conditions of the three thieves.
Realizing the nirvana of permanence and bliss, one is forever liberated from the three thieves.
Those with wisdom in this world should deeply loathe their own bodies, seeking the nirvana of permanence and bliss; they should be diligent and never negligent.
I have heard these words from the Blessed One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!
There are, in brief, three kinds of meritorious deeds that should be cultivated, practiced, and frequently cultivated."
What are the three?
First, the meritorious action of giving; second, the meritorious action of ethical discipline;
[and third, the meritorious action of cultivation].
Third is the cultivation of meritorious deeds through giving (*dāna-puṇya-kriyā-vastu*). What is called the meritorious deed of giving?

It refers to any son or daughter of good family who possesses pure faith and is able to give various kinds of food and drink, delicacies, perfumes, garlands, clothing, vehicles, bedding, halls, rooms, houses, lamps, torches, and all manner of requisites for life; this is called the meritorious deed of giving.
"What is called the meritorious action of ethical discipline?
It refers to a son or daughter of good family who possesses pure faith and is able to abstain from taking life, achieving ultimate perfection, being without transgression, and remaining pure;
and who abstains from taking what is not given, achieving ultimate perfection, being without transgression, and remaining pure."
He is perfectly complete and pure in abstaining from sexual misconduct, being free from transgression;
he is perfectly complete and pure in abstaining from false speech, being free from transgression;
and he is perfectly complete and pure in abstaining from intoxicants that cause heedlessness, being free from transgression.
This is called the meritorious action of ethical discipline.
What is called the meritorious action of cultivation?
It refers to a son or daughter of good family with pure faith who cultivates a mind imbued with loving-kindness, pervading one direction and dwelling therein fully and securely.

In this way, the second, third, and fourth directions, as well as the zenith, nadir, and intermediate quarters—all worlds throughout—were entirely filled and fully established, causing the mind associated with loving-kindness to become vast and immeasurable, free from enmity and harm, pervading all while remaining steadfast.
One cultivates a mind imbued with compassion, pervading one direction, and dwells therein fully and stably.

Likewise, one pervades the second, third, and fourth directions, as well as the zenith, nadir, and all intermediate points; thus, throughout the entire world, one pervades everywhere, dwelling fully and stably, causing this mind imbued with compassion to become vast and immeasurable, free from enmity and free from malice, pervading all while remaining established.
He cultivates a mind imbued with joy, pervading one direction, dwelling therein fully and stably.

Likewise, he dwells pervading the second, third, and fourth directions, as well as above, below, and across the intermediate points; he dwells pervading the entire world, having made this mind imbued with joy vast and immeasurable, free from enmity and free from ill will.
He cultivates a mind imbued with equanimity, pervading one direction, and dwells therein fully and stably.

Likewise, he pervades the second, third, and fourth directions, as well as the zenith, the nadir, and the intermediate points; throughout the entire world, he dwells pervading all, having cultivated a mind imbued with equanimity that is vast, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from malice. He dwells pervading it completely.
This is called the practice of meritorious deeds.
Regarding these three types of meritorious deeds thus described, one should cultivate them, practice them, and cultivate them extensively.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“There are three dharmas that should be cultivated, practiced, and frequently developed;
they can bring about three kinds of happiness, namely: giving, morality, and cultivation.”
By practicing generosity one gains abundant wealth; by practicing ethical discipline one attains long life.
By cultivating loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, one shall be born in the pure heavens.
For those wise people in the world who seek preeminent happiness, [this is the path].
"One should cultivate these three merits; one will certainly attain them, without doubt.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
In this world, there are briefly three kinds of supreme beings.
What are these three?

First, among all designated sentient beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; whether with form or formless; with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—the Buddha is the most supreme. He is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Person, the Trainer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the Bhagavān.
If one gives rise to pure faith toward the Buddha, it is the foremost among all forms of faith.
The karmic fruit induced by such pure faith is the foremost among those of gods and humans.

Second, among all established doctrinal gateways—whether mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned, and so forth—Nirvana is supreme. It is the state where all pride is abandoned, all craving is stilled, the ālayavijñāna is extinguished, all pathways are severed, and there is the extinction of craving and detachment from desire: tranquil Nirvana.
If one gives rise to pure faith toward such a Dharma of nirvāṇa, it is the foremost among all forms of faith.
The karmic fruit induced by such pure faith is the foremost among those of gods and humans.

Third: Among all designated assemblies, groups, circles, and gatherings, the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s noble disciples is the most excellent—namely, the eight types of individuals consisting of those on the four paths and those who have attained the four fruits. Among all sentient beings, they are the true, the sublime, and the foremost.

One should respectfully invite them, pay homage, provide offerings, and praise them with acclaim; being unstinting with one's body or wealth, they are the unsurpassed field of merit for all beings in the world, including gods and humans.
If one gives rise to pure faith within such a noble Sangha of the Aryas, it is the foremost among all forms of faith.
The karmic fruit induced by such pure faith is the foremost among those of gods and humans.
"These are called the three most excellent.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to summarize this meaning, spoke in verse:
"There are three kinds of most excellent: Namely, the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha."
By relying on the arising of pure faith, one is able to see the most supreme Dharma.
Relying on the Buddha, one gives rise to pure faith; knowing him as the Honored One among two-legged beings, who has realized unsurpassed Bodhi and is worthy of offerings by devas and humans alike.
Generating pure faith in the Dharma, one knows it as the most honored among those free from desire;
realizing unsurpassed nirvāṇa, one dwells in constant peace and bliss.
Generating pure faith in the Saṅgha, one knows it as the most honored among all assemblies.
Having realized the unsurpassed field of merit, worthy of offerings by devas and humans alike;
giving to this most excellent and fertile field produces the most excellent merit, bringing about the most excellent peace and happiness: longevity, beauty, strength, and renown.
Making offerings to the Most Supreme Person, practicing the Most Supreme Dharma,
one attains the most supreme peace and happiness, whether among the devas or among humans.
Bestowing gifts upon the Triple Gem, the field of merit, is called the most supreme act of giving.
"Wherever one dwells, there shall always be peace and happiness; later, one shall realize nirvāṇa.
To summarize the preceding sūtra, the uddāna says:
Child, respect, the two trainings, merit, firmness, roots, and pūra.
Impurity and so forth, as well as enemies, meritorious deeds, and the most excellent—
this is what I have heard from the World-Honored One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!..."

There appear in the world three Great Masters who benefit and bring peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, out of compassion for the world’s multitudes of devas and humans, enabling them to attain immeasurable benefit and well-being.
What are these three? "They are:

the appearance in the world of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Perfectly Endowed in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Hero, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the Bhagavat; who, for the sake of all sentient beings, proclaims the True Dharma—excellent in its beginning, middle, and end, skillful in its words and meaning, and which reveals the pure, complete, and stainless holy life."

That is to say: this is the truth of suffering, this is the truth of the origin of suffering, this is the truth of the cessation of suffering, and this is the truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

This is called the first Great Teacher appearing in the world to benefit and bring peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, out of compassion for the world’s multitudes of devas and humans, so that they may attain immeasurable benefit and happiness.

Furthermore, there appear in the world disciples of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha who are beyond training—those who are Arhats, whose taints are exhausted, whose holy life is established, who have accomplished what was to be done, who have laid down the heavy burden, who have attained their own welfare, who have exhausted the fetters of existence, who have correctly practiced the noble teaching of the Tathāgata, who have attained liberation, and who have realized full knowledge. For the sake of all sentient beings, they expound the True Dharma, which is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end; its words and meanings are skillful; it reveals the pure, complete, and stainless holy life, namely: "This is the Truth of Suffering, this is the Truth of the Origin of Suffering, this is the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and this is the Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering."

Thus is described the appearance of the second Great Teacher in the world, who brings benefit and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, out of compassion for the world and its multitudes of gods and humans, so that they may attain immeasurable purpose, profit, peace, and happiness.

Furthermore, there appear in the world disciples of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha who are still in training—those who have fully cultivated the holy life and possess extensive learning, meaning they have correctly heard the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, avadānas, vaipulyas, and adbhutadharmas, and are well-versed in their meanings. For the sake of all sentient beings, they expound the True Dharma, which is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end; its words and meanings are skillful and subtle; it reveals the pure, complete, and stainless holy life, namely: "This is the Truth of Suffering, this is the Truth of the Origin of Suffering, this is the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and this is the Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering."

"This is called the third Great Teacher appearing in the world to benefit and bring peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings; out of compassion for the world and its multitudes of devas and humans, he causes them to attain immeasurable benefit and happiness."

Thus, it is said that there appear in the world three Great Teachers who benefit and bring peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, out of compassion for the world’s multitudes of gods and humans, enabling them to attain immeasurable benefit and well-being.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to summarize this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“There are three kinds of Great Teachers; if they appear in the world, they are able to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to the world of devas and humans.”
The first is the Tathāgata; the second, the disciples beyond training (aśaikṣa);
and the third, the disciples still in training (śaikṣa), who possess pure precepts and great learning.
These three great masters are worthy of offerings by devas, humans, and all others.
Able to proclaim the True Dharma, widely opening the gate of the ambrosia,
causing immeasurable sentient beings to forever exhaust all fetters of existence,
to be liberated from the suffering of birth and death, and to realize the eternal bliss of Nirvana.
Just as a skilled guide can show people the good path,
those who proceed correctly and in accordance with it will attain peace and happiness without doubt.
In this same way, the Three Great Teachers show the Four Truths to sentient beings.
"Practicing without negligence, one will surely transcend the limits of birth and death.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
There are three occasions when the devas assemble, rejoice, deliberate together, and exhort one another to descend to the human world.
What are these three? They are:

"My disciples—whether possessing little wealth or much wealth, few attendants or many attendants, or of noble lineage or humble lineage—have initially conceived pure faith, become weary of and turned their backs on the household life, and joyfully delight in renouncing the world."
At that time, the devas gathered together in great joy and said to one another:

"O celestial seers, you should know that the disciples of the Buddha are now about to engage in battle with the armies of Māra. We ought to lead the hosts of devas down to the human realm to secretly provide assistance and support, increasing their faith and ensuring they encounter no obstacles."
Having spoken these words, they descend to the human realm to perform what is to be done.
This is called the first occasion when the devas assemble in joyful deliberation and, exhorting one another, descend to the human realm.

"Furthermore, my disciples shave off their hair and beards, don the saffron robes, and with right faith, renounce the household life to go forth into homelessness. Together with the bhikṣus, they cultivate harmony and respect, dwelling securely in the observance of the Prātimokṣa vows. Their conduct and deportment are entirely perfect; they perceive great dread even in the slightest fault, and they train themselves in all the precepts that ought to be learned. They achieve purity in the actions of body, speech, and mind, achieve pure livelihood, and achieve pure view."
At that time, the devas gathered in great joy and said to one another:

"O celestial seers, you should know that the disciples of the Buddha are now engaged in battle with the armies of Māra. We ought to lead the hosts of devas down to the human realm to provide secret assistance and augment their power, so that they may triumph over the demonic forces."
Having spoken these words, they descend into the human realm to perform what is to be done.
This is called the second occasion when the devas assemble, rejoice, deliberate in detail, and exhort one another to descend into the human realm.

“Furthermore, my disciples have forever exhausted all taints and realized true taintlessness; their minds are well-liberated and their wisdom is well-liberated. In this very life, they have personally realized higher knowledge and dwell fully established in it, being able to know for themselves:
‘Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence.’”
At that time, the devas gathered in joyful assembly and said to one another:

"O celestial sages, you should know that the disciples of the Buddha have now engaged in battle with the armies of Māra; they have severed the heads of Māra and crushed his hosts. They have declared for themselves:
'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence.'"

"We ought to lead the hosts of devas, carrying exquisite incense and flowers, descend to the human realm to pay homage and make offerings, extol and praise him, and request that he preach the True Dharma, so that we ourselves may be delivered from birth, old age, sickness, and death."
Having spoken these words, they descend to the human world to perform what ought to be done.
This is called the third occasion when the devas assemble, rejoice, deliberate together, and encourage one another to descend to the human world.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

If there are kingdoms, cities, towns, or villages where those with pure faith seek to leave the household life; where those shave their hair and beards and truly go forth; and where, having gone forth, some have exhausted all outflows—then within those kingdoms, cities, and so forth, the great celestial sages and benevolent deities will all descend to diligently protect them, causing them to be abundant and joyful, with wind and rain falling in season and no epidemics.

The sentient beings therein will face one another with hearts of loving-kindness and together cultivate wholesome deeds, attaining long-term peace and security throughout the present and the future, and swiftly realizing the unsurpassed, eternal bliss of Nirvāṇa.”
"This is what is meant by the three times when the devas assemble in joyful consultation, exhorting one another to descend to the human world.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"At the three times, the devas Assemble together in joy."
Having deliberated and encouraged one another, they descended to the human realm.
First, he sought to leave the household life; second, he shaved his beard and hair;
third, his outflows were forever exhausted, as he subdued all the armies of Māra.
Seeing one who has gone forth, capable of bringing all outflows to an eternal end, the various devas all pay respectful homage and offer sustenance, praising him with these words:
"We take refuge in the most excellent person; we take refuge in the supreme being."
I take refuge in the one who subdues the hosts of Māra and has attained great renown;
The various devas, with hearts full of joy, assist him as he practices offerings;
Seeking to shave his hair and beard, he realizes the state of no-birth with the exhaustion of outflows.
Therefore, one should apply oneself with right diligence, fixing the mind and delighting in meditative concentration;
being courageous and free from negligence, one shall subdue all the hosts of Māra.
For those who have gone forth with right faith within the Dharma and Vinaya of the Buddha, [this is the path].
"One is able to be liberated from all outflows, forever reaching the end of all suffering.
Thus have I heard from the World-Honored One:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
Briefly, there are three matters in which the devas surpass humans.
What are these three?
First, longevity;
Second is physical excellence;
third is happiness.
These three matters show that the gods surpass humans by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, beyond all calculation.
Why is this so? "The measure of fifty human years is equivalent to one day and night in the heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*).
Counting such days and nights up to thirty makes one month, and accumulating twelve such months makes one year."
By such years, the lifespan of the gods of the Four Great Kings is five hundred years, which corresponds to nine million years in the human realm.
"In this manner, one hundred years in the human realm constitutes one day and one night for the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three."
In this manner, thirty such days and nights constitute one month, and twelve such months accumulate to form one year.
By such years, the lifespan of the gods in the Heaven of the Thirty-three is one thousand years, which corresponds to thirty-six million years in the human realm.
"Two hundred years of human measure constitute one day and one night in the heavenly realm of the Yāma devas.
Counting thirty such days and nights as one month, and twelve such months as one year."
In such years, two thousand years in the lifespan of the Yāma Heaven correspond to one hundred forty-four million years in the human world.
"Likewise, a period of four hundred years in the human world corresponds to one day and night in the Tuṣita Heaven above."
In this manner, thirty such days and nights constitute one month, and twelve such months accumulate to form one year.
By such years, the lifespan in the Tuṣita Heaven is four thousand [years], which corresponds to five hundred and seventy-six million years in the human realm.
"Thus, eight hundred human years constitute one day and night for the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati).
Counting thirty such days and nights as one month, and twelve such months as one year."

In such years, the lifespan of the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati) is eight thousand [years], which corresponds to twenty-three hundred and forty million years in the human realm.
"In this way, one thousand six hundred human years correspond to one day and one night in the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin)."
In this manner, thirty such days and nights constitute one month, and twelve such months accumulate to form one year.

By such years, the lifespan of the gods of the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*) is sixteen thousand years, which corresponds to nine hundred twenty-one million six hundred thousand years in human reckoning—in this calculation, ten million is termed a *koṭi*.
"Such are the long lifespans of the devas;
such is the physical beauty of the devas; such is the happiness of the devas—none of which can be compared to anything found in the human world.
These three superior qualities of the devas are all impermanent and unstable, unreliable, subject to change and decay, swallowed by the power of death, and bound to death."
When those celestial beings are approaching the end of their lives, other celestial beings come to them and instruct and admonish them, saying:

"O celestial seers, may you all be reborn in a happy realm; having been reborn in a happy realm, may you obtain excellent benefits; and having obtained excellent benefits, may you accomplish what is to be achieved."
In this regard, to what happy destinies do these devas go?
What beneficial gains do they obtain?
What is it that they accomplish?
This means that when those gods have passed away and are reborn among human beings, attaining the human state (*manuṣya-sabhāgatā*), they are said to have "gone to a happy destination.
Having reached the human realm, they attain right faith in the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Buddha; this is called "attaining a wholesome benefit."

When right faith has thus increased and expanded, its roots becoming deep and firm, no śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa in the world, nor any deva, māra, or brahmā, can lawfully lead one to regress; therefore, it is called "accomplishment."

Because of this accomplishment, one performs much within the Buddha-dharma; that is to say, with pure faith, one leaves the household life and receives the precepts, cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā, contemplates the Four Noble Truths, eternally severs all outflows (āsravas), realizes nirvāṇa, and reaches the ultimate end of suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One, summarizing this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“The gods excel in three matters: long life, physical beauty, and bliss.
When compared with those among humans, they are beyond calculation; it is extremely difficult to reach their measure.”
These three supreme things are neither eternal nor permanent;
they are fragile phenomena subject to decay, bound by the power of Death.
When a deva is about to relinquish his life, other devas gather at his side.
Through excellent instruction and admonition, may you give rise to a heart of joy.
O celestial being, may you aspire to be reborn in a happy realm,
to enter the human class, and to be born in a central land with intelligence.
Within the Dharma and Vinaya of the Buddha, having attained right faith, one’s faculties increase and become firm; false teachings cannot turn them aside.
One is able to skillfully abandon unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind.
The faults produced therein can also be skillfully eliminated.
By extensively cultivating the three types of sublime virtuous karma of body, speech, and mind,
and by reflecting correctly according to principle, one causes them to become immeasurable and vast.
One cultivates various meritorious deeds, namely generosity, ethical discipline,
and extensive learning; within the Buddha’s True Dharma, one leaves the household life to cultivate the holy life,
practices the Dharma with right faith, and remains ever patient and gentle.
Some are born among gods or humans, while others realize the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Thus these various celestial beings come to admonish and instruct;
as the heavenly hosts are about to relinquish their lives, they show compassion for them like a mother for her child.
May the various devas always make vows, so that their rebirths in the happy realms may ever increase,
and cause the asuras and their like to retreat and disperse, never to increase again.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle Seven.
